subtopic_detail: Metabolic monitoring schedule after commencing an atypical antipsychotic
stem: A 24-year-old man is reviewed 12 weeks after starting olanzapine 15 mg at night for a first episode of psychosis. His weight has risen from 74 to 82 kg and his waist from 88 to 96 cm.

data_table.Baseline metabolic screen: Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, fasting lipids normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan now?

options.text: Send serum prolactin instead of glucose and lipids in this age group
Defer repeat bloods to 12 months and follow weight and waist meanwhile
Order fasting glucose and lipids now but omit HbA1c as unvalidated
Add a resting electrocardiogram and troponin to 12 week screening
Repeat fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipids now and continue anthropometry

subtopic_detail: Interpreting weight gain and switching agent on olanzapine
stem: A 27-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder has taken olanzapine 20 mg nightly for nine months and is well. Three months of dietitian and gym input have not reduced her weight and she is anxious about gaining more.

data_table.Anthropometry: Weight 71 kg (baseline 62 kg), waist 87 cm (baseline 76 cm), body mass index 26.1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her medication?

options.text: Continue olanzapine and repeat metabolic bloods at the annual review
Cross-titrate olanzapine to aripiprazole and continue lifestyle measures
Add metformin and defer any change of antipsychotic agent
Reduce olanzapine to 10 mg nightly and monitor for relapse
Cross-titrate olanzapine to clozapine for its comparable metabolic burden

subtopic_detail: Hyperprolactinaemia workup on risperidone
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 32-year-old woman on risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months for schizophrenia presents with 6 weeks of non-cyclical breast tenderness, milky bilateral nipple discharge, and secondary amenorrhoea. She has previously had regular cycles and is not sexually active.

She has no headaches, visual changes, weight loss or heat intolerance and is not on other regular medications. Home pregnancy test yesterday was negative. She is symptomatically well from a psychiatric standpoint and has partial insight into her illness.

On examination she is not distressed. Blood pressure is 118/72, pulse 72 regular. Visual fields to confrontation are full. Serum prolactin is 2400 mIU/L (reference <500), TSH 1.8 mIU/L, morning cortisol within normal limits, and beta hCG negative.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea; visual fields full; no goitre or thyromegaly
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2400 mIU/L (<500); TSH 1.8 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); morning cortisol within normal limits; beta hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 4 mg daily for 8 months; no other medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Order an urgent MRI pituitary before any change in psychotropic therapy because of the risk of adenoma
Reduce risperidone to 2 mg daily and repeat prolactin in 6 weeks if symptoms are unchanged with dose reduction
Add cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly while continuing risperidone at the current dose to normalise prolactin
Cross-titrate risperidone to aripiprazole and reassess prolactin and symptoms 6 weeks after the switch is complete
Continue risperidone unchanged and refer to endocrinology for consideration of oestrogen replacement therapy

subtopic_detail: Long-term surveillance schedule for lithium
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 42-year-old woman who is 18 months into lithium prophylaxis for bipolar I disorder. She has been well with no admissions since starting lithium and takes her dose reliably.

Her most recent trough lithium level (12 hours post dose) is 0.7 mmol/L, taken 6 months ago. She has no polyuria, polydipsia, tremor, ataxia, or heat intolerance. She takes no other regular medications, is not planning pregnancy, and drinks 1.5 litres of fluid daily.

On assessment blood pressure is 122/76, pulse 74 regular. Weight is stable at 68 kg. She asks how often she now needs bloods and what tests should be done.

data_table.Most recent bloods (6 months ago): Lithium 0.7 mmol/L (0.6-0.8 target); eGFR 92 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH 2.1 mIU/L; corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg nocte; no other regular medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term monitoring plan?

options.text: Trough lithium level yearly with renal function only when clinical concern arises about toxicity or dehydration
Trough lithium level every 3 to 6 months and eGFR, TSH and corrected calcium every 6 to 12 months
Trough lithium level every 3 months plus quarterly parathyroid hormone in place of corrected calcium
Trough lithium level every 6 weeks and 24 hour urinary volume routinely to screen for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Trough lithium and full blood count every 3 months in place of thyroid function surveillance whilst on therapy

subtopic_detail: Interpreting lithium level in the context of new medication
stem: A 58-year-old man on lithium 1000 mg nightly for 15 years has three days of unsteady gait, coarse tremor and slurred speech. Perindopril was started two weeks ago. He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea but has drunk less during a hot spell.

data_table.Neurology: Oriented to person only, coarse resting tremor, gait ataxia, horizontal nystagmus
data_table.Bloods: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (0.6-0.8), creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 82), eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73m2, sodium 141 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, give intravenous fluids and repeat the level in 6 hours
Give repeated activated charcoal four hourly and withhold both drugs
Withhold both drugs, give intravenous fluids and arrange urgent haemodialysis
Give sodium polystyrene sulfonate with a forced alkaline diuresis
Continue lithium at 500 mg nightly and repeat the level in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Contraception planning for a woman of childbearing potential on valproate
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 22-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been well for 2 years on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily. She has never been pregnant, is in a new relationship, and uses condoms inconsistently. She hopes to have children in the next 5 years but not immediately.

Her weight is 62 kg. Blood pressure is 118/74, pulse 72 regular. She has no history of migraine, VTE, hypertension, or smoking. Liver enzymes, full blood count and beta hCG are within normal limits today. She does not wish to change her mood stabiliser as she has previously failed lithium and lamotrigine trials.

data_table.Investigations: LFTs, FBC within normal limits; beta hCG negative
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 2 years
data_table.History: No smoking, no migraine, no VTE, no hypertension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to comply with the Australian valproate pregnancy prevention program?

options.text: Switch valproate to carbamazepine 400 mg daily as a safer mood stabiliser option during her fertile years
Continue valproate and advise continued condom use with review of contraception if she becomes sexually active
Continue valproate and start high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily as sufficient risk mitigation without changing contraception
Provide written information about teratogenicity and arrange a highly effective contraception method before continuing valproate
Stop valproate abruptly and start lithium 500 mg nocte pending contraception planning at the next visit

subtopic_detail: Mood stabiliser choice in first trimester bipolar
stem:
You are the perinatal psychiatry registrar. A 29-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is 7 weeks pregnant. She has been well on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 3 years after two severe manic episodes.

The pregnancy was unplanned. Her last episode was 3 years ago and required admission and a period of involuntary treatment. She has previously trialled lithium with acceptable tolerance but was switched to valproate for superior symptom control. She has taken folic acid 500 micrograms daily only since finding out she was pregnant last week.

On assessment she is euthymic with intact insight. Blood pressure is 116/72, pulse 74 regular. Booking bloods including TFTs, FBC, LFTs, and renal function are within normal limits. Beta hCG confirms viable intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound today.

data_table.Investigations: TFTs, FBC, LFTs, renal function within normal limits; viable intrauterine pregnancy at 7 weeks on ultrasound
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily; folic acid 500 micrograms daily (started last week)
data_table.Psychiatric history: Two prior severe manic admissions; well for 3 years on valproate; previous lithium trial tolerated but less effective

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her medication regimen?

options.text: Stop valproate abruptly and commence olanzapine 10 mg nocte as sole prophylaxis for the remainder of pregnancy
Continue valproate at the current dose because organogenesis is already underway and switching risks relapse
Cross-titrate valproate to carbamazepine at an equivalent mood stabilising dose to maintain relapse prevention
Cross-titrate valproate to lithium with weekly levels and increase folic acid to 5 mg daily during the switch
Stop valproate and rely on structured psychological therapy alone for mood stabilisation across the pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
stem: A 24-year-old man is brought in 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of his father's amitriptyline. He had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the ambulance which self-terminated.

data_table.Examination: GCS 11, dilated pupils, dry warm skin
data_table.ECG: QRS 138 ms, dominant R wave in aVR

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe for QRS narrowing over four hours
Intravenous flumazenil 200 micrograms to reverse the reduced conscious level
Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis after the seizure
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 minutes for the wide complex tachycardia
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeated until QRS narrows

subtopic_detail: Varenicline black box warning for a patient with depression history
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 46-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has done so for 25 years. His most recent quit attempt using nicotine patches alone lasted 3 weeks 2 years ago.

He has a history of a single moderate depressive episode 5 years ago that resolved with 12 months of sertraline, ceased 3 years ago; he is currently euthymic with no suicidal ideation and works full time as an electrician. He has no history of seizures, eating disorder, or alcohol use disorder. He has stable angina on aspirin and atorvastatin.

On assessment he is calm and future-focussed. Blood pressure is 132/82, pulse 78 regular. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. He asks what the most effective medication for quitting would be.

data_table.Psychiatric history: Single moderate depressive episode 5 years ago; euthymic 3 years; no suicidal ideation
data_table.Medical history: Stable angina; no seizures; no eating disorder; no alcohol use disorder
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily; atorvastatin 40 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus lozenge as required) with behavioural support
Varenicline titrated over the first week to 1 mg twice daily with behavioural support and standard neuropsychiatric monitoring
Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to twice daily with behavioural support and quit date at week 2
Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg with behavioural support and a set quit date at 2 weeks
Nicotine vaping product prescription with 6 monthly review and no other pharmacotherapy at this stage

subtopic_detail: Bupropion contraindication
stem:
You are the GP registrar. A 34-year-old woman wants to stop smoking after 15 years of a 20 cigarette a day habit. She has previously used nicotine gum without success.

Her medical history includes anorexia nervosa in her early twenties requiring inpatient treatment, currently in stable recovery, and one witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure last year attributed to sleep deprivation and heavy alcohol use during a stressful period at work. She has since abstained from alcohol and takes no regular medications.

On assessment she is well. Blood pressure is 122/78, pulse 70 regular. BMI 20.1. She is not pregnant and uses a copper IUD. She has read online about bupropion and asks whether it would suit her.

data_table.History: Anorexia nervosa in stable recovery; one unprovoked-appearing seizure last year in context of alcohol and sleep deprivation; alcohol abstinent 12 months
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrating to 150 mg twice daily with behavioural support
Nortriptyline 25 mg nocte titrated to 75 mg with behavioural support and a set quit date at week 2
Nicotine patch 21 mg daily alone as monotherapy without a fast-acting nicotine product added on
Varenicline titrated over the first week to 1 mg twice daily with behavioural support and quit date at day 8
Behavioural counselling alone without any pharmacotherapy for a further 12 weeks before reconsidering options

subtopic_detail: Prescribing authority and driving in adult ADHD
stem:
You are the GP registrar in NSW. A 28-year-old software engineer has been diagnosed with ADHD by a psychiatrist after a formal assessment. Recommendation letter recommends a trial of lisdexamfetamine.

He drives daily to work over the Sydney Harbour Bridge and works from a home office 3 days a week. He has no history of substance use disorder, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, glaucoma, or psychosis. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week.

On assessment he is calm and focused. Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular. ECG at the psychiatrist's assessment showed sinus rhythm with a QTc of 400 ms and no structural abnormality on echocardiogram. He asks whether you as his GP can prescribe the stimulant and whether he needs to notify Roads and Maritime Services.

data_table.Cardiac: ECG sinus rhythm; QTc 400 ms; echocardiogram no structural abnormality
data_table.History: No substance use disorder; no cardiovascular disease; no psychosis; no glaucoma
data_table.Occupation: Software engineer; drives daily; works from home 3 days per week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach with respect to prescribing and driving?

options.text: Notify Roads and Maritime Services of the ADHD diagnosis directly under mandatory notification requirements
Write a private prescription for lisdexamfetamine without any regulatory notification given the psychiatrist has assessed him
Refer him back to the psychiatrist for all ongoing prescribing because GPs are not permitted to prescribe stimulants in NSW
Advise him he must surrender his driver licence for 12 months from the date of starting stimulant medication
Apply to NSW Health for a Schedule 8 stimulant authority as the primary prescriber before writing any stimulant script

subtopic_detail: Second-line stimulant choice in comorbid substance use
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic. A 34-year-old man with confirmed adult ADHD presents for pharmacotherapy planning. He has never trialled medication.

He has a 6 year history of methamphetamine use disorder in sustained remission for 18 months, engaged with a drug and alcohol counsellor, and has been out of correctional supervision for 2 years. He works as a self-employed carpenter and drives his own ute daily to job sites. He has no psychosis, cardiovascular disease, or hypertension.

On assessment he is calm with intact insight. Blood pressure is 126/78, pulse 72 regular. ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms. Urine drug screen today is negative. He is worried about relapse and asks what medication would be safest for him.

data_table.History: Methamphetamine use disorder in sustained remission 18 months; engaged with counsellor
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative today
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Immediate-release dexamfetamine tablets titrated to therapeutic dose with weekly dispense supervision
Bupropion sustained release 150 mg daily titrated to 300 mg daily as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD
Atomoxetine titrated over 2 weeks to a maintenance dose of 80 mg daily with 4 to 6 weekly review of efficacy and BP
Lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily titrated up as a long-acting stimulant with prodrug formulation reducing misuse risk
Modafinil 200 mg daily with slow uptitration to 400 mg daily as a wakefulness-promoting agent for ADHD symptoms

subtopic_detail: Discriminating brief psychotic disorder from schizophreniform and schizophrenia
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 26-year-old woman is brought in by her partner. She has had 3 weeks of fixed persecutory beliefs that her neighbours are broadcasting her thoughts, disorganised speech, and 2 witnessed episodes of speaking to voices only she can hear.

She has no previous psychiatric history. There was no clear trigger and no bereavement or trauma. She uses no illicit substances (urine drug screen negative) and has not started any new medications. She has been sleeping only 3 to 4 hours a night for the past fortnight.

On examination she is guarded and preoccupied but oriented. Blood pressure is 118/76, pulse 82 regular. Physical examination and routine bloods including TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC, and CT brain are unremarkable. Her mood is not persistently elevated or depressed and there is no history of prior manic episodes.

data_table.Mental state: Guarded and preoccupied; oriented; persecutory delusions of thought broadcasting; auditory hallucinations; disorganised speech; no persistent mood disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; TSH, calcium, LFTs, FBC within normal limits; CT brain normal
data_table.Medications: Nil

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis at this presentation?

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder as psychosis has been present for less than one month total duration
Schizophreniform disorder as the presentation is typical of an early primary psychotic illness in this age group
Schizophrenia because thought broadcasting and persistent auditory hallucinations are pathognomonic first rank features
Delusional disorder because the persecutory belief is non bizarre and there are no other prominent symptoms
Schizoaffective disorder given the co-occurrence of sleep disturbance and prominent psychotic features

subtopic_detail: Recognising delusional disorder
stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought by her daughter because for 15 months she has been convinced that her husband is having an affair with the neighbour. She has hired a private investigator and repeatedly examines his phone. She works part time, cooks and sees friends as usual.

data_table.Mental state: Cooperative and euthymic; single fixed belief; no hallucinations, disorganised speech or negative symptoms; no alcohol use
data_table.Investigations: MoCA 28/30; thyroid function, calcium and B12 normal; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features
Late onset schizophrenia given the persistence of a fixed belief
Delusional disorder, jealous type, outside any mood or psychotic illness
Alcohol-induced psychotic disorder presenting as morbid jealousy
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with fixed beliefs about her spouse

subtopic_detail: Synthetic cannabinoid intoxication vs primary psychosis
stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 19-year-old university student is brought in by ambulance after collapsing at a music festival. His friend reports he smoked what he called "K2" from a vape 90 minutes before symptoms started.

He has no known psychiatric history. On arrival he is agitated, sweating profusely, and describes visual distortions and paranoid ideation. He has no headache, focal neurology, chest pain, or dysuria. He last ate 4 hours ago and drank 3 beers earlier.

On assessment: pulse 138 regular, blood pressure 168/104, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1. He is agitated but redirectable. Pupils 6 mm equal and reactive. There is a fine tremor and diaphoresis. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with normal intervals. Urine drug screen (immunoassay) is negative for cannabinoids, amphetamines, cocaine and opioids. Creatine kinase is 2400 U/L, sodium 140, potassium 4.0.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 regular, BP 168/104, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.1
data_table.Examination: Agitated but redirectable; pupils 6 mm reactive; fine tremor; diaphoresis; no focal neurology
data_table.Mental state: Visual distortions, paranoid ideation, agitation
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen (immunoassay) negative for cannabinoids, amphetamines, cocaine, opioids; CK 2400 U/L; sodium 140; potassium 4.0

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonist intoxication with sympathomimetic and agitation features
Serotonin syndrome triggered by an undisclosed ingestion of an MDMA-containing tablet at the festival
First episode schizophrenia presenting with a substance triggered acute psychotic episode at a festival
Anticholinergic toxidrome from a novel psychoactive substance sold as a cannabinoid at the festival stall
Acute alcohol withdrawal in a young man now presenting 6 hours after his last drink at the festival

subtopic_detail: Rapid tranquillisation of an acutely disturbed adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a metropolitan ED. A 32-year-old man with a known diagnosis of schizophrenia is brought in by police after threatening his neighbour with a knife. He is now in a seclusion room and is verbally hostile, pacing, and threatening to punch staff.

He is not on any regular antipsychotic (defaulted 6 months ago) and denies substance use today. Attempts at verbal de-escalation over the past 20 minutes have not settled him. He refuses oral medication.

He weighs approximately 80 kg. There is no known cardiac history, no recent head injury, and no known allergies. Blood pressure taken through the seclusion window is 138/86, pulse 118 regular, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 98% room air. Bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L. He has not been assessed for QTc as an ECG has not been feasible.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, pulse 118 regular, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Behaviour: Verbally hostile, pacing, threatening staff; declines oral medication; verbal de-escalation failed after 20 minutes
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L; ECG not feasible

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological approach?

options.text: Intramuscular lorazepam 4 mg as sole first-line therapy for acute behavioural disturbance in this patient
Intramuscular midazolam 10 mg immediately followed by intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg from a separate syringe
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg as a single loading dose without ECG availability given the acuity of the situation
Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg/kg as a rapid dissociative sedative given the failure of verbal de-escalation
Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with a minimum 1 hour interval before considering a repeat dose

subtopic_detail: DBT skill selection for acute distress
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 27-year-old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder attends her scheduled DBT session in acute distress after an argument with her partner.

She describes an urge to cut her forearm which she rates 9/10, tearfulness, and an impulse to "do something to feel real". She denies suicidal ideation or a plan. She is not currently intoxicated, has no acute medical concerns, and has attended 4 months of the DBT program.

On assessment she is tearful but engageable and cooperative with the session. She has completed the mindfulness module and is currently working through distress tolerance. She asks which skill she should use right now to get through the next hour without self-harming.

data_table.Presentation: Acute distress after interpersonal conflict; urge to self-harm 9/10; denies suicidal ideation
data_table.Treatment: 4 months into DBT; completed mindfulness module; currently in distress tolerance module

lead_in: Which DBT skill is most appropriate for her to use in the next hour?

options.text: DEAR MAN interpersonal effectiveness skill to negotiate a resolution with her partner about the argument now
TIPP skills (temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation) to rapidly reduce arousal
Radical acceptance to acknowledge the reality of the conflict as the primary short-term response now
Check the facts from the emotion regulation module to appraise the argument objectively before acting
Wise mind observation from the core mindfulness module as the primary intervention to prevent the self-harm

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy limits in BPD per NHMRC
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar. A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is currently on quetiapine 300 mg nocte, sertraline 100 mg daily, and lorazepam 1 mg PRN twice weekly, all started over the last 12 months by different clinicians during acute crises. She has never had a manic episode or a primary psychotic disorder.

She has gained 8 kg over 6 months and reports daytime sedation. She has not engaged with structured psychological therapy and asks whether she really needs so many medications. There is no current suicidal ideation, no episode of self-harm in the last 6 weeks, and no comorbid substance use disorder.

On assessment she is euthymic. Blood pressure is 128/78, pulse 72 regular. Fasting glucose is 5.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.7%, LDL 3.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L. She is otherwise well.

data_table.Fasting bloods: Glucose 5.6 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.7%; LDL 3.4 mmol/L; triglycerides 1.6 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Quetiapine 300 mg nocte; sertraline 100 mg daily; lorazepam 1 mg PRN twice weekly
data_table.Psychiatric history: BPD; no manic or primary psychotic episodes; no substance use disorder; no recent self-harm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her pharmacological management?

options.text: Continue current medications unchanged given clinical stability and reassess in 12 months for streamlining
Increase quetiapine to 600 mg nocte to address the affective instability more effectively while she waits for therapy
Structured deprescribing plan targeting all three agents while enrolling her in a formal psychological therapy program
Substitute lamotrigine for quetiapine because mood stabilisers have proven efficacy for BPD emotional dysregulation
Convert PRN lorazepam to scheduled diazepam 5 mg twice daily to reduce impulsive PRN use and taper later

subtopic_detail: Clozapine myocarditis surveillance in the first month
stem: A 31-year-old man is three weeks into clozapine titration for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, on 200 mg nightly. Over three days he has been increasingly fatigued with low grade fever and mild ankle swelling. He denies chest pain.

data_table.Investigations: Troponin 82 ng/L (<14), C reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), ECG sinus tachycardia with lateral ST depression
data_table.Baseline: Troponin, C reactive protein and echocardiogram normal before clozapine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine and refer urgently to cardiology for echocardiography
Continue clozapine and repeat troponin and C reactive protein in 48 hours
Halve clozapine to 100 mg nightly and add oral prednisolone
Continue clozapine and start ivabradine for the tachycardia
Add amoxicillin with clavulanic acid and continue clozapine

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing akathisia from anxiety in first-episode psychosis
stem: A 22-year-old man started risperidone 2 mg nocte ten days ago for a first psychotic episode, and his positive symptoms are settling. For three days he has had an inner restlessness and cannot sit still. He says he feels physically compelled to move rather than driven by any belief.

data_table.Examination: Shifts weight from foot to foot standing, taps his feet seated, no tremor and no rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add propranolol 20 mg twice daily and reduce risperidone to 1 mg nocte
Increase risperidone to 3 mg nocte to control the psychomotor agitation
Add benzatropine 2 mg orally twice daily as first line for the movements
Commence diazepam 5 mg twice daily as the primary anxiolytic treatment
Cross-titrate risperidone to haloperidol to settle the restlessness

subtopic_detail: Medical admission thresholds in anorexia nervosa
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 17-year-old woman brought in by her mother after her general practitioner faxed a referral requesting admission for restrictive eating over 8 months. She has been drinking water only for the past two days before a school swimming carnival.

She is alert, tearful and denies feeling unwell. She has no chest pain and no syncope. She takes no regular medications and has never purged.

Weight 41.2 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 15.1). Pulse 38 regular supine, blood pressure 96/58 supine falling to 78/48 on standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius. Peripheral capillary refill 3 seconds and fingers dusky. Venous blood gas: pH 7.42, potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), glucose 3.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 regular, BP 96/58 supine to 78/48 standing, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate disposition?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient dietitian and community eating disorder team follow up within 48 hours
Commence oral high energy supplements in ED and reassess for admission after 24 hours of ambulatory monitoring
Refer directly to a specialist eating disorders inpatient unit and delay any refeeding until formal admission
Arrange short stay ED observation for four hours of fluid resuscitation then discharge if vitals normalise
Admit to a general paediatric or adolescent ward for medical stabilisation with cardiac monitoring and cautious refeeding

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome prevention
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 19-year-old man with a 10 month history of severe restriction. He is currently 44 kg (BMI 14.9) and has been eating around 400 kcal/day for the past three weeks.

He is haemodynamically stable now with pulse 52, blood pressure 104/68 supine to 96/62 standing, temperature 35.9 degrees Celsius. He has no diarrhoea and no recent vomiting.

Admission bloods: sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium 2.30 mmol/L, glucose 3.9 mmol/L, urea 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, LFTs mildly deranged with ALT 88 U/L. ECG shows sinus bradycardia with QTc 440 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52, BP 104/68 supine to 96/62 standing, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 35.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 138 mmol/L; potassium 3.6 mmol/L; phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 3.9 mmol/L; ALT 88 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial refeeding plan?

options.text: Commence 20 kcal/kg/day divided across three meals with prophylactic oral thiamine and daily electrolyte monitoring
Start at 5 kcal/kg/day of continuous nasogastric feed with weekly bloods for the first fortnight of admission
Commence 50 kcal/kg/day oral diet from day one with twice weekly electrolytes and no supplements
Delay all feeding for 48 hours to correct electrolytes to mid-normal range before offering any calories
Start intravenous 10% dextrose infusion at 100 mL/hour as the sole energy source for the first 72 hours

subtopic_detail: EPDS thresholds and next step in perinatal screening
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 32-year-old woman at her 6 week postnatal check. Her first baby is feeding well and gaining weight. She reports she has been tearful, waking with anxiety before the baby wakes, and losing interest in things she previously enjoyed.

She has no personal history of mental illness. She has good partner support and does not use alcohol or other substances.

The practice nurse has completed an EPDS today: total score 14 with item 10 (self-harm) scored 0. Her previous EPDS at 28 weeks antenatal was 6. There is no evidence of psychotic symptoms, mania, or plans to harm herself or the baby. She is willing to accept help and asks what happens next.

data_table.Screening: EPDS 14/30 today, item 10 score 0; antenatal EPDS at 28 weeks 6/30
data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful; no psychotic features; no thoughts of harm to self or baby

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that a score of 14 is a normal postnatal adjustment reaction and repeat the EPDS in three months
Repeat the EPDS in two weeks before making any diagnostic decision, given that a single score is unreliable
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily today as first line for postnatal depression before considering therapy
Refer to a mother and baby unit for admission because the EPDS score exceeds the community management cut off
Undertake a structured diagnostic assessment and offer psychological therapy with review in one to two weeks

subtopic_detail: SSRI choice in breastfeeding for moderate postnatal depression
stem:
You are the community perinatal psychiatry registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman 9 weeks postnatally. She has moderate depression with early morning waking, anhedonia and pervasive guilt over the past 5 weeks. Two sessions of CBT with the perinatal service have not yet produced improvement.

She is exclusively breastfeeding her healthy term infant who is thriving. She has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder, no psychotic symptoms, and no active thoughts of self-harm.

She took sertraline 50 mg daily during a previous non-perinatal depressive episode 4 years ago with good response and tolerability. She has no other medical conditions and takes no regular medications. She is worried about drug transfer into breast milk and wants to continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Examination: Depressed mood; no psychotic features; no thoughts of self-harm or infant harm
data_table.Prior response: Sertraline 50 mg daily 4 years ago with good response and no adverse effects
data_table.Breastfeeding: Exclusive breastfeeding; infant thriving on growth chart

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological choice now?

options.text: Commence agomelatine 25 mg orally at night titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
Commence citalopram 20 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
Commence venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily titrating as tolerated with continued breastfeeding and infant observation

subtopic_detail: Postpartum psychosis emergency management
stem:
You are the ED registrar called by the community midwife about a 30-year-old primiparous woman 12 days postpartum. Over the past 48 hours she has slept 2 hours per night, is speaking rapidly about her baby being sent by God to save the family, and has been overheard saying the baby has divine protection and does not need feeding.

Her partner reports she has been holding the baby at the second story window because angels will catch him if he falls. She has a family history of bipolar I disorder in her mother.

She has no fever and no localising infective signs. Bloods including full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is negative. She refuses admission and says she must remain at home to protect her baby from the doctors.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Mental state: Elevated mood, pressured speech, grandiose religious delusions, poor insight; infant safety concerns
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC, TFTs within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Contact child protection to remove the infant and discharge the mother with community mental health follow up
Commence olanzapine 5 mg orally daily at home with community follow up in 24 hours by the perinatal team
Refer for urgent outpatient psychiatry appointment within 72 hours and arrange for the partner to supervise
Admit informally to the postnatal ward for observation with midwifery review only and no psychiatric input overnight
Arrange same day involuntary admission under the NSW Mental Health Act to a mother and baby unit or acute psychiatry bed

subtopic_detail: Consent and indication for ECT in severe depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on a NSW acute inpatient unit reviewing a 62-year-old woman with severe melancholic depression. Over the past 3 weeks she has stopped eating and drinking, has lost 5 kg, and expresses a persistent belief that her internal organs have rotted away.

She has failed adequate trials of two SSRIs and one SNRI over the past 8 months. She is dehydrated and requires IV fluids. Her renal function is preserved and her ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 430 ms.

She accepts admission voluntarily but says she does not want any tablets or any procedures because they will not work. Her son has enduring guardianship for medical decisions. The treating consultant is proposing bilateral ECT under general anaesthesia and asks you to organise consent for the first treatment tomorrow.

data_table.Mental state: Severe melancholic depression; nihilistic delusion of rotted organs; refusing oral intake
data_table.Prior trials: Sertraline 200 mg 8 weeks, escitalopram 20 mg 10 weeks, venlafaxine 225 mg 12 weeks all inadequate
data_table.Investigations: Renal function preserved; ECG sinus rhythm QTc 430 ms; dehydration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate consent pathway to enable ECT tomorrow?

options.text: Proceed under the son's enduring guardianship consent as she has effectively delegated medical decisions to him
Obtain her signed consent tomorrow before the procedure as her refusal today is likely to change overnight
Rely on the doctrine of necessity given the medical risk of continued refusal of oral intake
Apply to the Mental Health Review Tribunal for an ECT authorisation given she lacks capacity to consent
Defer ECT and continue an eighth week of antidepressant trial while monitoring hydration in hospital

subtopic_detail: Cognitive side effects and electrode placement
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 74-year-old man three days after his fourth session of bilateral ECT for severe psychotic depression. He is responding well with resolution of nihilistic delusions and improved oral intake.

However he is markedly confused during the day, cannot recall visiting relatives from yesterday morning, and has become disoriented walking back from the bathroom. Baseline cognition was intact with an MoCA of 27 before commencing ECT.

He has no fever, no focal neurology, and no new medications. His electrolytes, glucose, and inflammatory markers are within normal limits. Non contrast CT brain is unchanged from admission. His consultant asks how to modify the ECT plan to preserve response while reducing his cognitive burden.

data_table.Neurology: Confused, poor short term memory recall, no focal signs
data_table.Cognition: MoCA 27 at baseline; not repeated during acute confusion
data_table.Investigations: Electrolytes, glucose, inflammatory markers within normal limits; CT brain unchanged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate modification to his ECT plan?

options.text: Switch to right unilateral ultra-brief pulse ECT and continue the treatment course
Continue bilateral ECT at current dose and add donepezil 5 mg orally daily to counter cognitive symptoms
Stop ECT permanently and switch to a trial of ketamine infusion given the cognitive concern
Reduce ECT frequency to weekly at the current bilateral placement and dose per session
Increase the anaesthetic propofol dose to induce a longer post-ictal recovery and reduce recall of confusion

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 34-year-old man brought in by ambulance with agitation, sweating and shivering. He is on sertraline 200 mg daily for depression and was started on tramadol 3 days ago after a workplace back injury.

His partner says he took an extra tramadol tablet at 4pm today and became agitated over the next 3 hours. There has been no recent illicit drug use and urine screen is pending.

On examination he is anxious with pressured movements. Pulse 128 regular, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Pupils are 6 mm and reactive. There is spontaneous inducible clonus in both ankles worse on the right, hyperreflexia at knees and ankles, and diaphoretic warm skin. Muscle tone is increased but does not have lead-pipe rigidity. Creatine kinase is 220 U/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 158/98, RR 24, SpO2 98%, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Bilateral inducible ankle clonus (right greater than left); hyperreflexia at knees and ankles; increased tone without lead-pipe rigidity; pupils 6 mm reactive
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 220 U/L (30-200); urine drug screen pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management alongside supportive care?

options.text: Continue current medications, give paracetamol for temperature and observe over the next 12 hours
Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add IV dantrolene
Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add oral bromocriptine
Cease serotonergic agents, give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and add oral cyproheptadine
Cease serotonergic agents, give IV haloperidol for agitation and observe temperature response

subtopic_detail: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome recognition
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to see a 42-year-old man on the psychiatric ward. He was admitted 8 days ago with a first episode of psychosis and started on haloperidol 5 mg twice daily titrated up to 10 mg twice daily 4 days ago.

Over the past 24 hours he has become mute and immobile. Nursing report he was well overnight but reduced oral intake this morning. He is not currently on any other regular medications and has never used antidepressants.

On examination he is diaphoretic. Pulse 118 regular, BP 168/104 fluctuating to 128/78 within minutes, RR 20, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius. He has generalised lead-pipe rigidity through all limbs, cogwheeling at the wrists, and hyporeflexia. Pupils are 4 mm equal and reactive. Bloods: creatine kinase 6800 U/L (30-200), white cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, urea 9.1 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 168/104 fluctuating to 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 98%, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Mute, diaphoretic; generalised lead-pipe rigidity; cogwheeling; hyporeflexia; pupils 4 mm reactive
data_table.Bloods: Creatine kinase 6800 U/L (30-200); WCC 14.2 x10^9/L; urea 9.1 mmol/L; creatinine 108 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue haloperidol at current dose, add procyclidine for extrapyramidal symptoms and give oral paracetamol
Cease haloperidol, transfer to a monitored bed for IV fluids and cooling, and commence bromocriptine
Cease haloperidol, give IV lorazepam for suspected catatonia, and repeat CK in 12 hours before further action
Cease haloperidol, commence cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, and observe on the psychiatric ward
Continue haloperidol, commence IV dantrolene as monotherapy and manage on the psychiatric ward overnight

subtopic_detail: CIWA-Ar symptom triggered diazepam regimen
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 52-year-old man who normally drinks a bottle of vodka per day. His last drink was 16 hours ago. He is admitted for elective inguinal hernia repair scheduled in 3 days and is on the ward for preoperative alcohol withdrawal management.

He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens in previous withdrawals. He has no chronic liver disease, no cognitive impairment and takes no regular medications.

On examination he is tremulous with mild sweating. Pulse 96 regular, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius. He is oriented, without hallucinations. His CIWA-Ar score is 12 on admission. Bloods including electrolytes, magnesium and glucose are within normal limits, and he has already received parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 148/92, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tremulous, mild sweating, oriented, no hallucinations
data_table.Assessment: CIWA-Ar 12; no prior seizures or delirium tremens; parenteral thiamine 300 mg IV already given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate benzodiazepine regimen now?

options.text: Lorazepam 2 mg orally every 6 hours regularly with no CIWA-Ar guided as-needed doses
Diazepam 10 mg orally four times daily for 3 days then 5 mg four times daily for 3 days
Diazepam 20 mg orally every 2 hours as needed while CIWA-Ar stays at 10 or above
Chlordiazepoxide 25 mg orally every 8 hours for 5 days without any symptom triggered doses
Withhold benzodiazepines until CIWA-Ar reaches 20 then diazepam 10 mg every 4 hours as needed

subtopic_detail: Thiamine and Wernicke prevention in dependent drinking
stem:
You are the ED registrar assessing a 48-year-old woman brought in confused after being found in the street. Her partner reports she drinks around 750 mL of spirits daily and eats poorly. Her last drink was 8 hours ago.

She is alert but disoriented to place and time. She has a wide-based gait and nystagmus on lateral gaze bilaterally. She is not febrile and has no focal weakness.

Pulse 108 regular, BP 152/94, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Bloods: sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.4 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), glucose 4.8 mmol/L. Non contrast CT brain shows no acute pathology and blood alcohol is 0.12%.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 152/94, RR 18, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurology: Disoriented to place and time; wide-based gait; bilateral lateral gaze nystagmus; no focal weakness
data_table.Bloods: Sodium 137 mmol/L; potassium 3.4 mmol/L; magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); glucose 4.8 mmol/L; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of her thiamine and glucose needs?

options.text: Give IV thiamine 100 mg once daily for 5 days without magnesium replacement and delay any glucose until day 2
Give oral thiamine 100 mg three times daily and IV 5% dextrose 1 L over 4 hours to correct suspected hypoglycaemia
Give IV thiamine 500 mg three times daily for 2-3 days, replace magnesium, and give IV dextrose only after the first thiamine dose
Withhold thiamine until blood test confirms low thiamine levels and manage confusion with diazepam alone
Give IM thiamine 100 mg once daily and multivitamin tablet daily and defer magnesium correction to the ward

subtopic_detail: Buprenorphine-naloxone induction and precipitated withdrawal
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman who has been using illicit oxycodone up to 200 mg per day for 8 months. She is motivated to commence opioid agonist therapy and prefers buprenorphine-naloxone.

Her last oxycodone use was 8 hours ago. She has not previously been on OST. She has no chronic pain condition and no other regular medications. She has no known QT prolongation and hepatitis serology is negative.

On examination she is anxious with mild sweating and yawning. Pulse 92, BP 128/78, pupils 5 mm and reactive. Objective Opioid Withdrawal Scale (OOWS) score is 4 (mild). She asks how quickly you can start buprenorphine-naloxone today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/78, RR 16, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Anxious; mild sweating and yawning; pupils 5 mm reactive; OOWS 4
data_table.History: Illicit oxycodone up to 200 mg/day for 8 months; last dose 8 hours ago; no prior OST

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait until objective withdrawal is at least moderate then give buprenorphine-naloxone 4/1 mg sublingually and titrate
Give buprenorphine-naloxone 4/1 mg sublingually now and titrate up to 12/3 mg over 4 hours
Give methadone 40 mg orally now instead as it does not require prior withdrawal to induct safely
Give oral naltrexone 50 mg today and arrange buprenorphine induction after 7 days of abstinence
Give sublingual buprenorphine mono product 8 mg now and add naloxone tomorrow to reduce diversion

subtopic_detail: Take away doses on methadone maintenance in NSW
stem:
You are the GP registrar in a NSW clinic accredited for OST prescribing. A 39-year-old man has been on methadone 80 mg daily for opioid use disorder for 7 months. He attends the pharmacy daily for supervised dosing.

He has been abstinent from illicit opioids and stimulants on random urine drug screens for the past 4 months. He is employed as a plumber, engaged with his GP, and takes no other medications. He has no history of overdose since starting methadone.

He requests two take-away doses per week to make working on outer suburb jobs easier. He has not previously had take-aways. He has a locked medicine box at home and lives alone.

data_table.History: Methadone 80 mg daily for 7 months; 4 months of clean UDS; employed; no overdoses; lives alone with lockable storage
data_table.Assessment: Stable, engaged, no diversion concerns; requesting 2 take-away doses/week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in managing his take-away request?

options.text: Grant four take-away doses per week immediately as he clearly meets the primary NSW stability criteria
Grant two take-away doses per week with documented risk assessment, secure storage plan and structured review
Refuse take-away doses because NSW policy prohibits take-aways in the first 12 months of maintenance treatment
Convert him to buprenorphine-naloxone this week as it allows unsupervised dosing without formal take-away approvals
Refer to a specialist addiction physician for a subcutaneous depot buprenorphine trial to eliminate his daily pharmacy attendance

subtopic_detail: OCD pharmacotherapy first line and dose
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with obsessive compulsive symptoms for 3 years. She spends about 4 hours per day on contamination checking and hand washing, which now interferes with her Masters coursework.

She has trialled 12 sessions of exposure and response prevention (ERP) with a psychologist over the past 4 months with only partial improvement. She has no bipolar history, no psychotic symptoms, and no active suicidal thoughts.

She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no other medical conditions, does not smoke, drinks alcohol only socially, and takes no regular medications. She is not currently sexually active but has been prescribed the combined oral contraceptive pill for cycle regulation. She is asking about adding a medication to her ERP.

data_table.History: Contamination and washing OCD for 3 years, 4 hours/day rituals; ERP 12 sessions partial response
data_table.Mental state: No bipolar, no psychosis, no active suicidal ideation
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill; no antidepressant history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Fluvoxamine 100 mg orally daily, titrated toward 200-300 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
Sertraline 50 mg orally daily, titrated toward 150-200 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
Clomipramine 25 mg orally at night, titrated toward 150-250 mg/day over 6-8 weeks
Diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily short term while continuing ERP
Risperidone 1 mg orally at night added to ongoing ERP as first line augmentation

subtopic_detail: Panic disorder first line SSRI selection and dose ramp
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 33-year-old man with recurrent panic attacks over the past 4 months. He has had 3-4 attacks per week with palpitations, chest tightness and a sense of impending doom, plus persistent anticipatory anxiety about further attacks. He has stopped taking public transport.

He has had a normal ECG, TFTs and urine drug screen. He does not use caffeine excessively and drinks alcohol only socially. He is not on any regular medications.

He has agreed to a course of CBT with a psychologist and is asking about medication. He is worried that antidepressants might make his panic worse initially. He has no personal or family history of bipolar disorder and no active suicidal ideation.

data_table.History: Panic attacks 3-4/week for 4 months; agoraphobic avoidance of public transport
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal; TFTs normal; urine drug screen negative
data_table.Mental state: No bipolar features; no active suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial SSRI regimen?

options.text: Alprazolam 0.5 mg orally three times daily as monotherapy with review in 4 weeks
Sertraline 100 mg orally daily from day one to reach target dose quickly and review at 2 weeks
Sertraline 25 mg orally daily for 1 week then increase to 50 mg daily with review at 2 weeks
Propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily as monotherapy for autonomic symptoms with review in 4 weeks
Mirtazapine 30 mg orally at night as first line pharmacotherapy with review in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Adult autism spectrum diagnosis in women
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 28-year-old woman who suspects she is on the autism spectrum. She has always found social situations exhausting, rehearses conversations before work meetings, and copies expressions from colleagues. She struggles with unexpected changes to her routine and has strong food texture preferences.

She completed a Bachelor of Design and works as a graphic designer. She has been treated for anxiety and depression with sertraline and CBT over 6 years with only partial response. Her older brother has an established autism spectrum disorder diagnosis from childhood.

She scores 34 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-50). Standard developmental screens as a child were reportedly unremarkable and she was described as a quiet, well behaved child. She is asking about the next step in her diagnostic assessment.

data_table.History: Social masking, routine dependence, sensory sensitivities; anxiety and depression only partial response to sertraline and CBT
data_table.Screening: AQ-50 score 34 (cut off 32); AQ-50 subthreshold in childhood
data_table.Family history: Brother with autism spectrum disorder diagnosed in childhood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure her that her successful career and normal childhood screens exclude autism and continue current mental health treatment
Refer for a specialist multidisciplinary autism assessment using ADOS-2 and ADI-R with a developmental history informant
Commence methylphenidate for suspected undiagnosed ADHD as it commonly presents this way in adult women
Diagnose autism spectrum disorder in the room today based on the AQ-50 score above cut off and issue a formal report
Switch her sertraline to venlafaxine given anxiety and depression are the primary problem and defer any autism assessment

subtopic_detail: Conduct disorder versus oppositional defiant disorder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community mental health team seeing a 13-year-old boy brought by his mother because of behavioural problems that have escalated over the past 18 months. He has been suspended from school twice this term.

Behaviours over the past year include starting fights that resulted in another student needing sutures, using a knife to threaten a peer during an argument, setting a fire in the bike shed, and staying out overnight three times without contact. Two nights ago the local police returned him after finding him breaking into a shed.

His mother describes him as argumentative and refusing chores since age 7, but says the more serious behaviours started about 18 months ago. He has no diagnosed intellectual disability, no epilepsy, and no substance use disclosed. He shows little remorse for the injuries he has caused.

data_table.History: Fighting causing injury, knife threat, fire setting, staying out overnight, breaking and entering over 18 months
data_table.Longstanding: Argumentative and refusing chores since age 7
data_table.Mental state: Little remorse; no substance use disclosed; no intellectual disability; no epilepsy

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Oppositional defiant disorder with intermittent explosive features
Disruptive mood dysregulation disorder with behavioural escalation
Conduct disorder, adolescent-onset with limited prosocial emotions
Antisocial personality disorder with early adolescent onset
Substance-induced disruptive behaviour disorder with cannabis use

subtopic_detail: First episode psychosis EPPIC pathway referral
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing an 18-year-old man brought by his father. Over the past 6 weeks he has withdrawn from friends, stopped attending university lectures, and has become preoccupied with the belief that a particular lecturer is monitoring his thoughts via the campus WiFi.

He describes hearing the lecturer's voice commenting on him at least once a day. He is not agitated and has no plans to harm the lecturer or himself. He has no personal or family history of bipolar or schizophrenia. He does not use cannabis or methamphetamine and urine drug screen is negative.

He is well groomed, calm and cooperative. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination and routine bloods including TFTs, electrolytes and B12 are within normal limits. Non contrast CT brain is unremarkable. He has agreed to review and to accept treatment.

data_table.History: 6 weeks of social withdrawal, delusion of thought monitoring via WiFi, auditory hallucinations of running commentary; no substance use
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; FBC, UEC, TFTs, B12 within normal limits; CT brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that transient psychotic experiences are common in adolescence and review
Commence olanzapine 10 mg orally at night in general practice and review at four weeks
Arrange a routine outpatient adult mental health team appointment in eight to twelve weeks
Refer to a youth focused early psychosis service (headspace Early Psychosis or equivalent) for assessment
Arrange involuntary admission under the NSW Mental Health Act 2007 for containment and treatment

subtopic_detail: Social and emotional wellbeing framework in Aboriginal mental health
stem:
You are the GP registrar in a regional NSW clinic seeing a 46-year-old Aboriginal man for a routine health check. He mentions he has been feeling flat since his uncle died three months ago on Country. He struggles with sleep and has lost interest in football, which he used to coach.

He does not describe hopelessness, has no thoughts of self-harm, and drinks alcohol occasionally. He has stable employment and lives with his wife and children. He has not previously accessed mental health care and expresses concern that psychiatric labels might affect his contact with his community.

He would like some help but is unsure what would be appropriate. He asks whether he needs medication and whether he has to see a psychologist in the city. His K10 score today is 21 (moderate distress) and he has no active psychotic symptoms.

data_table.History: Grief over uncle's death 3 months ago; low mood, sleep disturbance, loss of interest in football
data_table.Assessment: K10 score 21 (moderate distress); no psychosis; no self-harm; hesitant about mainstream psychiatric care

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.text: Refer to an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Service or social and emotional wellbeing worker
Commence sertraline 50 mg orally daily today given his K10 of 21 indicates moderate distress
Reassure him that grief is normal, no intervention is needed and review him again in six months
Refer to metropolitan psychiatry services for formal DSM diagnostic assessment before any support
Arrange voluntary admission to the acute psychiatric unit for containment given his bereavement

subtopic_detail: SSRI failure in generalised anxiety disorder augmentation choice
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic reviewing a 42-year-old woman with generalised anxiety disorder for 3 years. She has had adequate trials of escitalopram 20 mg daily for 12 weeks and then sertraline 200 mg daily for 12 weeks with only a 20% reduction in her GAD-7 score.

She has also completed a 16 session CBT program with a psychologist during the sertraline trial. She has ongoing pervasive worry, muscle tension and initial insomnia. She works as a solicitor and drives to work daily. She has no history of substance use disorder and no bipolar features.

She has never had a benzodiazepine. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 445 ms. Renal and hepatic function are within normal limits. She takes no other regular medications and does not smoke. She is asking about the next step in medication.

data_table.History: GAD 3 years; failed escitalopram 20 mg 12 weeks; failed sertraline 200 mg 12 weeks; 16-session CBT during sertraline trial
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 445 ms; renal and hepatic function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Add quetiapine 25 mg orally at night, titrated to 150-300 mg/day as SSRI augmentation
Add diazepam 5 mg orally three times daily long term as SSRI augmentation for residual anxiety
Add pregabalin 75 mg orally twice daily, titrated to 300-600 mg/day divided doses as SSRI augmentation
Switch to venlafaxine XR 75 mg orally daily, titrated toward 150-225 mg/day over 4-6 weeks
Add propranolol 40 mg orally three times daily as SSRI augmentation for somatic anxiety symptoms

subtopic_detail: Erythrocytosis detected on routine monitoring during masculinising hormone therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner providing shared care for a 27-year-old trans man who has been receiving intramuscular testosterone undecanoate 1000 mg every 12 weeks for 14 months. He feels well, works night shifts as a baker, and has no chest pain, breathlessness or visual symptoms.

He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has done so since he was 18. He takes no other regular medicines and drinks alcohol rarely. His last injection was six weeks ago and he attends today for his routine monitoring bloods, which you review with him in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haematocrit 0.57 (0.40-0.54), haemoglobin 188 g/L (130-175), ferritin within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, total testosterone 17 nmol/L (8-27)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of these results?

options.text: Continue the current dose and interval, and repeat the full blood count in 12 months
Cease testosterone permanently and refer him back to the gender service for further review
Reduce the testosterone dose, offer smoking cessation support, and repeat in three months
Commence low dose aspirin and continue testosterone at the current dose and interval
Refer him for venesection today and continue testosterone at the current dose and interval

subtopic_detail: Choosing an oestrogen formulation when vascular risk factors are present
stem:
A 32-year-old trans woman attends your general practice asking to move her hormone therapy into supervised care. For the past seven months she has been taking oestrogen tablets bought through an overseas website, without any monitoring.

She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. She has had migraine with visual aura roughly monthly since her twenties, and her mother had a pulmonary embolism at 52. Her body mass index is 31 kg/m2. She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism. She wants to continue feminising therapy and asks what you would put her on.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, fasting lipids within normal limits, oestradiol 210 pmol/L, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: Which regimen would you first recommend?

options.text: Transdermal oestradiol patch 50 micrograms per 24 hours, with dose review in three months
Oral ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms daily, with a dose review in three months
Oral conjugated equine oestrogens 1.25 mg daily, with dose review in three months
Intramuscular oestradiol valerate 20 mg once every two weeks, with dose review in three months
Withhold all oestrogen until she stops smoking, with readiness review in three months

subtopic_detail: New vaginal bleeding after established amenorrhoea on testosterone
stem:
A 34-year-old trans man comes to your clinic because he has been getting light bleeding on and off for six weeks, which he describes as spotting that stains his underwear. He has been on testosterone gel for three years and had no bleeding at all for the 30 months before this.

He has never had a cervical screening test and finds pelvic examination intolerable. He has not had chest or genital surgery and takes no other medicines. He has no pelvic pain, and his last testosterone level and haematocrit were within the expected range.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, no palpable mass, external examination declined
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-175), total testosterone 19 nmol/L (8-27), urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the testosterone dose and review the bleeding pattern again in three months
Prescribe a course of norethisterone and review the bleeding pattern again in three months
Reassure him this is an expected effect of testosterone and review again in three months
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and offer a self collected cervical screening test now
Refer him for endometrial ablation and review the bleeding pattern again in three months

subtopic_detail: Antiandrogen adverse effects during feminising therapy
stem:
A 28-year-old trans woman has been on oestradiol valerate 6 mg daily and cyproterone acetate 100 mg daily for 10 months, prescribed before she moved interstate and never reviewed since.

Over the past three months she has felt flat and persistently tired, and she has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples when she showers. She has no headaches and no change in her vision. She is not taking an antipsychotic or any other regular medicine. She is pleased with her physical changes and does not want feminising therapy interrupted.

data_table.Examination: Visual fields full to confrontation, fundoscopy normal, bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, no breast mass
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1450 mIU/L (less than 600), alanine aminotransferase 74 U/L (less than 35), oestradiol 380 pmol/L, total testosterone less than 0.5 nmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue the current regimen unchanged and repeat the prolactin level in six months
Cease cyproterone, start spironolactone 100 mg daily, and repeat levels in eight weeks
Start cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly and continue the current antiandrogen dose
Cease oestradiol, continue cyproterone, and repeat the prolactin level in eight weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before making any change to therapy

subtopic_detail: Pregnancy prevention while established on masculinising hormone therapy
stem:
A 22-year-old trans man attends for a sexual health check. He has been on testosterone for 10 months and has had no periods for the last seven of those.

He has a new male partner and they have been having condomless vaginal sex for about two months. He has a uterus and ovaries and has had no surgery. He tells you he assumed that being on testosterone meant he could not get pregnant. He does not want to be pregnant now or in the next few years, but is unsure about the longer term.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, abdominal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Urine beta human chorionic gonadotropin negative, sexually transmitted infection screen pending, haemoglobin and haematocrit within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend for pregnancy prevention?

options.text: Advise that no contraception is required while amenorrhoea continues on testosterone
Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel
Advise fertility awareness based methods with condoms while he remains amenorrhoeic
Increase the testosterone dose to maintain amenorrhoea and supply condoms alone
Offer a levonorgestrel intrauterine device now and continue his current testosterone

subtopic_detail: Sequencing gender assessment alongside a first episode of psychosis
stem:
You are the registrar on an early psychosis team reviewing a 19-year-old trans woman admitted three weeks ago with a four month history of persecutory beliefs about her neighbours and auditory hallucinations. She is responding to risperidone and her beliefs are no longer held with conviction.

She has been living as a woman since she was 16 and asks daily about starting hormone therapy. Her mother's collateral history describes her consistently identifying as female since the age of 12, with no change during this episode. The psychotic content has never involved her gender or her body. The team is divided about what to do with her request.

data_table.Examination: Calm and cooperative, no formal thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance in the past week, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Medications: Risperidone 2 mg orally at night
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, urine drug screen negative on admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue antipsychotic treatment and refer concurrently to the gender service for assessment
Defer gender service referral until she has been free of psychotic symptoms for two years
Refer to the gender service and withhold antipsychotic treatment until assessment is complete
Interpret her stated gender identity as part of the delusional system and treat accordingly
Commence feminising hormone therapy today and review the psychotic symptoms in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Medical instability thresholds in a gender diverse young person with restrictive eating
stem:
A 17-year-old non binary young person, who uses they and them pronouns, is brought to your clinic by a parent after losing 12 kg over five months. They have been eating one small meal a day and running before school.

They tell you that the eating changes began as a way to stop their periods and to flatten their chest, and that the weight loss has done both. They are on a waiting list for a gender service and are not on any hormone therapy. They deny wanting to harm themselves. They feel cold constantly and fainted once last week while getting out of bed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 41 beats per minute, blood pressure 86/54 mmHg lying with a fall of 22 mmHg systolic on standing, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 35.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 15.1 kg/m2, cool peripheries, dry skin, no oedema, alert and oriented
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), phosphate 0.75 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), magnesium within normal limits, electrocardiogram sinus bradycardia with corrected QT interval 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to a community eating disorder service for outpatient family based treatment this week
Refer to the gender service for prioritised assessment before starting eating disorder treatment
Arrange admission to hospital today for supervised refeeding and continuous cardiac monitoring
Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg at night and arrange outpatient dietitian review within the week
Arrange twice weekly general practice weight and vital sign checks with supervised family meals

subtopic_detail: Raised potassium in a person taking spironolactone as an antiandrogen
stem:
A 36-year-old trans woman attends for routine review. She has taken oestradiol valerate 6 mg daily and spironolactone 200 mg daily for 14 months and is happy with her progress.

Six weeks ago another doctor at the practice started her on perindopril for hypertension. She feels well, with no palpitations, weakness or muscle cramps. She takes no over the counter medicines and uses no salt substitutes. You review the monitoring bloods taken yesterday before she leaves.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 5.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 94 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate 68 mL/min/1.73m2, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal T wave morphology

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue both medicines at current doses and repeat the potassium level in three months
Cease the oestradiol, continue spironolactone at the current dose, and repeat in one week
Refer her to the emergency department today for insulin dextrose and cardiac monitoring
Cease spironolactone permanently and offer her no alternative antiandrogen agent from now on
Withhold spironolactone, review the perindopril, and repeat the potassium in one week

subtopic_detail: Legal authorisation for stage two hormone treatment when parents disagree
stem:
You are the registrar at a multidisciplinary gender service reviewing a 16-year-old trans boy who has been on puberty suppression for 18 months. The service has diagnosed gender dysphoria and the team, including the treating psychiatrist and paediatric endocrinologist, has assessed him as competent to consent to testosterone.

He lives with his mother, who supports the treatment and has signed the consent form. His father, who shares parental responsibility under a parenting order, has written to the service stating that he does not accept the diagnosis and opposes any hormone treatment. The young person is clear and consistent about wanting to proceed, and the clinic appointment today is to plan next steps.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage suppressed, height and weight tracking along the 50th centile, mood euthymic, no self-harm
data_table.Investigations: Bone age consistent with chronological age, bone mineral density within expected range, liver function and lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before testosterone can be commenced?

options.text: Proceed on his own consent, since the treating team has assessed him as competent to decide
Apply to the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia for authorisation of the treatment
Proceed with the consenting parent's authority, documenting the other parent's objection in full
Refer the disagreement to the hospital clinical ethics committee for a binding determination
Defer all hormone treatment until he turns eighteen and can give consent as an adult

subtopic_detail: Perceptual experiences of a deceased relative during bereavement in a resettled family
stem:
A 58-year-old Hazara woman is referred to you by her general practitioner with a note asking you to start an antipsychotic. She was resettled in Australia 14 months ago and her husband died of cancer four months ago.

Through an accredited interpreter she tells you that most nights she sees her husband sitting at the end of the bed and hears him speaking to her, usually telling her to look after the grandchildren. She finds these visits comforting and says several women in her community have described the same thing after a death. She sleeps about five hours, has lost 2 kg, and still cooks, prays and minds her grandchildren daily. She knows her husband has died and does not believe anyone is watching or following her.

data_table.Examination: Alert, tearful when speaking of her husband, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no responding to unseen stimuli during interview
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits, no cognitive concerns on collateral history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night and review the perceptual experiences in four weeks
Arrange urgent psychiatric admission for assessment of a suspected first episode of psychosis
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for a depressive episode and review her symptoms in four weeks
Provide bereavement support with an accredited interpreter and review her again in two weeks
Arrange computed tomography of the brain and formal cognitive testing before any management

subtopic_detail: Low mood and fatigue at the post-arrival health assessment of a newly arrived refugee
stem:
A 31-year-old woman from Myanmar attends your general practice five months after arriving on a humanitarian visa. Through an accredited interpreter she describes four months of tiredness, poor concentration, low mood and, in her words, thinking too much at night.

She spent six years in a camp in Thailand before resettlement. She denies suicidal thoughts and is caring for her two children, though she says everything takes more effort than it used to. Her Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score is 14. The post-arrival screening bloods requested at her first visit are back today.
