data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, conjunctival pallor, no goitre, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 71 fL (80-100), ferritin 5 micrograms/L (30-300), vitamin D 29 nmol/L (more than 50), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, eosinophil count within normal limits, hepatitis B and strongyloides serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and arrange psychological review for her in six weeks
Commence iron replacement, investigate the cause, and reassess her mood in six weeks
Refer her to the state torture and trauma service and review her mood in six weeks
Commence mirtazapine 15 mg at night for sleep and appetite and review her in six weeks
Repeat the questionnaire in six weeks and take no further action at this consultation

subtopic_detail: Episodic unresponsiveness in a survivor of torture already treated for trauma symptoms
stem:
A 44-year-old Tamil man has been attending your clinic for two years with nightmares, hypervigilance and avoidance following detention and repeated beatings in his country of origin, which included blows to the head with a rifle butt. He takes sertraline 100 mg daily and has completed trauma-focused therapy with an interpreter.

His wife reports that twice in the past month he has stopped responding mid conversation, stiffened, and had jerking of both arms for about a minute. Afterwards he was confused for twenty minutes and on one occasion he had bitten the side of his tongue. He has no memory of either episode. He has been getting daily headaches and losing his thread in conversation.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, cranial nerves intact, no focal limb weakness, gait normal, healed scar over the left parietal scalp
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, glucose and electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose and re-refer him for trauma-focused therapy with an interpreter
Attribute the episodes to dissociation and refer for grounding focused therapy with an interpreter
Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night for the symptoms and review him in four weeks
Reassure him that memory difficulty is expected and repeat a symptom checklist in three months
Refer for neurological assessment with brain imaging and an electroencephalogram this week

subtopic_detail: Adding pharmacotherapy after an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy
stem:
A 38-year-old man who arrived from Iraq six years ago has been treated at your service for post-traumatic stress disorder. He has completed 14 sessions of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy delivered with the same accredited interpreter throughout.

His avoidance has improved and he has returned to part time work. He still wakes most nights after nightmares, sleeps about four hours, and is easily startled. His Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist score has fallen from 55 to 44 over four months and has been unchanged for the last six weeks. He is not drinking alcohol, has stable housing and permanent residency, and takes no regular medicines.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, no psychomotor slowing, no suicidal ideation elicited
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence diazepam 5 mg at night for sleep and review his symptoms in four weeks
Commence quetiapine 25 mg at night for sleep and review his symptoms in four weeks
Commence sertraline 50 mg each morning and continue the psychological work in parallel
Commence prazosin 1 mg at night for nightmares and review his symptoms in four weeks
Repeat an identical course of the same psychological therapy and review his symptoms in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Involuntary detention decision for an asylum seeker presenting with self harm
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a New South Wales hospital. A 27-year-old man who arrived by boat and is living in the community on a bridging visa is brought in by a friend at 9 pm after cutting his left forearm with a razor blade.

Through a telephone interpreter he says he has kept a box of his housemate's medication for weeks and intends to take it all tonight, and that nothing will change while his protection claim is unresolved. He is not intoxicated, has no psychotic symptoms, and is oriented and coherent. He says he wants to leave now and is standing by the door with his jacket on. His friend says he has not eaten for two days.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Three superficial forearm lacerations with haemostasis achieved, tearful, guarded, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas, electrolytes, paracetamol level and ethanol level within normal limits or not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Complete a mental health certificate under the Act and arrange transfer to a declared facility
Discharge him with a written safety plan and a community mental health appointment in three days
Ask security to hold him while you seek advice from the immigration department about his visa
Defer the decision until an on-site interpreter in his language can attend early tomorrow morning
Contact the police to take him into custody under the Act as he refuses to remain

subtopic_detail: Structuring the consultation when a parent answers for an adolescent from a resettled family
stem:
A 14-year-old girl is brought to your general practice by her father because she has not attended school for six weeks. Her family arrived from Syria two years ago and she completed a year of intensive English before entering mainstream classes.

Her father answers every question you ask her, tells you she is simply lazy, and declines an interpreter for himself, saying his English is adequate. He reports that she complains of stomach aches and headaches on school mornings. When you ask her directly how she has been, she looks at her father and says nothing. Her physical examination is normal and she has grown along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, abdomen soft and non-tender, no organomegaly, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, coeliac serology and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this consultation?

options.text: Commence sertraline 25 mg daily for presumed anxiety and review her in four weeks
Refer her to the school counsellor and review the attendance pattern again in four weeks
Agree a graded return to school plan with her father and review the attendance in four weeks
Interview her alone for part of the consultation and offer her father an interpreter
Refer her to paediatrics for investigation of the headaches and abdominal pain in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Interpreter selection when the allocated interpreter is known within the patient's community
stem:
A 29-year-old Rohingya woman attends a refugee health clinic for her first mental health appointment. The nurse who booked the appointment recorded that she wanted to talk about what happened to her in the camp.

The accredited interpreter who arrives is a man from the same small community who greets her by her family name and mentions knowing her uncle. She lowers her gaze, answers in single words, and says everything is fine. Earlier, in the waiting room, she had told the nurse through a phone interpreter that she had not been sleeping and had been having bad memories. Her brother is waiting outside and has offered to help if needed.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, guarded, reduced eye contact, no psychomotor agitation
data_table.Investigations: Post-arrival screening bloods within normal limits, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue with the booked interpreter and revisit the sensitive history at a later appointment
Change to a female accredited interpreter by telephone today and continue the assessment
Ask her adult brother in the waiting room to interpret for the remainder of the consultation
Proceed in English without an interpreter, using short sentences and written information sheets
Reschedule her to a clinic in three months when a local female interpreter becomes available

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a non-trough lithium level during fasting and concurrent anti-inflammatory use
stem: A 34-year-old man stable on lithium for three years has fasted between dawn and sunset for ten days and moved his dose to 4.30 am, working outdoors through a heatwave. He started ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily five days ago.

data_table.Examination: Nausea, coarse tremor and unsteadiness for two days; dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 1.3 mmol/L at 9.30 am (12 hour trough range 0.6-0.8), sodium 147 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 116 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management today?

options.text: Continue the dose, as the sample was not a trough level
Halve the dose, continue ibuprofen and repeat in two weeks
Refer for urgent haemodialysis given the level and renal function
Switch to sodium valproate today and review within two weeks
Withhold lithium, cease ibuprofen, rehydrate and repeat a trough tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Concurrent diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in an adult with autism
stem:
A 24-year-old woman was diagnosed with autism last year after presenting with exhaustion following social contact. She now describes lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, losing essential items and leaving tasks unfinished, which her primary school reports and her mother both confirm.

These difficulties affect her university course and her casual job equally. A clinician she saw previously told her that attention problems are simply part of autism and cannot be diagnosed separately. She is not depressed, sleeps well, and takes no medicines.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, mental state examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Explain that attention symptoms within autism cannot be separately diagnosed or treated
Repeat the autism assessment to check whether the original diagnosis was correct
Arrange an assessment for a co-occurring attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review her concentration in six weeks
Refer for cognitive testing to see whether an intellectual disability explains this

subtopic_detail: Starting dose of an antidepressant for anxiety in an autistic adult
stem:
A 29-year-old autistic man has generalised anxiety that has persisted despite 12 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for autistic adults. He worries most days about work and travel, sleeps poorly and has stopped catching trains.

He lives independently and works as a data analyst. At 22 he was prescribed fluoxetine 20 mg daily and stopped it after five days because he felt wound up and could not keep still, which resolved within two days of stopping. He drinks no alcohol and takes no other medicines. He would like to try medication again alongside continuing therapy.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows anxious mood, no psychomotor agitation, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits, electrocardiogram within normal limits

lead_in: Which prescribing plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Sertraline 25 mg daily, increasing slowly after four weeks if it is tolerated
Sertraline 50 mg daily, increasing to 100 mg after two weeks if it is tolerated
Diazepam 5 mg as required for anxiety, with review of his response after four weeks
Risperidone 0.5 mg at night, increasing to 1 mg after two weeks if it is tolerated
Propranolol 10 mg three times daily, with review of his response after four weeks

subtopic_detail: Restlessness emerging after an antidepressant dose increase in an autistic adult
stem:
A 31-year-old autistic woman was started on sertraline 50 mg daily twelve days ago for a moderate depressive episode. Three days ago a colleague increased the dose to 100 mg because her partner reported that she had become more agitated.

She now paces the house from morning until night, has slept four hours in three days, and repeatedly stands up and sits down during your consultation. She describes a feeling in her legs that only walking relieves, and says it is nothing like her usual hand movements, which she has done since childhood and finds calming. Her partner says the pacing started two days after the first prescription and has worsened since the increase. She has no thoughts of self-harm and her mood is unchanged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal tone, reflexes normal and symmetrical, no clonus, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and creatine kinase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 150 mg daily and review her symptoms again in one week
Add diazepam 5 mg twice daily and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily for now
Add quetiapine 25 mg at night for sleep and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily
Reduce the sertraline dose immediately and review her in person within 48 hours
Add propranolol 10 mg three times daily and continue the sertraline at 100 mg daily

subtopic_detail: New physical symptoms in an autistic adult already labelled as anxious
stem:
A 27-year-old autistic man attends with four months of abdominal pain and 6 kg of unintentional weight loss. Two clinicians have told him the pain is anxiety and advised breathing exercises.

He finds it hard to localise the pain and describes it as a feeling that something is wrong low down in his belly. He has been opening his bowels four to six times a day, sometimes waking him at night, which is a change from his lifelong routine of once each morning. He has no history of an eating disorder and his appetite is unchanged. His mother says he stopped going to his weekly board game group two months ago because of the pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19.4 kg/m2, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, no mass, no perianal abnormality seen
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-300), C-reactive protein 34 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 32 g/L (35-50), coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him to a psychologist for anxiety focused therapy and review in eight weeks
Commence sertraline 25 mg daily for anxiety and review his symptoms in four weeks
Refer him urgently for specialist assessment and endoscopic investigation of the bowel
Commence oral iron and repeat the full blood count in eight weeks without investigation
Explain that the symptoms reflect differences in bodily perception and review in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Functional decline after a role change in an autistic adult on a stable antidepressant
stem:
A 34-year-old autistic woman has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for two years for a depressive episode, with full remission until three months ago. Four months ago she was promoted from a solo laboratory role into a client facing position in an open plan office.

She now sleeps twelve hours on weekends, has stopped cooking and has let her driving lapse because it takes too much effort. At work she has started making errors. On a two week holiday last month she felt like herself again within four days and resumed cooking. She still enjoys her home routines and her weight is stable. She has no suicidal thoughts and denies guilt or worthlessness.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows reactive mood, normal speech rate, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase the sertraline dose to 150 mg daily and review her mood again in four weeks
Arrange workplace adjustments with a graded reduction in demands and review in four weeks
Add quetiapine 25 mg at night and review her mood and function in four weeks
Refer her for a repeat diagnostic assessment and review her mood and function in four weeks
Commence lithium augmentation at 500 mg at night and review her mood again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Gender assessment request from an autistic adult declined by the referral service
stem:
A 26-year-old autistic person who uses they and them pronouns is referred back to you by a gender service, which has written that assessment should wait until the autism is better understood.

They have identified as non binary consistently since the age of 16, have used their current name for four years, and describe persistent distress about their chest and voice. They live independently, manage their own finances and work full time in logistics. They understand the effects of hormone therapy, its reversible and irreversible components, and its effect on fertility, and they can explain these back to you accurately. They have no psychotic symptoms and no current depressive episode.

data_table.Examination: Vital signs within normal limits, mental state examination shows congruent affect and no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, lipids and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Defer the gender assessment until a further autism specific assessment has been completed
Explain that gender affirming hormone therapy is not offered to autistic people
Refer them for social skills training before revisiting the request for gender assessment
Arrange a capacity assessment by an independent psychiatrist before taking any further steps
Proceed with gender assessment, adjusting the communication format and appointment length

subtopic_detail: Attention symptoms first appearing in middle adult life
stem:
A 41-year-old accountant asks to be referred for assessment after scoring highly on an online attention questionnaire. For three years he has been forgetful, easily distracted, irritable with his children and unable to finish reports, and he has twice fallen asleep at his desk in the afternoon.

He brought his school reports, which describe him as attentive and consistently near the top of his class, and his mother recalls no difficulties. His wife says he snores loudly and that she has watched him stop breathing several times a night. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and his body mass index is 34 kg/m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Neck circumference 44 cm, oropharynx crowded, no goitre, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function, iron studies and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a formal sleep study before proceeding with any attention deficit assessment
Refer him to a psychiatrist for adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder assessment
Commence a trial of lisdexamfetamine 30 mg each morning and review in four weeks
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily for a presumed depressive episode and review shortly
Reassure him that attention symptoms at this age are age related and review annually

subtopic_detail: Self-injurious behaviour after a change of accommodation in a minimally speaking autistic adult
stem:
You are asked to review a 23-year-old autistic man who moved into a new supported accommodation house five weeks ago. Over the past three weeks he has been striking the side of his head with his palm, leaving bruising.

He communicates with single words and a picture based system. Staff record that the striking happens almost entirely between four and six in the afternoon in the shared lounge, when the television is on and the staff shift changes. His previous house had a quiet room and a visual timetable on the wall, and neither is in place at the new house. A dental review and a physical examination last week were unremarkable. The house manager has asked you to prescribe something to be given when he becomes distressed.

data_table.Examination: Bruising over the left temporal scalp, no laceration, ears and oropharynx normal, abdomen soft, gait normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function, thyroid function and urine microscopy within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg at night and review the behaviour in four weeks
Commence diazepam 2 mg as required and review the behaviour in four weeks
Arrange admission to an inpatient mental health unit for assessment and behavioural stabilisation
Arrange a functional behaviour assessment with sensory and communication supports in place
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review the behaviour and sleep in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive advice for a commercial vehicle driver commencing a sedating antipsychotic
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 44-year-old man with schizophrenia whose olanzapine was increased three days ago after a relapse of persecutory beliefs. He is settling well and wants to return to work on Monday.

He drives a semi-trailer interstate and holds a commercial vehicle licence. He tells you he feels groggy until about lunchtime each day and has been sleeping 11 hours. He asks you not to write anything that might cost him his job, and says he will simply drink more coffee.

data_table.Mental state: Residual persecutory beliefs held with reduced conviction, no command hallucinations, no thoughts of harming himself or others, insight partial, cognition grossly intact but subjectively slowed
data_table.Examination: Mild psychomotor slowing, no parkinsonism, no akathisia, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg with no postural drop
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests and fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Clear him to drive as his psychotic symptoms have improved on treatment
Notify the driver licensing authority today without telling the patient
Advise him not to drive, document the advice and arrange review
Halve the olanzapine dose so that he can return to driving on Monday
Leave the decision to him since he knows his own tolerance to the drug

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant associated sexual dysfunction in sustained remission where the agent rather than the treatment is changed
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 34-year-old man who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 14 months after a single severe depressive episode. His mood, sleep, appetite and concentration have been back to baseline for 8 months and he has returned to full time work.

Over that time he has found it takes far longer to reach orgasm and his interest in sex has dropped noticeably. This is causing tension with his partner and he says he is close to stopping the tablets himself. He has no erectile difficulty and no early morning erections have been lost.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic mood with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no suicidal ideation, body mass index 25 kg/m2, normal secondary sexual characteristics and testicular examination
data_table.Investigations: Total testosterone 18 nmol/L (8 to 30), TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), HbA1c 33 mmol/mol (less than 42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to an antidepressant with a lower sexual adverse effect profile
Advise weekend drug holidays from sertraline before planned intimacy
Continue sertraline unchanged and reassure him this resolves with time
Stop sertraline now given that he has been well for eight months
Add sildenafil 50 mg to be taken before intercourse and review

subtopic_detail: Herbal preparation interacting with a serotonergic antidepressant and hormonal contraception
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman who has taken escitalopram 10 mg daily for 7 months for a depressive episode and uses a combined oral contraceptive pill. Three weeks ago she bought a herbal preparation from a health food shop to help her mood and has taken it daily since.

Over the past week she has felt restless and jittery, has been sweating through her shirts, and her hands shake when she holds a coffee. She has also had two episodes of unexpected vaginal bleeding, which has not happened before on the pill.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of the outstretched hands, brisk reflexes with three beats of inducible ankle clonus, pupils 5 mm and reactive, no rigidity, alert and fully oriented
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 units/L (30 to 200), urea and electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits, beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop escitalopram and continue the herbal preparation and the pill
Stop the herbal preparation and review her within 48 hours
Continue all three and arrange review in 4 weeks as planned
Add cyproheptadine 8 mg orally and continue current medication
Increase the escitalopram dose to 20 mg daily to control symptoms

subtopic_detail: Blood injection injury phobia with vasovagal syncope requiring applied tension rather than anxiolysis
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 22-year-old nursing student who needs immunisations before her first clinical placement in 5 weeks. She tells you she has fainted at every blood test since she was 14 and once hit her head on a desk after a school vaccination.

She describes feeling hot and sweaty when she sees the needle, then her vision greys out and she wakes on the floor. She has no difficulty with heights, enclosed spaces, flying or public speaking, and is otherwise confident and outgoing.

data_table.Examination: Cardiovascular examination normal with no postural drop in blood pressure, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, no generalised worry, no panic attacks outside medical settings, no avoidance of any other situation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg orally one hour before each procedure
Prescribe propranolol 10 mg orally one hour before each procedure
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and review her in four weeks
Advise that she lie supine for all future blood tests and stop there
Refer for applied tension training with graded exposure therapy

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection in an older woman with weight loss, insomnia and previous drug induced hyponatraemia
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 78-year-old woman who has been persistently low, tearful and uninterested in her craft group since her husband died 14 months ago. She has lost 6 kg without trying, pushes her meals around the plate, and lies awake for two hours before she gets to sleep.

Last year a trial of sertraline was stopped after 3 weeks when her sodium fell to 126 mmol/L, which corrected within a fortnight of ceasing it. She takes no regular medications, lives alone and has no thoughts of harming herself.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 19 kg/m2, no postural hypotension, Mini-Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, no focal neurological signs, thyroid not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45 to 90), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 2.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 155), B12 and folate within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Re-trial sertraline 25 mg daily with sodium checked at one week
Commence venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily and review her in two weeks
Commence amitriptyline 25 mg at night for sleep and appetite
Commence mirtazapine 15 mg at night and monitor weight and mood
Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night and review the mood in a month

subtopic_detail: Recurrent disproportionate aggressive outbursts with normal interepisode function and genuine remorse
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26-year-old electrician referred by his employer after he punched a hole through a plasterboard wall when a delivery arrived late. He has had about two shouting outbursts a week for the past year and three episodes of breaking his own property.

He describes the outbursts as coming on within seconds, being over within half an hour, and leaving him ashamed and apologetic. He gains nothing from them and has never planned one. Between episodes his mood is steady, he sleeps well, he holds down his job and he has close friendships he values.

data_table.History: No history of deliberate deception, theft, cruelty or disregard for others' rights before age 15, no self-harm, no fear of abandonment, no unstable self image
data_table.Substance history: Drinks 4 standard drinks on a Friday night only, no illicit drug use, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no pressured speech, no grandiosity, no psychotic features, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Intermittent explosive disorder
Antisocial personality disorder
Bipolar disorder with mixed features
Borderline personality disorder
Alcohol induced mood disorder

subtopic_detail: Next line treatment for treatment resistant depression when lithium and quetiapine augmentation are unsuitable
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42-year-old accountant with a moderate depressive episode that has persisted for 11 months. He has completed 8 weeks of escitalopram 20 mg daily and 10 weeks of venlafaxine 225 mg daily, both at full dose with good adherence, alongside 14 sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy.

A quetiapine trial 6 months ago was stopped after he gained 9 kg in 7 weeks and was too sedated to work. He continues to work full time, has no psychotic features, is eating and sleeping adequately and denies any thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Mental state: Reactive but persistently low mood, no psychomotor retardation, no delusions or hallucinations, no suicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Rating scale: Montgomery Asberg Depression Rating Scale 26, indicating moderate severity
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 132 micromol/L (60 to 110), eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73m2, TSH 1.9 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits, no history of seizures or intracranial metal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.text: Refer urgently for a course of electroconvulsive therapy
Augment with lithium and monitor levels and renal function
Add quetiapine 50 mg at night as an augmenting agent
Refer for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
Switch to a third antidepressant from a different class

subtopic_detail: Functional seizures with atypical semiology and repeated normal routine electroencephalograms
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 29-year-old woman who has had events described as seizures for 2 years, now occurring up to five times a week. She takes levetiracetam 1500 mg twice daily and lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily and reports no reduction in frequency on either.

Her partner has filmed an event. It lasts 9 minutes, with her eyes squeezed tightly shut throughout, side to side head movements, and thrashing of the arms and legs that is out of phase between the two sides. Afterwards she is immediately oriented and tells you she could hear her partner talking to her during it. She has never bitten her tongue and has never been incontinent.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no injuries or scarring, no focal deficit
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with epilepsy protocol reported as normal, two routine interictal electroencephalograms normal, serum prolactin taken 20 minutes after an event within normal limits, electrolytes and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add sodium valproate as a third antiseizure medication
Refer for prolonged video electroencephalographic monitoring
Increase levetiracetam to the maximum tolerated dose
Commence sertraline 50 mg daily and discharge from neurology
Repeat the routine electroencephalogram with sleep deprivation

subtopic_detail: Emergent depressive symptoms with passive suicidal ideation during isotretinoin treatment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 16-year-old boy brought by his mother, 8 weeks into a course of isotretinoin prescribed by a dermatologist for severe nodulocystic acne. His skin has improved considerably.

His mother says he has withdrawn to his room, resigned from his football team and is sleeping 12 hours a night. When you see him alone he says he feels flat most of the day, has stopped enjoying anything, and over the past fortnight has had recurring thoughts that his family would be better off without him, although he has no plan and has not acted on them. He has never been depressed before and uses no alcohol or drugs.

data_table.Mental state: Reduced eye contact, slowed speech, restricted affect, pervasive anhedonia, passive suicidal ideation with no plan, intent or preparatory acts, no psychotic features
data_table.Examination: Marked improvement in facial and truncal acne, weight stable, no dry mucous membranes requiring treatment change, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests, fasting lipids and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that the evidence shows no causal link and continue
Halve the isotretinoin dose and review him again in four weeks
Commence fluoxetine 20 mg daily and continue the isotretinoin course
Continue the course and arrange dermatology review within a month
Cease isotretinoin now and arrange urgent mental health assessment

subtopic_detail: Progressive drowsiness and vomiting on valproate with a therapeutic level and normal liver function
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the ward to see a 34-year-old man admitted 3 weeks ago with a manic episode. His sodium valproate was increased from 500 mg to 1000 mg twice daily 9 days ago and his mania has settled.

Over the past 5 days the nursing staff have noticed he is increasingly drowsy, has vomited three times, and today could not tell them the day or the month. He has had no fever, no headache, no neck stiffness and no seizure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, disoriented to time, asterixis present on outstretched hands, no focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate 620 micromol/L (therapeutic range 350 to 700), ALT 28 units/L (less than 40), bilirubin 12 micromol/L (less than 20), INR 1.0, sodium 138 mmol/L (135 to 145), venous ammonia 98 micromol/L (less than 50), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Attribute the drowsiness to sedation and reduce the evening dose
Arrange computed tomography of the head and a lumbar puncture
Cease sodium valproate and monitor ammonia and conscious state
Continue valproate since the serum level is within the target range
Give lorazepam 1 mg for agitation and review in the morning

subtopic_detail: Additive upper gastrointestinal bleeding risk from a serotonergic antidepressant with dual antiplatelet therapy
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 68-year-old man who has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 2 years for recurrent depression, currently in remission. Eight months ago he had a drug eluting stent inserted and takes aspirin 100 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg daily.

He mentions three weeks of burning discomfort behind the lower sternum, worse after meals. He has had no vomiting, no difficulty swallowing, no weight loss and has not noticed any black or bloody stool. He takes no anti-inflammatory medicines.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness with no guarding, no mass, rectal examination shows brown stool negative on faecal occult blood testing
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130 to 180), mean cell volume 89 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30 to 300), urea and electrolytes and liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: Which single change is most likely to reduce his risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding?

options.text: Stop aspirin and continue clopidogrel as single antiplatelet therapy
Commence a proton pump inhibitor alongside his current medicines
Switch sertraline to another selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Halve the sertraline dose and review his mood in four weeks
Replace aspirin and clopidogrel with a direct oral anticoagulant

subtopic_detail: Escalating gaming and school refusal in an adolescent as avoidance driven by an anxiety disorder
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-year-old boy whose parents are worried that he games for around 10 hours a day and has not attended school for 6 weeks. He becomes irritable when they take the console away and has stopped seeing the friends he used to skate with, although he speaks nightly to the same group online.

Seen alone, he tells you he stopped going after a class presentation where he lost his place and some students laughed. He now feels sick and shaky from the moment he wakes on a school day, dreads being looked at in the corridor, and lies awake going over things he has said. He says gaming is the only time his mind is quiet.

data_table.Mental state: Anxious affect, no pervasive low mood, no anhedonia outside school related activities, no suicidal ideation, no psychotic features, insight into the pattern of avoidance
data_table.History: No alcohol or drug use, no gambling or in-game purchasing, no bullying reported beyond the presentation incident, was a competent student until this term
data_table.Examination: Physical examination normal, growth tracking on the 50th centile, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Set a graded screen time limit contract and review in four weeks
Diagnose internet gaming disorder and refer for addiction counselling
Commence melatonin 2 mg at night to correct the sleep cycle first
Assess for an anxiety disorder driving the school avoidance
Refer the family for therapy focused on parental limit setting

subtopic_detail: Massive modified release paracetamol ingestion where a level below the nomogram line does not exclude toxicity
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 19-year-old woman brought in by her housemate 5 hours after she swallowed a bottle of tablets following the end of a relationship. She now regrets it and is cooperative.

The pack is a modified release paracetamol preparation containing 665 mg per tablet, and 40 tablets are missing. She weighs 55 kg, has vomited once, and has taken no other substance and no alcohol. Her housemate confirms the timing. A blood sample drawn at 4 hours after ingestion has returned, and the resident has plotted it below the treatment line and suggests she be referred to the mental health team for discharge planning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and fully oriented, no abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, no asterixis, no evidence of other ingestion
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol concentration at 4 hours after ingestion 110 mg/L, ALT 22 units/L (less than 40), INR 1.0, creatinine 64 micromol/L (45 to 90), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22 to 32), lactate 1.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0), beta hCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge her as the four hour level sits below the treatment line
Give activated charcoal now and repeat the paracetamol level at 12 hours
Commence acetylcysteine now and repeat the level in 4 hours
Withhold treatment and recheck the level and liver tests at 8 hours
Measure the international normalised ratio and treat only if it rises

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to initiate sleep before the early hours who sleeps normally when free of a school schedule
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old boy brought in by his mother because he cannot get up for school and has missed twelve days this term. He says he lies awake until about three in the morning however early he goes to bed, then cannot be woken at seven.

On school holidays he falls asleep at about three and wakes around eleven, sleeps straight through, and describes himself as fine and full of energy. He denies feeling flat or hopeless, still plays basketball twice a week, sees his friends, and is not worried about school or being bullied. He drinks no coffee or energy drinks and uses no substances.

data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged with normal affect and reactive mood, no psychomotor slowing, body mass index 21 kg/m2, no goitre, tonsils not enlarged, no snoring reported by the family
data_table.Investigations: Sleep diary over two weeks confirms sleep onset between 2.30 and 3.30 am with a spontaneous wake time of 11 am when unconstrained, full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a short course of temazepam to be taken at his intended bedtime
Commence sertraline and arrange psychological review for underlying depression
Advise low dose melatonin several hours before sleep with morning bright light
Refer for overnight polysomnography before beginning any specific treatment
Advise removing devices from the bedroom as the sole intervention for now

subtopic_detail: Repetitive hair pulling with relief afterwards and broken hairs of varying length without scalp inflammation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old university student who has two bald patches at the crown of her scalp. She tells you she pulls her hair out, mostly while studying at night or watching television, and that she feels a building tension beforehand and a sense of relief once she has pulled.

She has been doing this for about three years, has tried wearing a beanie and cutting her nails short, and is embarrassed enough that she has stopped going to the gym. She is not distressed by thoughts of contamination or harm, does not check or count, and has no rituals she feels compelled to perform. She swallows no hair and has no abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Two irregular patches of hair loss at the crown containing broken hairs of varying lengths, scalp skin normal with no scaling, erythema, pustules or scarring, no exclamation mark hairs, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for habit reversal training with an appropriately trained therapist
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a dose used for compulsions
Prescribe topical minoxidil solution to the affected areas of the scalp
Commence oral N acetylcysteine and review the response after three months
Commence a low dose antipsychotic to augment behavioural strategies she has tried

subtopic_detail: Accumulation of possessions with distress at discarding and unusable living space in a late middle aged adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to see a 58-year-old woman after her daughter contacted the practice. On a home visit you find narrow walkways between stacked newspapers, boxes and shopping bags, the kitchen bench unusable and the bath full of stored items.

She tells you each item might be needed one day and becomes visibly distressed and tearful when her daughter suggests removing anything. She does not describe intrusive thoughts about contamination or harm, performs no washing, checking or counting rituals, and says she simply cannot bear to waste things. She is oriented, manages her own finances and medication accurately, and shops for herself. She has no delusional beliefs about the items and knows the state of the house is a problem.

data_table.Examination: Well groomed, normal affect with appropriate reactivity, no psychomotor change, no evidence of psychosis, clock drawing test normal
data_table.Investigations: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30, full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, thyroid function and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a high dose serotonin reuptake inhibitor as used for compulsions
Arrange a council clean out of the property while she stays with her daughter
Refer for a capacity assessment with a view to guardianship for her affairs
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy developed specifically for hoarding
Commence a low dose antipsychotic to reduce her attachment to the possessions

subtopic_detail: Severe irritability and low mood confined to the week before menstruation with prospective rating over two cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 33-year-old woman who says she becomes a different person for about a week each month. She describes irritability that has frightened her children, tearfulness, a sense of being overwhelmed and food cravings, and says it lifts within a day or two of her period starting and she then feels completely well.

This has gone on for two years and has worsened since the birth of her second child. She has kept daily symptom ratings for the past two cycles at your request, and they show scores in the normal range throughout the first half of each cycle. She is using condoms for contraception and does not wish to start hormonal contraception. She has no history of depression outside this pattern and no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Normal affect at today's visit on day 6 of her cycle, no psychomotor change, body mass index 26 kg/m2, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Prospective daily symptom ratings over two consecutive cycles show a greater than 50 per cent rise in scores in the luteal phase with full remission by day 4, thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What would you first recommend?

options.text: Commence a combined oral contraceptive containing drospirenone continuously
Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken from ovulation until menstruation
Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously every day of the cycle
Recommend a calcium supplement with regular aerobic exercise for three cycles
Refer for a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy

subtopic_detail: Third relapse of psychosis each following cessation of oral medication with full response while taking it
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man on the ward two weeks into his third admission in two years. Each admission has followed him stopping his tablets, and on each occasion his symptoms have fully resolved within three to four weeks of restarting the same medication.

He is now settled, no longer describes voices, and can discuss his illness openly. He tells you the tablets do help but that he forgets them once he is feeling well and finds taking something every day a daily reminder that he is unwell. He uses no alcohol or other drugs, and urine drug screens on each admission have been negative. He has had no movement side effects and his weight has been stable.

data_table.Examination: Calm, cooperative, no thought disorder, no perceptual disturbance elicited, partial insight with agreement that medication has helped, no rigidity, tremor or abnormal involuntary movements
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, fasting lipids and glucose all within normal limits, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management on discharge?

options.text: Switch to clozapine given that he has now relapsed on three separate occasions
Increase the oral dose and arrange weekly community follow up after discharge
Add a mood stabiliser to reduce the frequency of further relapses of illness
Apply for a community treatment order to enforce ongoing oral medication
Offer transfer to a long-acting injectable form of his current antipsychotic

subtopic_detail: Early prescription requests and multiple prescribers on long term opioid therapy for non cancer back pain
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old man who has taken modified release oxycodone for six years for back pain following a work injury. He has asked for his script eight days early on three occasions this year, saying the pain has been worse.

The real time prescription monitoring system shows he has also received oxycodone from two other practices in the past four months. He has stopped attending the gym program he was doing, sleeps poorly, and says the tablets take the edge off but no longer help as they once did. He does not inject, uses no heroin or stimulants, drinks two beers most evenings, and has never had an overdose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 per minute, blood pressure 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No pinpoint pupils, no sedation, no track marks, lumbar movement restricted by pain with negative straight leg raise, power reflexes and sensation in both legs within normal limits, no saddle anaesthesia
data_table.Investigations: Current daily dose equivalent to 80 mg of oral morphine, liver function and renal function within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for oxycodone only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop the oxycodone immediately and prescribe oral naltrexone to prevent relapse
Continue the current dose and add pregabalin for a neuropathic component
Establish a single prescriber agreement and begin a gradual dose reduction
Increase to transdermal fentanyl to provide more stable analgesic blood levels
Refer for a lumbar epidural corticosteroid injection before changing prescribing

subtopic_detail: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved attention three weeks into abstinence after repeated withdrawals
stem: A 58-year-old man is due for discharge tomorrow to his flat alone, three weeks after admission for alcohol withdrawal. He tells staff about fishing with his brother yesterday, which did not happen, and greets you as though you had not met this morning. He had three days of oral thiamine on admission.

data_table.Examination: Attention sustained, three word recall 0/3 at five minutes, unsteady gait
data_table.Investigations: MoCA 19/30 with losses on delayed recall; macrocytosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give high dose parenteral thiamine and defer the decision about where he lives
Commence donepezil for probable Alzheimer disease with clinic follow up
Discharge him tomorrow as planned with community alcohol and drug follow up
Arrange a capacity assessment today and apply for a guardianship order
Commence an antipsychotic to address the false accounts he gives staff

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal eating with complete amnesia for the episodes months after starting a non benzodiazepine hypnotic
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42-year-old woman who has taken zolpidem nightly for four months for insomnia that began during a stressful period at work.

Her partner tells you that she gets up an hour or two after falling asleep, goes to the kitchen and eats large quantities of whatever is there, including frozen bread and uncooked pasta, and does not answer when he speaks to her. She has no memory of any of it and has twice found the kitchen in disarray and been upset and frightened by it. She has sent two incoherent text messages overnight that she cannot recall writing. She does not eat in this way during the day, has no concerns about her weight or body shape, sleepwalked at no point in childhood, and drinks no alcohol.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2 having risen from 24 kg/m2 over four months, normal affect with no low mood or anhedonia, no psychomotor change, neurological examination within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and fasting glucose all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the zolpidem dose and continue it alongside a consistent bedtime routine
Refer for eating disorder assessment and commence fluoxetine for binge eating
Arrange overnight polysomnography before making any change to her medication
Switch to temazepam at an equivalent dose to maintain her sleep through the night
Cease the zolpidem and treat the insomnia with cognitive behavioural therapy

subtopic_detail: Seizure with profound hyponatraemia and maximally dilute urine in a man observed drinking continuously
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the emergency department where a 38-year-old man with schizophrenia, treated with olanzapine for six years, has had a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting ninety seconds. He is now post ictal and drowsy but protecting his airway.

The nursing home staff who brought him in say he drinks constantly from taps and the bathroom shower, carries a two litre bottle everywhere, and that he looks visibly puffier in the evenings than in the mornings. He has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no recent change to his medication. He has not been started on any new drug and takes no diuretic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy and rousable with no focal neurology, moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, weight 4.1 kg above his documented morning weight
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 112 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), serum osmolality 238 mOsm/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 78 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits, computed tomography of the brain shows no acute abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Restrict all oral fluid with one to one observation and recheck the sodium
Give a bolus of hypertonic saline and recheck the sodium within the hour
Commence an infusion of isotonic saline at 125 mL per hour and monitor closely
Commence oral tolvaptan to promote free water clearance by the kidneys
Cease the olanzapine, since antipsychotic treatment is the likely precipitant

subtopic_detail: Large volume dilute urine on long term lithium with a therapeutic level and no response to desmopressin
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46-year-old woman who has taken lithium for twelve years for bipolar affective disorder, with no episode of mania or depression in the past nine years. She now passes very large volumes of pale urine, gets up four times a night, and drinks constantly to keep up.

She has had no tremor, no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no unsteadiness, and has not started any new medication. She is frightened of becoming unwell again and says the last manic episode cost her her job and nearly her marriage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert with no tremor, no ataxia, no hyperreflexia and no myoclonus, mucous membranes moist, no goitre, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.60-0.80), sodium 147 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 84 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60 mL/min/1.73m2, calcium and thyroid function within normal limits, 24 hour urine volume 5.2 litres, urine osmolality 105 mOsm/kg and unchanged after desmopressin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop lithium today and commence a thiazide diuretic to control the urine output
Give regular intranasal desmopressin to bring the urine output under control
Restrict her fluid intake to two litres daily and repeat the sodium in one week
Add amiloride and review whether lithium remains the best long term treatment
Increase the lithium dose to improve symptom control and recheck the level

subtopic_detail: Orofacial choreoathetoid movements emerging on long term depot treatment and worsening after a dose reduction
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 61-year-old man with schizophrenia who has received a haloperidol depot injection for nine years. His sister says his mouth has been moving on its own for about two years and that it has become much more noticeable since his dose was reduced three months ago.

He is not troubled by the movements himself but they stop when he is asked to perform a task with his hands, and his sister reports he is now reluctant to eat in public. His psychotic symptoms have remained well controlled and he has had no relapse in five years.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing movements with choreoathetoid movements of the fingers, present at rest and suppressed briefly on distraction, no cogwheel rigidity, no resting tremor, no bradykinesia, gait normal with preserved arm swing
data_table.Investigations: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score 14, full blood count, urea creatinine and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the depot dose back to the previous level to settle the movements
Add benzatropine regularly to treat the abnormal involuntary movements
Switch to an antipsychotic with a substantially lower risk of movement effects
Add propranolol to reduce the frequency of the abnormal movements
Cease all antipsychotic treatment immediately and observe over three months

subtopic_detail: Delusional misidentification of a spouse with fluctuating attention, dream enactment and later emerging parkinsonism
stem: A 76-year-old man has insisted for eight months that his wife is an impostor. He sees small children and a cat in the hallway. He is sharp on some days and stares into space on others. For three years he has shouted and thrashed in his sleep while recalling vivid dreams.

data_table.Examination: Mild bradykinesia, low amplitude left rest tremor, fluctuating attention, slow gait with two recent falls
data_table.Investigations: Mini Mental State Examination 24 out of 30 with visuospatial impairment; bloods and brain computed tomography normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence rivastigmine and advise against antipsychotic treatment
Commence low dose risperidone and monitor for movement side effects
Commence low dose quetiapine, which has the least dopamine blockade
Commence levodopa for the parkinsonism and reassess the psychosis
Commence a benzodiazepine at night and review again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Persistent yearning and preoccupation with a deceased spouse fourteen months after the death with preserved self worth and no pervasive anhedonia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68-year-old woman fourteen months after her husband died. She says she thinks about him almost all day, sets his place at the table, has not been able to give away his clothes, and finds it hard to believe he is really gone.

She has stopped seeing the friends they had as a couple because being with them is unbearable, but she still enjoys her grandchildren and her garden, eats normally and does not feel worthless. She has no thoughts of ending her life and says she wants to feel able to live again.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband and brightens when discussing her grandchildren, no psychomotor retardation, speech normal in rate and volume, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact on brief testing, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the response after four to six weeks
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for sleep and emotional distress
Advise that this is expected after a long marriage and review her in six months
Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy with planned review
Refer to a bereavement support group as the sole intervention for her symptoms

subtopic_detail: Adolescent using a nicotine vaping device hourly with morning use and failed unassisted quit attempts
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old boy who asks for help stopping vaping. He tells you he uses a disposable device roughly every hour, reaches for it within fifteen minutes of waking, and gets irritable and unable to concentrate in class when he cannot use it.

He has tried three times to stop on his own and lasted at most two days each time. He has never smoked cigarettes, uses no other drugs, has no respiratory or cardiac history, and is attending school and doing reasonably well.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear with no wheeze, no cyanosis or clubbing, mental state examination shows no depressive or psychotic features, engaged and motivated in the consultation
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation with a written quit date and review in one month
Prescribe varenicline with weekly telephone contact through the quit attempt
Offer behavioural support with nicotine replacement therapy and structured follow up
Advise switching to a lower nicotine concentration device and gradual reduction
Refer to a specialist drug and alcohol service and defer treatment until assessed

subtopic_detail: Young adult with irresistible daytime sleep episodes and sudden bilateral leg weakness triggered by laughter with retained awareness
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 22-year-old apprentice referred by his employer after falling asleep at a workbench. He says he cannot stay awake through the afternoon no matter how much he sleeps at night, and that a ten minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours.

His girlfriend has seen him sag at the knees and slump forward when he laughs hard, lasting under a minute, and he says he can hear everything while it happens and is not confused afterwards. He sometimes wakes unable to move for a few seconds and occasionally sees figures in the room as he falls asleep.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no goitre, cranial nerves and peripheral neurological examination normal, no proximal weakness, reflexes present and symmetrical, mental state examination shows no depressive features, oropharynx unobstructed with a Mallampati score of 1
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and glucose all within normal limits, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to investigate probable atonic seizures
Advise sleep hygiene measures and a regular bedtime and review in two months
Start a modafinil trial and assess the response to treatment after four weeks
Refer for psychiatric assessment of possible functional neurological symptoms
Refer to a sleep physician for overnight polysomnography and daytime nap testing

subtopic_detail: Evening leg discomfort relieved by walking with an iron store at the low end of the population range and no anaemia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54-year-old woman who describes a crawling, creeping discomfort deep in both calves that starts when she sits down after dinner and builds until she has to get up and walk. Walking relieves it within a minute and it returns when she sits again.

It is worst between 9 pm and midnight and it takes her more than an hour to fall asleep most nights. Her partner says her legs jerk repeatedly once she is asleep. She takes no regular medication and her periods stopped four years ago.

data_table.Examination: Calves non-tender with no swelling or varicosities, pedal pulses present, no sensory loss to light touch or pinprick, ankle reflexes present, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, no skin changes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 129 g/L (115 to 155), mean cell volume 88 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 32 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 16 percent (15 to 45), estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), vitamin B12 372 pmol/L (150 to 700)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start a dopamine agonist at a low dose and titrate to symptom control
Start oral iron replacement and reassess symptoms and iron stores after three months
Start an alpha 2 delta ligand at night and titrate the dose to effect
Start a low dose benzodiazepine at night to improve her sleep onset latency
Arrange nerve conduction studies before committing to any specific treatment

subtopic_detail: Adult woman with lifelong social exhaustion and rigid routines who has carried several psychiatric labels without sustained response to treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who brings a list of questions and asks whether she might be autistic, having recognised herself in an account written by another woman.

She describes rehearsing conversations beforehand, copying colleagues' phrases, and needing to lie in a dark room for hours after social events. She has eaten the same lunch daily for eleven years, is distressed by unexpected changes to plans, and has intense long standing interests in textile history. She has been treated for social anxiety and for depression over fifteen years with partial and short lived benefit. She works, has one close friend, and made eye contact throughout, which she tells you she finds effortful and has practised.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows no current depressive episode, no psychotic features and no current suicidal ideation, speech normal in form, insight good, no evidence of an eating disorder with a body mass index of 22 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase her antidepressant dose and review the response after six weeks
Reassure her that autism is unlikely given her employment and eye contact
Refer for a specialist diagnostic assessment with a developmental history
Administer a self report autism screening questionnaire and act on the score
Refer for personality disorder assessment given the chronic interpersonal pattern

subtopic_detail: Persistent sense of watching oneself from outside and of surroundings appearing unreal beginning after a cannabis episode with intact reality testing
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 21-year-old university student who says that for the past seven months he has felt as though he is watching himself from a few feet away and that the world looks flat, as if through glass. He is frightened that he is going mad.

It began during an episode of intense anxiety after using a high potency cannabis product at a party, and has continued daily since although he has not used cannabis or any other drug since that night. He knows the feeling is not real and says nothing has actually changed about the room or about him, and he has no hallucinations and no unusual beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and pressured when describing the symptom, oriented with intact attention and memory, no perceptual abnormality elicited, no delusional beliefs, insight fully retained, no depressive episode, neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone and urine drug screen all unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start an antipsychotic at a low dose and review the response in four weeks
Prescribe a regular benzodiazepine to reduce the anxiety driving the experience
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before offering any treatment
Reassure him that this resolves without treatment and review him in six months
Explain the diagnosis and refer for psychological therapy with planned review

subtopic_detail: Inner restlessness and constant pacing appearing days after an antipsychotic dose increase with resolving delusions and no tremor or rigidity
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man admitted eleven days ago with a first episode of psychosis. His risperidone was increased four days ago and since then the nurses report he cannot settle, paces the corridor from early morning, and stands up and sits down repeatedly through meals.

He tells you he no longer believes the neighbours are transmitting to him and that the voices have almost stopped, but that he feels a dreadful churning inside his legs that only walking eases, and that he would rather be dead than feel like this for another week. He is sleeping about three hours a night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Constantly shifting weight from foot to foot when standing and crossing and uncrossing his legs when seated, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no abnormal involuntary movements of the face or tongue, no myoclonus, no hyperreflexia, oriented with normal cognition, mental state examination shows resolving delusions and reduced auditory hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 130 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the antipsychotic dose and add propranolol with close observation
Increase the antipsychotic dose further to settle his agitation and improve sleep
Add benzatropine regularly and review the movement disorder in 48 hours
Cease the antipsychotic immediately and commence supportive care with cooling
Add a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for the emerging depressive symptoms

subtopic_detail: Older adult becoming confused and unsteady three weeks after starting an antidepressant with a low sodium and concentrated urine
stem: A 79-year-old woman started sertraline three weeks ago for a moderate depressive episode. Over four days she has become muddled about the day, twice could not find her own bathroom, and has been unsteady with one near fall. She also takes hydrochlorothiazide, unchanged for nine years.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy, oriented to person only; euvolaemic with no postural drop; unsteady broad based gait
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 468 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue the antidepressant and add an antipsychotic for the confusion
Give intravenous sodium chloride to correct the sodium over 24 hours
Halve the antidepressant dose and repeat the electrolytes in one week
Cease the antidepressant and admit for fluid restriction and monitoring
Arrange computed tomography of the brain and review the result first

subtopic_detail: First episode of persistent low mood in a woman with irregular cycles and night sweats who attributes everything to her hormones
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 49-year-old accountant who says she is sure her hormones are to blame and wants hormone therapy. Her cycles have become unpredictable over eighteen months, ranging from 21 to 60 days, and she wakes drenched two or three nights a week.

For the past three months she has had low mood every day, has lost interest in things she used to enjoy including her choir, wakes at four each morning, has lost 5 kg without trying and describes herself as a burden to her family. She is making errors at work she would never previously have made. She has never had a depressive episode before and has no thoughts of self-harm.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation with slowed speech and delayed responses, restricted affect, no psychotic features, cognition grossly intact with subjective poor concentration, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, calcium, thyroid stimulating hormone, vitamin B12 and ferritin all within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What would you recommend as initial treatment?

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy alone with review of her mood in three months
Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol and treat according to the result
An antidepressant with psychological therapy, and discuss hormone therapy as well
Psychological therapy alone with a review of her progress after six weeks
Recommend exercise, sleep scheduling and reduced alcohol and review in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Adolescent brought in after inhaling solvent from a bag with a perioral rash and new unsteadiness between episodes
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old boy brought in by his aunt, who is his carer. She found him last night behind the shed with a plastic bag and a can of spray paint, and says this is the fourth time in two months.

He tells you it makes everything feel far away for about twenty minutes and that his friends do it too. His aunt says that in the past few weeks he has been dropping things, his handwriting has changed, and his teachers report he seems slower. He has not used alcohol or other drugs and has never been in trouble with police.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous scaling rash around the mouth and nostrils, mild bilateral hand tremor, intention tremor on finger to nose testing with past pointing, broad based unsteady gait, no nystagmus, power and reflexes normal, no hepatomegaly, mental state examination shows no psychotic features and no depressive episode
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, creatine kinase and venous blood gas all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a benzodiazepine taper to manage withdrawal from the inhaled substance
Engage him and his carer, address the neurological signs, and involve youth services
Reassure the family that this is experimental behaviour and review him in three months
Report the matter to police so that supply of the product can be restricted
Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram to investigate the episodes of detachment

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with long standing distress about their developing body and a consistently stated cross sex identity presenting with self harm
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old who was assigned female at birth, attending with a supportive mother. They tell you they have felt since early primary school that they are a boy, have asked to be called Sam for two years, and that since their chest developed they bind daily and avoid showering or swimming.

They have cut their forearms four times in the past six weeks, describing it as relief from distress rather than an attempt to die, and say they feel hopeless about what their body is becoming. They are attending school, have two close friends, and their mother asks you what you can do and where they should go.

data_table.Examination: Four superficial healed linear scars on the left forearm with no active wounds, no signs of constriction injury to the chest wall on examination with air entry equal and full, Tanner stage 4, mental state examination shows distress about body but no psychotic features, no current plan or intent to end life, protective factors include supportive mother and engaged schooling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence testosterone after discussion of the risks and benefits with the family
Treat the self-harm with a psychological referral and set the gender question aside
Advise waiting until 18 years before any assessment, with review appointments meanwhile
Refer for family therapy to address the mother's response to the disclosure
Refer to a specialist gender service while providing safety planning and support

subtopic_detail: Low mood and tearfulness clearly tied to a recent redundancy with retained enjoyment and fleeting thoughts that life is not worth living
