stem: A 42-year-old man was made redundant seven weeks ago. He feels flattened and tearful, worries about the mortgage and lies awake after going to bed. He still enjoys his daughter's netball; appetite, weight and waking time are unchanged. Once or twice he has thought his family would be better off without him, which frightens him, and he has no plan. He asks for antidepressants.

data_table.Examination: Tearful about work but brightens describing his daughter, no psychomotor change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Safety planning with psychological therapy and early planned review
Start an antidepressant today as he asks and review in four weeks
Refer him urgently to the acute mental health team for same day review
Prescribe a short course of a hypnotic and review in one month
Reassure him this is a normal reaction and review only if it worsens

subtopic_detail: Older man with rooms impassable from accumulated possessions who feels distress only when others try to discard them and has no intrusive contamination thoughts
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a home visit on a 68-year-old man after his daughter rang the practice. Newspapers, containers and unopened purchases are stacked to shoulder height through the hallway and only a narrow path remains to the kitchen, where the stove cannot be reached.

He tells you calmly that everything has a use and he will sort it when he has time, and he becomes visibly distressed only when his daughter suggests a skip bin. He describes no repetitive washing, checking or counting, and no intrusive thoughts he is trying to neutralise. His mood is reactive and he denies anhedonia. He scores 28 out of 30 on cognitive screening and manages his own finances and medications accurately.

data_table.Examination: Well kempt and oriented, speech normal in rate and form, mood reactive with no psychomotor slowing, no delusional explanation offered for the accumulation, insight limited regarding the safety risk, Mini Mental State Examination 28 out of 30, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a high dose and review in eight weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy specifically adapted for difficulty discarding
Arrange a forced clean out by council officers with family present to remove the risk
Refer for comprehensive neuropsychological assessment for a frontal lobe syndrome
Refer to the aged care assessment team for placement in supported residential care

subtopic_detail: Adolescent girl with a widening area of missing scalp hair pulled out when studying, with relief afterwards and no scaling or broken hair of varying length on the rest of the scalp
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15-year-old girl brought by her mother because of a bald patch at the crown that has widened over six months. Her mother has noticed hair on the desk when she is studying for exams.

When you see her alone she tells you she pulls hairs out one at a time while she is concentrating or lying in bed, feels a build up of tension first and a sense of relief afterwards, and has tried to stop several times. She denies eating the hair. She is embarrassed and now wears her hair up to hide it. She is doing well at school, has friends, sleeps normally and denies low mood or thoughts of self-harm. There are no intrusive thoughts and no rituals.

data_table.Examination: Irregular patch of hair loss at the crown measuring about 5 cm with hairs of varying lengths within it, no scaling, erythema, scarring or broken hair beyond the patch, eyebrows and eyelashes intact, no palpable abdominal mass, mood euthymic with reactive affect, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, ferritin and thyroid function all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and review in six weeks
Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid scalp lotion and review the patch in eight weeks
Prescribe oral terbinafine for four weeks after sending scalp scrapings for fungal culture
Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for assessment of a possible gastric hair mass
Refer for habit reversal training delivered by a trained psychologist over several sessions

subtopic_detail: Adolescent unable to fall asleep before three in the morning on school nights who sleeps soundly until midday on holidays with normal total sleep time
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16-year-old boy whose mother is worried that he is depressed because he cannot get out of bed for school and has been late eleven times this term. He lies awake until about three in the morning however early he goes to bed, then has to be dragged out at seven.

During the recent two week school holidays he went to sleep at about three and woke spontaneously at about eleven, felt refreshed and had no difficulty. His mood is good on weekends and in the holidays, he enjoys skateboarding and his appetite is normal. He drinks no caffeine after midday and does not use cannabis. His sleep diary shows a consistent sleep period of eight hours whenever he is allowed to choose the timing.

data_table.Examination: Alert with reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, no anhedonia described on direct questioning, no suicidal ideation, weight stable, general physical examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits, two week sleep diary showing sleep onset between 2:45 and 3:15 am with an eight hour sleep period when the wake time is unconstrained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start low dose melatonin timed several hours before his current sleep onset with morning light
Start a sedating antidepressant at night and review his mood symptoms in four weeks
Start temazepam at night for two weeks and taper it once his sleep pattern has settled
Start a high dose of melatonin at his usual bedtime and continue it for at least three months
Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on any specific treatment approach

subtopic_detail: Older woman with two years of difficulty maintaining sleep requesting a repeat hypnotic after four weeks of temazepam with a normal screening for depression and sleep apnoea
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71-year-old woman who has come in asking for another script for the sleeping tablet another doctor started a month ago. She wakes at about two each morning and lies there for two hours, and this has been going on for two years.

She says the tablet worked well for the first fortnight and now she needs it just to get the same sleep she had before. She is not low in mood, still plays bridge twice a week and gardens most days. Her husband says she does not snore and has never stopped breathing at night. She drinks one glass of wine with dinner and no coffee after lunch. She naps for an hour most afternoons in her armchair and is in bed by nine each night.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg per square metre, neck circumference 33 cm, Geriatric Depression Scale 2 out of 15, Mini Mental State Examination 29 out of 30, no postural drop, gait steady with no aid
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the current hypnotic at the same dose and review her again in three months
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and plan a gradual hypnotic taper
Switch to a sedating antihistamine at night and review her sleep pattern in four weeks
Start mirtazapine at night for its sedating effect and review her sleep again in six weeks
Arrange overnight polysomnography before making any change to her current medication

subtopic_detail: Residual nightly trauma related nightmares with waking in a sweat after completing an adequate course of trauma focused psychological therapy that resolved the daytime symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41-year-old former soldier who completed sixteen sessions of trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy with an experienced psychologist four months ago. His avoidance, hypervigilance and intrusive daytime memories have largely resolved and he has returned to work full time.

What has not changed is that five or six nights a week he wakes at about two in the morning from a dream replaying a specific incident, drenched in sweat and with his heart racing, then stays awake. His partner says he shouts but does not get out of bed or act out the dreams. He drinks two standard drinks on a Friday and no more. He takes no regular medication and his physical examination and screening bloods are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no current suicidal ideation, no postural blood pressure drop, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and glycated haemoglobin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his treatment?

options.text: Start quetiapine at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
Start temazepam at night and review his nightmare frequency again in four weeks' time
Repeat a second full course of trauma-focused psychological therapy with a new therapist
Start prazosin at night and titrate the dose slowly against his nightmare frequency
Arrange polysomnography to look for a disorder of rapid eye movement sleep behaviour

subtopic_detail: Man presenting with debt and marital crisis after escalating sports betting with chasing of losses, no alcohol or drug use and no manic features
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 36-year-old man who says his wife has told him to get help or leave. Over three years his sports betting has grown from a weekly bet to daily in play betting, and he has taken out a personal loan of 40000 dollars and borrowed from his brother without telling her.

He describes needing larger stakes for the same excitement, returning the next day to win back what he lost, and lying about how much he bets. He has tried to stop four times and lasted at most a fortnight. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He has never had a period of reduced sleep with elevated mood or overspending outside gambling. He denies current suicidal thoughts but says he has felt hopeless about the debt.

data_table.Examination: Appears tired but well kempt, speech normal in rate and volume, mood described as flat with reactive affect, no grandiosity or pressured speech, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact, no signs of chronic liver disease or intravenous drug use
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and urine drug screen all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start naltrexone at 50 mg daily and review his gambling and his mood in eight weeks
Start a mood stabiliser for an underlying bipolar disorder and review his mood in eight weeks
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for gambling with financial counselling alongside
Refer to a residential withdrawal unit for supervised abstinence over the next two weeks
Advise him to self exclude from venues and review his gambling again in three months' time

subtopic_detail: Choice of relapse prevention pharmacotherapy after alcohol withdrawal in a man with compensated cirrhosis and normal renal function
stem: A 54-year-old man has completed a five-day inpatient alcohol withdrawal with no withdrawal signs for 48 hours. He drank 15 standard drinks daily for a decade and wants to stay abstinent. He has cirrhosis without ascites or encephalopathy, takes no opioids and is booked with the drug and alcohol counsellor.

data_table.Examination: Spider naevi, palmar erythema, firm liver edge, no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 22 micromol/L, albumin 37 g/L, INR 1.2, creatinine 74 micromol/L, eGFR above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, platelets 118 x10^9/L

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medication should you start?

options.text: Oral naltrexone daily for at least six months
Oral disulfiram with supervised daily administration
Oral baclofen at low dose titrated upwards
Oral diazepam tapered over a further month
Oral acamprosate for at least six months

subtopic_detail: Restarting a mood stabiliser after eleven days without any doses in a woman whose maintenance dose was previously well tolerated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder maintained on lamotrigine 200 mg daily for three years without any rash or other problem. She went interstate for a funeral, left her tablets at home and has taken none for eleven days.

She feels her mood starting to drop and wants to restart today. She takes no other medication, in particular no sodium valproate and no oral contraceptive. She has had no rash, no fever and no mouth ulceration at any time. She has no intercurrent illness and her renal and liver function were normal three months ago. She asks whether she can simply take her usual 200 mg tonight and carry on as before.

data_table.Examination: Skin entirely clear with no rash anywhere including the mucous membranes, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, mood mildly low with reactive affect, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits three months ago

lead_in: What should you advise about restarting her medication?

options.text: Restart at her previous maintenance dose tonight because she tolerated it for three years
Restart at half her previous maintenance dose and increase to the full dose in one week
Restart at the original starting dose and follow the full titration schedule again
Switch to sodium valproate at an equivalent mood stabilising dose to avoid re-titration
Restart at her previous maintenance dose with a short course of prophylactic corticosteroid

subtopic_detail: Confusion and unsteadiness three weeks after a dose increase of an enzyme inducing mood stabiliser in an older woman with a low serum sodium and concentrated urine
stem: A 74-year-old woman has been muddled and unsteady for three days. Her carbamazepine was increased from 400 mg to 600 mg daily three weeks ago. She takes no diuretic and has not vomited.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no postural drop or oedema; oriented to place but not date, no seizures
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 252 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid and adrenal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the carbamazepine, restrict fluid and substitute another mood stabiliser
Reduce the carbamazepine dose, restrict fluid and recheck sodium daily
Give a 500 mL bolus of 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and reassess
Give 100 mL of 3 per cent hypertonic saline, repeated twice if needed
Start oral tolvaptan and continue the carbamazepine unchanged

subtopic_detail: Constipation, fatigue and renal colic in a woman on long term lithium with a raised corrected calcium and a parathyroid hormone that is not suppressed
stem: A 52-year-old woman has taken lithium for bipolar I disorder for 18 years and has been well for a decade. She passed a kidney stone six weeks ago and has been tired and constipated for months. She takes no thiazide, calcium or vitamin D, and has no tremor or ataxia.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.82 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), parathyroid hormone 8.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L, lithium 0.7 mmol/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most likely explanation for her biochemistry?

options.text: Lithium associated overactivity of the parathyroid glands after years of use
Lithium toxicity from accumulation as her renal function has declined
Malignancy related hypercalcaemia from a parathyroid hormone related peptide
Excess vitamin D increasing intestinal absorption of dietary calcium
Familial benign hypercalcaemia unmasked by biochemistry taken after the stone

subtopic_detail: Persistent tongue and jaw movements emerging after years of an antipsychotic in a man already taking benzatropine, with no restlessness or subjective urge to move
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol for 22 years and benzatropine alongside it for most of that time. Over the last eight months his wife has noticed his tongue pushing against his cheek and a chewing movement of his jaw when he is watching television.

He is not distressed by the movements and does not feel any urge to move, and he describes no inner restlessness. The movements stop while he is speaking and are absent in sleep. His psychotic symptoms have been in remission for six years on the current dose. He takes no other medication, has no tremor and no cogwheel rigidity. There are no chorea elsewhere and no family history of a movement disorder.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive lateral tongue movements and chewing jaw movements at rest that cease during speech, occasional lip pursing, no truncal or limb chorea, no rigidity or bradykinesia, no tremor, gait normal, Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale score 12, no restlessness observed or reported
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Increase the anticholinergic dose and review his involuntary movements in six weeks
Increase the antipsychotic dose because the movements reflect inadequate symptom control
Start propranolol and titrate the dose against the severity of his involuntary movements
Cease the anticholinergic and discuss switching to an antipsychotic with lower risk
Stop the antipsychotic abruptly and monitor his movements over the following three months

subtopic_detail: Severe irritability and low mood confined to the week before menstruation with complete resolution within days of onset, documented prospectively over two cycles
stem: A 33-year-old woman describes a week each month of irritability, tearfulness and feeling unable to cope that lifts within two days of her period starting, with complete wellbeing in between. She has never been depressed outside this pattern.

data_table.Symptom charting: Two cycles of daily ratings: symptoms begin five to seven days before bleeding and clear by day 3
data_table.Examination: Euthymic on day 9 of her cycle
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone and full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken only in the luteal phase
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken continuously
A combined oral contraceptive taken in an extended regimen
Micronised progesterone through the second half of each cycle
A gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with add-back therapy

subtopic_detail: Young man requesting a fourth cosmetic procedure for a nose he believes is deformed, with hours of daily mirror checking and an unremarkable appearance on examination
stem: A 24-year-old man wants a referral to a fourth surgeon about his nose, after two rhinoplasties and a revision, each leaving him briefly relieved then convinced the result was worse. He spends three or four hours a day checking his profile in reflective surfaces, leaves the house only after dark and has lost his apprenticeship through absences.

data_table.Examination: Nose appears unremarkable; belief held with absolute conviction; passive thoughts that life is not worth living

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide the referral, assess suicide risk and refer for psychological therapy
Start an antipsychotic alone because his belief is held with full conviction
Reassure him that his nose looks normal and review him in a month
Refer for assessment of an eating disorder given his appearance concerns
Decline the referral, assess suicide risk and refer for psychological therapy

subtopic_detail: Daytime sleep attacks with knee buckling on laughter in a nineteen year old whose sleep diary shows eight hours nightly
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old apprentice who has fallen asleep at his workbench three times in the past month and was nearly stood down after dozing off during a safety briefing. He says the sleepiness comes on suddenly and that a ten minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours.

He has twice felt his knees give way while laughing with his friends, staying fully aware throughout and recovering within a minute. He sometimes cannot move for a few seconds as he wakes. A two week sleep diary shows a consistent bedtime with eight hours of sleep each night, and his partner reports no snoring and no witnessed pauses in breathing. He scores 3 on a depression screening questionnaire and describes his mood as good.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg per square metre, Mallampati class 1 oropharynx, no goitre, normal cranial nerve and peripheral neurological examination, no papilloedema
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, ferritin 88 micrograms/L (30 to 300), Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19 out of 24, two week actigraphy confirms eight hours of sleep nightly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
Start modafinil now and arrange a sleep study if there is no response
Arrange thyroid function and iron studies, then review in four weeks
Refer for polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Advise sleep hygiene measures and review him again in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Four consecutive winters of low mood with hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a woman living in Hobart
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34-year-old woman who has come in each of the last four Junes with the same complaint. She describes flat mood, sleeping ten to eleven hours and still feeling leaden, craving bread and sweet food, and gaining four or five kilograms over the winter that she loses again by December.

She moved to Hobart five years ago from Cairns. Her mood and energy are entirely normal from about October to April, and she has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or increased activity. She works indoors and leaves for work and returns home in the dark through winter. She is not suicidal, functions at work with effort, and her weight and sleep are the symptoms she most wants addressed.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg per square metre, no goitre, no tremor, affect reactive during the consultation, no psychomotor retardation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, ferritin 65 micrograms/L (30 to 200), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 46 nmol/L (greater than 50), Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 14 out of 27

lead_in: What would you first recommend for her current episode?

options.text: Start lithium as a mood stabiliser and arrange monitoring of the levels
Start high dose oral colecalciferol and review her mood in eight weeks
Refer for electroconvulsive therapy assessment at the local mental health unit
Advise increased outdoor exercise alone and review her again in three months
Start bright light therapy each morning and review her again in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Emotional exhaustion and cynicism in a surgical registrar whose symptoms lift entirely on annual leave and who has no impairment at work
stem: A 31-year-old surgical registrar consults you with eight months of dreading work, nothing left to give her patients and uncharacteristic impatience at handover. Two weeks of leave restored her by day five and the dread returned within a week of going back. She sleeps and eats normally, still enjoys netball, and would step back if a patient were at risk.

data_table.Examination: Affect reactive, no thoughts of self-harm
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 8/27, GAD-7 6/21, AUDIT-C 3

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Structured review with workload focused counselling and no notification
Mandatory notification to the regulator, with review arranged
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
Certify her unfit for work for three months and review after that
Refer to the employee assistance program and take no further action

subtopic_detail: Weight loss in a twelve year old boy restricting by food texture since toddlerhood with no body image concern or fear of weight gain
stem: A 12-year-old boy has lost 4 kg in six months, falling from the 25th to below the 3rd centile. Since age three he has eaten only about eight dry beige foods and gags on anything wet or lumpy. He has no fear of gaining weight.

data_table.Examination: Weight below the 3rd centile, height on the 25th, Tanner stage 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents this is ordinary fussy eating and review in a year
Start family based treatment for anorexia nervosa with weekly weighing
Refer to a paediatric eating disorder service with dietitian involvement
Refer for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to exclude an organic cause
Start fluoxetine for restrictive eating and review him in four weeks

subtopic_detail: Eight months of not speaking at school in a six year old who talks fluently at home and passed school hearing screening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has written a letter because she has not spoken a word at school since she started in February. Her parents bring a phone video in which she is chatting and singing at home with her younger brother, using full sentences and a wide vocabulary.

At school she nods, points and writes answers on a whiteboard, and she will speak to no one, including other children. She played normally in the waiting room but has not spoken to you during the consultation, standing close to her mother and answering by nodding. Her school hearing screening in March was normal. Her parents describe her as shy with strangers since she was a toddler but say she has always spoken freely with family.

data_table.Examination: Well grown child, alert and engaged with toys, makes intermittent eye contact and uses gesture and pointing appropriately, no speech during consultation, no dysmorphic features, normal gait and coordination
data_table.Investigations: School hearing screening normal, growth and development otherwise age appropriate, no formal language assessment yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for formal audiology assessment before considering any other referral
Refer to a speech pathologist for assessment of a developmental language disorder
Reassure the parents that this is shyness and review her again in twelve months
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with a graded school based program
Start a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in six weeks

subtopic_detail: An evening urge to move the legs relieved by walking in a man on risperidone whose ferritin is 22 micrograms per litre
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46-year-old man with schizophrenia who has been on the same dose of risperidone for three years without change. He complains of a crawling discomfort deep in both calves that builds while he is watching television after dinner and is worst when he first gets into bed.

Walking around the flat relieves it completely within a minute, and it returns when he sits back down. He has no symptoms in the morning or at work, and he is no more restless in the waiting room now than at any previous review. His partner says his legs jerk repeatedly in the first hours of sleep. He has had heavy nosebleeds this year and his diet is limited.

data_table.Examination: No akathisic pacing or inability to remain seated during a 20 minute interview, no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor, no abnormal involuntary movements of the face or tongue, normal power and reflexes in both legs with intact pinprick and vibration sense
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 128 g/L (130 to 180), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (16 to 45), urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting glucose within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Add propranolol for akathisia and review his symptoms in two weeks
Start oral iron replacement and investigate the cause of the iron loss
Add benzatropine at night and review his symptoms again in two weeks
Start a dopamine agonist at night and review his symptoms in two weeks
Reduce the risperidone dose and review his symptoms again in two weeks

subtopic_detail: A fourth relapse within two years each time oral antipsychotic is stopped, in an improving involuntary inpatient with no insight into the need for treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar preparing the discharge plan for a 27-year-old man with schizophrenia who was admitted involuntarily six weeks ago after a relapse. This is his fourth admission in two years, and on each occasion he stopped his oral medication within a month of discharge and was readmitted within three months.

His symptoms have responded well to the current oral antipsychotic and he is now settled on the ward, sleeping, eating and attending groups. He remains convinced that he has never been unwell and that the tablets are only to keep staff happy, and he says plainly that he will not take them once he is home. He has a supportive sister and stable public housing. He has no history of violence, and there is no substance use.

data_table.Examination: Settled and cooperative, speech normal in rate and form, no thought disorder, no current hallucinations, persistent belief that he has never had a mental illness, no suicidal or homicidal ideation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, fasting lipids and glucose within normal limits, electrocardiogram QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discharge plan?

options.text: Discharge on the oral antipsychotic with weekly community team review
Keep him in hospital as an involuntary inpatient until his insight improves
Discharge him with no order and ask his sister to supervise the medication
Discharge on clozapine and arrange the required haematological monitoring
Apply for a community treatment order with a long-acting injectable antipsychotic

subtopic_detail: Reported seizures in a toddler that occur only when the mother is present and stop during a period of covert nursing observation
stem: A 3-year-old girl is admitted for the fourth time this year for collapses. Her mother, an enrolled nurse, describes episodes of stiffening, perioral cyanosis and unresponsiveness lasting two minutes, none ever witnessed by a clinician. Nursing staff recorded seven episodes, all when the mother was alone with her, and none on the four nights she went home.

data_table.Examination: Thriving, developmentally normal, plays freely on the ward
data_table.Investigations: Two electroencephalograms, cardiac monitoring, brain MRI and metabolic screen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a third electroencephalogram with ambulatory recording
Start an antiepileptic drug empirically and review in a month
Convene a multidisciplinary meeting and make a child protection notification
Discharge her with an ambulance call plan and review in a month
Tell the mother you suspect she is causing the episodes and gauge her reaction

subtopic_detail: Escalating pregabalin use obtained from several prescribers by a man stable on methadone who reports it gives him a lift
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 38-year-old man who has been stable on methadone through your practice for two years, with negative urine drug screens and steady employment. He was prescribed pregabalin for sciatica by a locum eight months ago.

Today he asks for an early script, saying the pain is worse. When you ask how he takes it, he tells you he now uses about 900 mg in the evening rather than the prescribed 150 mg twice daily, because it gives him a lift and helps him sleep, and that he has been getting extra from two other practices. He has had two falls at home in the past month and his partner says he has been slurring his words in the evenings. His sciatica has otherwise settled and his straight leg raise is full and painless today.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no slurred speech at this morning appointment, no nystagmus, gait steady, straight leg raise full and painless bilaterally, no focal neurological deficit, no injection sites
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for methadone with no other substances detected, full blood count urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, estimated glomerular filtration rate greater than 90 mL/min/1.73m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Check the real time prescription monitoring record and plan a supervised taper
Stop the pregabalin immediately today and review him again in four weeks
Continue the current prescription and add a benzodiazepine for his sleep
Increase the prescribed pregabalin to match what he is currently taking
Cease the methadone program and refer him to a residential detoxification unit

subtopic_detail: Repetitive unwanted images of harming her baby in a woman six weeks postpartum who avoids bathing him and finds the thoughts abhorrent
stem: A 29-year-old woman six weeks after her first baby's birth discloses that she keeps getting sudden images of holding him under the bath water. She finds them horrifying and has never wanted to act on them. She has stopped bathing him, put the kitchen knives away and checks him repeatedly at night.

data_table.Examination: Fully oriented, no delusions about the infant, insight preserved, infant thriving
data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 11, self-harm item zero

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for assessment
Make a child protection notification and review her in one week
Start an antipsychotic and arrange psychiatric review within a week
Explain the nature of the thoughts and refer for exposure based therapy
Reassure her this is normal after birth and review in three months

subtopic_detail: Irritability and fidgety movements at forty two in a man whose father died in a nursing home at fifty five after a movement disorder
stem: A 42-year-old man is referred with two years of irritability, apathy and difficulty organising himself at work. While talking he makes brief finger flicks and facial grimaces he seems unaware of. His father died in a nursing home at 55 after an undiscussed movement disorder. His well 19-year-old daughter asks to be tested too.

data_table.Examination: Involuntary movements flowing into voluntary ones, milkmaid grip, MoCA 24/30
data_table.Investigations: Caeruloplasmin normal, MRI shows mild caudate atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the movements in six months
Refer to a neurogenetics service for diagnostic testing with counselling
Arrange genetic testing for him and his daughter at one appointment
Start tetrabenazine for the movements and review him in six weeks
Repeat neuroimaging in twelve months and review him at that point

subtopic_detail: Agitation with a hydrocarbon smell and a perioral rash in a fifteen year old brought in after inhaling from a paint tin
stem: A 15-year-old boy is brought in by police, found behind a shopping centre with a tin of spray paint. He is agitated and shouting that the walls are moving. He smells of solvent and has a glazed silver rash around his mouth.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 /min, BP 128/74 mmHg, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Slurred speech, ataxic gait, no focal deficit, no head injury
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L, ECG sinus tachycardia, normal QRS, QTc 430 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his agitation?

options.text: Give intramuscular adrenaline if he becomes more agitated and combative
Give intramuscular droperidol and apply physical restraint until he settles
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and admit for cardiac monitoring
Give activated charcoal and observe in the short stay unit for four hours
Nurse him in a quiet low stimulus area with continuous cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: A sixteen year old who cannot fall asleep until the early hours and cannot be woken for school but sleeps normally through the holidays
stem: A 16-year-old boy has missed 14 days of school this term because he cannot be woken. He lies awake until about 3 am whatever time he goes to bed, then sleeps until midday if left alone. Through the recent holiday he slept 3 am to 11 am with good mood and energy.

data_table.Investigations: Sleep diary: onset 2.30 to 3.30 am, waking 11 am to midday on free days; thyroid function and ferritin normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe an antidepressant and arrange psychology review
Advise a fixed earlier bedtime with no phone in the bedroom
Refer for overnight polysomnography before treatment
Give low dose melatonin early evening with morning bright light
Start a sedative hypnotic nightly and review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Writhing tongue and lip movements developing after years of haloperidol in a man already taking benzatropine for stiffness
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 54-year-old man with schizophrenia who has taken haloperidol 10 mg daily for nine years. Benzatropine 2 mg daily was added six years ago for muscle stiffness and has been continued since.

Over the past four months his wife has noticed continuous movements of his tongue and lips. He is largely unaware of them. His psychotic symptoms have been well controlled for several years and he takes his medication reliably. On examination there are continuous writhing movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, plus occasional choreiform movements of the fingers. The movements lessen briefly when you ask him to open his mouth and hold his tongue still, and increase when he is distracted by mental arithmetic. There is no cogwheel rigidity, no tremor and no subjective inner restlessness.

data_table.Examination: Continuous choreoathetoid movements of the tongue with lip smacking and intermittent grimacing, occasional choreiform finger movements, movements briefly suppressible on request and worse with distraction, no cogwheel rigidity, no resting tremor, no akathisia on questioning or observation
data_table.Investigations: Urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Increase the benzatropine dose to control the abnormal movements
Add propranolol and continue his current medications unchanged
Withdraw the benzatropine and switch him to a different antipsychotic
Stop the haloperidol abruptly today and review him again next week
Arrange genetic testing and brain imaging for an inherited chorea

subtopic_detail: A fifteen year old playing online until dawn with falling grades and rage when the console is removed, whose parents want the internet cut off
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 15-year-old boy with his parents, who are exhausted and want the home internet disconnected. Over the past year he has played online games for eight to ten hours most days, often until dawn, and his school reports have fallen from solid passes to failures.

He has stopped attending football and no longer sees the friends he used to. He becomes verbally abusive and once punched a door when his father removed the console. He denies low mood and says he would be fine if everyone left him alone, though he admits he has tried to cut back several times and could not. He has lost 3 kg and often skips breakfast to keep playing. He uses no alcohol or other drugs and there is no history of gambling or in-game purchasing.

data_table.Examination: Slim, tired looking, engaged and articulate when discussing gaming, reactive affect with no psychomotor change, no evidence of intoxication or withdrawal, no self-harm marks
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, ferritin 48 micrograms/L (30 to 300), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Support the parents to disconnect the internet at home immediately
Refer for family based behavioural therapy with a structured sleep and school plan
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review in four weeks
Reassure the parents that this is a normal phase of adolescent development
Refer him to a residential drug and alcohol withdrawal service for admission

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of tearfulness and poor sleep after being made redundant in a man who still enjoys his weekends and has no diurnal variation
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 47-year-old man three weeks after he was made redundant from a job he had held for eighteen years. He asks for antidepressants because he feels he is not coping.

He describes tearfulness when he thinks about telling his extended family, difficulty getting to sleep as he worries about the mortgage, and a preoccupation with how unfairly the process was handled. He still enjoys cycling at the weekend and went to a friend's birthday dinner last week and had a good time. He denies any diurnal variation in mood, no loss of appetite and no weight change, and his concentration is intact when he is doing something he chooses. He has no thoughts of self-harm, no previous episodes of depression and no family history of mood disorder. He drinks two standard drinks most evenings, up from one.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when describing the redundancy but settles quickly and engages, affect reactive with preserved humour, no psychomotor retardation, speech and thought form normal, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, urea electrolytes and creatinine within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, HbA1c within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start sertraline at 50 mg daily and review him again in two weeks
Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for his initial insomnia
Reassure him that no intervention is required and review in three months
Refer urgently to the acute mental health team for same day assessment
Refer for structured problem solving therapy with review of his alcohol use

subtopic_detail: A new father screening above threshold at the six week check with irritability and withdrawal while his partner is being treated for postnatal depression
stem: A 33-year-old man attends his baby's six week check. His partner is being treated for postnatal depression. For a month he has felt flat and irritable, wakes at 4 am and enjoys nothing. He drinks four or five beers most nights, up from two on weekends.

data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 14, self-harm item negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Explain the scale is not validated in men and take no further action
Arrange his own assessment and care plan, addressing his alcohol use
Advise his symptoms will settle once his partner's treatment works
Refer the couple for relationship counselling as the main intervention
Notify child protection services because of his reported irritability

subtopic_detail: A wife who has lost 6 kg and sleeps in a chair by the door because her husband with dementia wanders at night, presenting about her own back pain
stem: A 74-year-old woman attends with low back pain. Her husband has moderate Alzheimer disease and tries to leave the house at night, so she sleeps in an armchair by the door. She has lost 6 kg in eight months, stopped her swimming class, cries most days and feels guilty. She refuses residential care.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful; denies suicidal ideation; no psychotic features
data_table.Examination: Lumbar paraspinal tenderness, no neurological deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Treat the back pain and arrange a carer assessment with respite
Treat the back pain and review her in three months as planned
Prescribe a sedative for her husband so she can sleep at night
Arrange urgent permanent residential placement for her husband
Refer her for urgent psychiatric admission for guilt and crying

subtopic_detail: Episodes of watching himself from outside his body with the world looking flat and two dimensional, while knowing the experience is not real
stem: A 24-year-old man has eight months of episodes, several times a week, of watching himself from behind his own head while the world looks flat and artificial. Episodes last twenty minutes to several hours and throughout them he knows the experience is not real. There is no palpitation, breathlessness or fear of dying. He has never used drugs.

data_table.Examination: Insight fully retained, no hallucinations, no memory gaps
data_table.Investigations: Brain imaging and electroencephalogram normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start an antipsychotic, as the experiences indicate psychosis
Refer for psychological therapy with psychoeducation about the symptoms
Start an antiepileptic after repeating the electroencephalogram
Treat him for panic disorder with an antidepressant and exposure
Arrange assessment for dissociative identity disorder with a specialist

subtopic_detail: Prolonged thrashing episodes with eyes squeezed shut and preserved awareness afterwards in a woman already on two antiepileptic drugs
stem: A 29-year-old woman diagnosed with epilepsy four years ago takes levetiracetam and lamotrigine at therapeutic doses. Three episodes this week lasted eight to fifteen minutes, with asymmetric limb thrashing, pelvic movement and eyes squeezed shut against attempts to open them. Afterwards she is tearful and can recount what staff said during the episode.

data_table.Examination: No tongue biting, incontinence or postictal confusion
data_table.Investigations: Video electroencephalography captured two typical episodes with no epileptiform change; drug levels therapeutic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange a saline injection to provoke an event and confirm the diagnosis
Tell her the tests are normal and discharge her to her general practitioner
Treat her for factitious disorder and notify the driving licence authority
Add a third antiepileptic drug and refer for epilepsy surgery assessment
Explain the diagnosis positively and plan supervised antiepileptic withdrawal

subtopic_detail: A man convinced he has motor neurone disease after eleven months of normal investigations who examines his own tongue daily and requests another neurology opinion
stem: A 41-year-old man has been preoccupied for eleven months with the conviction that he has motor neurone disease. He examines his tongue several times daily and reads patient forums for hours each evening. He accepts that two specialist assessments were normal but says they were done too early, and requests a third opinion.

data_table.Examination: Normal bulk, tone and power, no fasciculation, reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography normal twice, most recently six weeks ago; creatine kinase 118 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange the third neurology opinion he requests to provide reassurance
Repeat the electromyography now to settle the question definitively
Consolidate his care with one clinician and refer for psychological therapy
Tell him firmly that nothing is wrong and decline further appointments
Start an antipsychotic, since his belief about the diagnosis is fixed

subtopic_detail: Elation, pressured speech and reduced need for sleep starting five days after prednisolone was increased for a vasculitis flare
stem: A 52-year-old woman admitted five days ago with a vasculitis flare had her prednisolone increased from 10 mg to 75 mg daily. For three nights she has slept two hours without tiring, telephoned relatives at 3 am planning to sell her house, and speaks uninterruptibly.

data_table.Examination: Elated and irritable, flight of ideas, attention intact, MMSE 29/30, no fluctuating conscious level; no past mood disorder
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, glucose 11.4 mmol/L, CRP 18 down from 96 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat as hyperactive delirium and search for occult infection
Start an antidepressant, as grandiosity reflects agitated depression
Give regular diazepam alone and review her in seventy two hours
Discuss steroid dose reduction with the renal team and start an antipsychotic
Start lithium as maintenance for a first episode of bipolar disorder

subtopic_detail: Small figures seen at the end of the bed in a man with a four year tremor and shuffling gait whose levodopa was increased last month
stem: A 76-year-old man has had a resting tremor and shuffling gait for four years, and his levodopa with carbidopa was increased four weeks ago. He now sees small figures of children at the end of his bed and a cat crossing the lounge room, is frightened, and accuses his wife of letting people into the house.

data_table.History: Alertness varies through the day
data_table.Examination: Resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, Mini Mental State Examination 24 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative; electrolytes, calcium and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and make no other change
Treat empirically for a urinary tract infection and reassess
Start risperidone at a low dose and review him in one week
Give haloperidol as required for the frightening hallucinations
Review his antiparkinsonian medications and reduce the dopaminergic load

subtopic_detail: Crying that starts and stops abruptly without sadness between episodes in a man eight weeks after a left hemisphere stroke
stem: A 68-year-old man is in rehabilitation eight weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. His wife reports he bursts into tears several times a day, often when greeted or during a television advertisement, and the crying stops as abruptly as it starts. He says he is not sad. Between episodes he engages in therapy and sleeps and eats well.

data_table.Examination: Abrupt onset and offset crying with rapid return to baseline, no anhedonia
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the symptom and start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Start an antidepressant at full dose for a post-stroke depressive episode
Refer for grief focused psychological therapy to process his disability
Reassure the team that the crying needs no treatment and will settle
Start a low dose antipsychotic to control the emotional lability

subtopic_detail: Choosing analgesia for a fractured ankle in a man taking an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor whose last dose was this morning
stem: A 44-year-old man has a closed displaced ankle fracture needing operative fixation today and severe pain. He has taken tranylcypromine 30 mg daily for eight months for treatment resistant depression, after four failed trials, with the best response of his life. His last dose was this morning.

data_table.Examination: Neurovascularly intact fracture, no clonus or hyperreflexia
data_table.Investigations: Bloods normal; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What analgesia and antidepressant management is most appropriate?

options.text: Give fentanyl now and postpone surgery for two weeks after stopping it
Give pethidine now and stop the antidepressant until after surgery
Give tramadol now and continue the antidepressant perioperatively
Give titrated morphine now, continue the antidepressant, and alert the anaesthetist
Withhold all opioids, give a regional block and stop the antidepressant

subtopic_detail: A six year old who speaks freely at home but has not spoken at school for eighteen months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has asked her parents to seek help. She has not spoken a word at school since she started, although she nods, points and will write answers on a whiteboard.

At home she chatters constantly, argues with her brother and tells long stories to her grandmother. At the shops she goes silent if a stranger speaks to her and hides behind her mother. Her parents say she was a cautious toddler who took a long time to warm to new people, and her hearing was tested last year and was normal.

data_table.Examination: Sits close to her mother and does not speak during the consultation, makes brief eye contact, nods and shakes her head appropriately to questions, completes a drawing task and hands it over, no repetitive movements or unusual mannerisms, plays reciprocally with a doll offered to her, articulate speech heard on a video recorded at home showing age-appropriate sentences and pretend play

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for behavioural therapy delivered with the school, using graded exposure to speaking situations
Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her speech at school in six weeks
Refer for a multidisciplinary autism assessment before any anxiety focused intervention is commenced
Advise the school to require a spoken answer before she is allowed to move on to the next activity
Arrange repeat audiology and a speech pathology assessment before considering any psychological treatment

subtopic_detail: Defiance and explosive tantrums at home and school in a seven year old with normal development and no aggression to others
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the mother of a 7-year-old boy who has had a year of daily arguments, refusal to follow instructions and tantrums lasting up to forty minutes when asked to turn off the television.

His teacher reports the same pattern at school with peers but no fighting or bullying, and his academic progress is on track. His mother says she spends most of the evening shouting and has begun to give in to stop the noise. He is well, sleeps through the night, and has no history of fire setting, cruelty to animals or stealing.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative and chatty during the consultation, normal vocabulary and comprehension for age, no motor overactivity or impulsivity observed across a twenty minute consultation, no low mood or anhedonia on direct questioning, reciprocal social interaction with normal eye contact and shared attention, growth parameters on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Teacher report scale showing elevated oppositional and defiant items with inattention and hyperactivity items in the normal range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence a trial of a stimulant medication and arrange review of his behaviour at home and school in four weeks
Refer the family to a structured parenting program that teaches consistent limits and positive reinforcement
Prescribe low dose risperidone for the tantrums and arrange metabolic monitoring at baseline and twelve weeks
Refer him for individual play therapy weekly and review his progress with the therapist after three months
Arrange a paediatric review for a formal neurodevelopmental assessment before offering any behavioural intervention

subtopic_detail: Discharge planning after inpatient opioid withdrawal in a man whose tolerance has fallen
stem:
You are the registrar discharging a 34-year-old man from a six day inpatient withdrawal admission for heroin dependence. He has used intravenously for eight years and has had two previous non fatal overdoses.

He has declined opioid agonist treatment for now and plans to stay with his sister, who is in the room and asks what she should do if she finds him unresponsive. He says he intends to stay off heroin but acknowledges he has relapsed after previous admissions.

data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented with no withdrawal features, pupils 3 mm and equal, no track marks with surrounding cellulitis, chest clear, no oedema, gait steady
data_table.Investigations: Liver function tests within normal limits, hepatitis C antibody positive with undetectable viral load after treatment, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 420 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate step to take before he leaves the ward?

options.text: Give him written overdose prevention information and a follow up appointment with the community drug service
Arrange a naltrexone implant before discharge to block the effect of any opioid he uses in the coming months
Supply take home naloxone and train both him and his sister to recognise an overdose and give it
Prescribe a short course of diazepam to manage the anxiety and insomnia that commonly follow withdrawal treatment
Defer naloxone supply until he has decided about opioid agonist treatment at his community appointment next week

subtopic_detail: Subacute cognitive complaints with prominent self reported memory failure and poor effort on testing in a seventy four year old
stem: A 74-year-old man says his memory has gone, dating the onset to four months ago, shortly after his wife died. He lists in detail what he has forgotten. He has stopped going to bowls, wakes at 4 am and has lost 6 kg. His daughter says he manages his medications and banking without error.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor slowing; answers I do not know to most questions; Montreal Cognitive Assessment 21 out of 30, recall improving with cueing
data_table.Investigations: Screening bloods normal; imaging shows age-appropriate atrophy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer to a memory clinic for amyloid positron emission tomography
Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and repeat testing in three months
Refer for driving assessment and notify the licensing authority
Treat the depression and repeat cognitive testing once mood responds
Reassure him that grief explains this and review in six months

subtopic_detail: Six weeks of morning abdominal pain with school non attendance in a thirteen year old who is well on weekends
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13-year-old girl who has attended school four days in the last six weeks. Each school morning she has stomach pain and nausea from about seven o'clock and cries when her mother insists she gets in the car.

On weekends and during the recent school holidays she was symptom free and went to a sleepover without difficulty. Her mother works from home and has been letting her stay in her room on the laptop. She has no truancy history, wants to keep up with her friends and says she feels sick at the thought of walking through the school gate.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no organomegaly or masses, growth tracking along the 50th centile with no weight loss, no pallor, no mouth ulcers, no joint swelling, mood reactive with normal affect during the consultation, no thoughts of self-harm on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), coeliac serology negative with normal immunoglobulin A, faecal calprotectin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Certify her as medically unfit for school for four weeks and arrange educational materials to be sent home
Refer her for an abdominal ultrasound and gastroenterology review before addressing the school attendance pattern
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review her attendance and side effects in four weeks
Recommend enrolment in distance education so that she can continue learning without the distress of attending
Arrange a graded return to school plan with the school wellbeing team and cognitive behavioural therapy

subtopic_detail: Excessive water drinking with a large diurnal weight gain and a falling sodium in a man with chronic schizophrenia
stem: A 41-year-old man with long-standing schizophrenia drinks from bathroom taps and carries a two litre bottle. He is more confused in the late afternoon than the morning and vomited twice last night. He takes no diuretic.

data_table.Weights: 78.4 kg at 7 am, 82.1 kg at 4 pm
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg, urine osmolality 88 mmol/kg, urine sodium 12 mmol/L, urea 2.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Restrict fluid with a supervised plan and monitor twice daily weights
Start a 3 per cent sodium chloride infusion with hourly levels
Start demeclocycline and repeat his electrolytes in three days
Cease olanzapine and substitute an antipsychotic less linked to hyponatraemia
Give intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride and recheck in six hours

subtopic_detail: Longstanding sensory based food restriction with faltering growth in a thirteen year old with no body image concern
stem: A 13-year-old boy has dropped from the 50th to below the 10th centile for weight over two years. He eats six foods, all beige and dry, and gags at the smell of cooked vegetables. He has eaten this way since he was three. He wants to be bigger for football and has never felt fat.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index on the 5th centile, no lanugo or dental erosion
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 14 micrograms/L (30-200), zinc low, sinus bradycardia 52 /min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence family based treatment focused on parental control of eating
Prescribe an appetite stimulant and review his weight in three months
Refer for dietetic nutritional rehabilitation with graded sensory exposure
Admit for nasogastric feeding and cardiac monitoring for his bradycardia
Arrange gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude an organic cause

subtopic_detail: Persistent dense amnesia with confabulation four weeks after treated Wernicke encephalopathy in a man who has stopped drinking
stem: A 58-year-old man is four weeks past an admission with confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia treated with parenteral thiamine. Those signs have resolved and he has not drunk alcohol since. He describes a fishing trip yesterday that did not happen.

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal digit span, no recall at five minutes despite cueing, disoriented to date
data_table.Investigations: Mean cell volume 104 fL, B12 and thyroid function normal, brain computed tomography shows atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor and review in the cognitive clinic
Continue thiamine and arrange neuropsychological assessment after abstinence
Correct each confabulated account as it occurs to reorient him
Apply for a guardianship order now to arrange supported accommodation
Give a further three days of high dose parenteral thiamine

subtopic_detail: Repugnant intrusive thoughts of harming her baby with avoidance of bathing in a woman with intact reality testing
stem: Six weeks after the birth of her first baby, a 30-year-old woman discloses that images of drowning the baby come to her when she runs the bath, so her husband now does all the bathing. She calls the thoughts horrible and not like her, checks the baby's breathing twenty times a night and has hidden the knives. She delights in the baby.

data_table.Examination: Thoughts unwanted and repugnant, no delusional beliefs about the baby, insight intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit urgently to a mother and baby unit with supervised contact
Advise another adult be present at all times and review in four weeks
Explain the nature of intrusive thoughts and refer for exposure therapy
Commence a low dose antipsychotic and arrange psychiatric review this week
Report to child protection on the basis of her disclosure

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antipsychotic for a first psychotic episode in a man with focal epilepsy taking carbamazepine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old man with focal epilepsy since childhood, controlled on carbamazepine with his last seizure two years ago. Over three months he has developed the belief that his neighbours are broadcasting his thoughts, and he now hears two voices discussing him.

The symptoms are present every day and are unrelated to his seizures, and there has been no change in seizure frequency or aura. He uses no substances, and a urine drug screen is negative. His neurologist has confirmed that his antiepileptic dose is unchanged and his last electroencephalogram was stable.

data_table.Examination: Guarded with persecutory delusions of thought broadcasting and third person auditory hallucinations, no clouding of consciousness, fully oriented with intact attention, no postictal confusion, no focal neurological deficit, no tremor or rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L (135 to 145), liver function tests within normal limits, carbamazepine level within the therapeutic range, electrocardiogram with a corrected QT interval of 408 milliseconds, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showing left mesial temporal sclerosis unchanged from previous imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Commence clozapine now, given that psychosis arising with epilepsy is typically refractory to other antipsychotic agents
Withhold antipsychotic treatment and ask the neurologist to increase the carbamazepine dose to suppress the psychosis
Commence chlorpromazine at night, titrating the dose upwards according to his response over the next two weeks
Commence risperidone at a low dose and titrate slowly, anticipating that carbamazepine will lower its plasma concentration
Treat this as a postictal phenomenon and observe him without antipsychotic treatment for a further two weeks

subtopic_detail: Agitation with tremor and autonomic arousal on day three after surgery in a patient whose long term night sedation was omitted
stem: A 72-year-old woman is agitated and climbing out of bed on the third night after a total hip replacement, having been oriented and calm for two days. Her daughter mentions she has taken a tablet for her nerves nightly for twenty five years, never asked about on admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 /min, BP 168/94 mmHg, temperature 37.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Restless, coarse tremor, diaphoretic, disoriented, attention impaired
data_table.Investigations: CRP 42 mg/L falling from 88, urine and chest radiograph clear
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol, as required oxycodone; no benzodiazepine charted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommence a benzodiazepine at an equivalent dose with a slow supervised taper
Prescribe regular haloperidol for the agitation with daily liaison review
Stop the oxycodone and treat her pain with regular paracetamol alone
Start empirical intravenous antibiotics for presumed postoperative sepsis
Arrange urgent CT of the brain and withhold sedating medication

subtopic_detail: Fever with rigidity and a very high creatine kinase two days after antiparkinsonian medication was withheld before surgery
stem: A 71-year-old man with nine years of Parkinson disease was admitted two days ago with small bowel obstruction and kept nil by mouth; his levodopa with carbidopa and entacapone have not been given since. He has never taken an antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 126 /min, BP swinging between 165/95 and 105/60 mmHg, temperature 39.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Severe generalised lead-pipe rigidity, sweating, fluctuating conscious state, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 6800 U/L (<200), white cell count 15.8 x10^9/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L, brain imaging normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene and transfer to intensive care for cooling
Give intramuscular olanzapine for his agitation and reassess the rigidity
Start empirical intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis and continue nil by mouth
Give a benzodiazepine and restart his usual medication when bowel function returns
Reinstate his dopaminergic therapy now by nasogastric tube or transdermal patch

subtopic_detail: Prolonged episodes with closed eyes and side to side head movement captured on video telemetry with a normal trace
stem: A 24-year-old woman has two years of episodes in which she falls, shakes and is unresponsive, unchanged on levetiracetam. Video electroencephalogram telemetry captured three typical episodes, each about eight minutes with eyes held closed, side to side head movement and asynchronous waxing and waning limb shaking, with a normal awake rhythm throughout.

data_table.Examination: No tongue biting or incontinence during any event
data_table.Investigations: Brain magnetic resonance imaging normal, postictal prolactin normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Increase levetiracetam, add lamotrigine and review in six weeks
Tell her the episodes are not genuine seizures and discharge her
Explain the positive diagnosis, refer for therapy and plan drug withdrawal
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor as primary treatment
Repeat the imaging with an epilepsy protocol and further telemetry

subtopic_detail: Sudden uncontrollable crying spells months after a stroke in a man whose sleep, appetite and interests are unchanged
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 68-year-old man in a stroke follow up clinic four months after a right hemisphere infarct. His wife reports that he bursts into tears several times a day, often triggered by something trivial like a television advertisement, and that the crying stops as abruptly as it starts.

He is embarrassed by it and says he does not feel sad when it happens. He has returned to lawn bowls twice a week and enjoys it, sleeps through the night and eats normally. His wife says his weight has been steady and he has not spoken about wanting to die.

data_table.Examination: Mild residual left sided weakness with independent mobility, speech fluent, euthymic affect between episodes with reactive expression, no psychomotor retardation, mini mental state examination 28 out of 30, no anhedonia elicited on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, vitamin B12 and folate within normal limits, sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence a low dose selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and explain that it reduces the frequency of the episodes
Commence a full antidepressant dose for post stroke depression and review his mood using a structured rating scale in six weeks
Commence a low dose atypical antipsychotic to reduce the emotional lability and review his response in the clinic in four weeks
Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting the depressive cognitions underlying his frequent episodes of crying
Reassure his wife that the crying is a normal grief reaction to his stroke and review him again in the clinic in three months

subtopic_detail: Four days of reduced sleep need with overspending and pressured speech six weeks into treatment for a depressive episode
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32-year-old man who was started on sertraline six weeks ago by his general practitioner for a moderate depressive episode. His partner brought him in today because for the past four days he has been sleeping about three hours a night and waking full of energy.

He has spent 14000 dollars on recording equipment he does not need, is talking so fast that his partner cannot interrupt, and has emailed his manager a plan to restructure the company. He says he has never felt better. His mother was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in her thirties for something his family never discussed.

data_table.Examination: Elevated and expansive mood with pressured speech and flight of ideas, grandiose but not delusional content, no hallucinations, insight absent, orientated with intact attention, no tremor, no clonus and no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60 to 110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue the sertraline at the current dose and add a short course of a hypnotic to restore his sleep while his mood is monitored
Halve the sertraline dose, arrange review in two weeks and advise his partner to bring him back sooner if his behaviour worsens
Add lithium to the sertraline as an augmentation strategy and arrange measurement of his serum level in one week
Cease the sertraline and commence an atypical antipsychotic with antimanic efficacy, arranging urgent specialist psychiatric review
Switch him from sertraline to a different class of antidepressant such as mirtazapine and review his sleep and mood in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Severe pain from a fractured tibia in a man maintained on sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone for opioid dependence
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar providing addiction medicine liaison to the orthopaedic ward. A 34-year-old man was admitted overnight with a tibial shaft fracture after falling from a ladder and is awaiting internal fixation this afternoon.

He takes sublingual buprenorphine with naloxone 16 mg daily, dispensed daily at his community pharmacy, and has been abstinent from other opioids for two years. He rates his pain 9 out of 10 despite regular paracetamol, and the orthopaedic intern has telephoned you because he is reluctant to prescribe opioids to a patient on an opioid treatment program.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Distressed by pain with the right leg in a backslab, no sedation with a normal level of alertness, pupils mid position, no withdrawal signs, no track marks, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, liver function tests within normal limits, urine drug screen positive for buprenorphine only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to his analgesia?

options.text: Withhold all opioid analgesia and manage his pain with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory and a regional nerve block alone
Cease the buprenorphine immediately and transfer him to methadone so that full agonist analgesia can work without receptor competition
Halve his buprenorphine dose today so that receptor occupancy falls and any full agonist opioid given afterwards becomes more effective
Continue his usual buprenorphine dose and add titrated short-acting full agonist opioid analgesia with multimodal and regional adjuncts
Prescribe regular tramadol as the sole opioid agent because its partial mechanism is considered safer in a person with opioid dependence

subtopic_detail: Private disclosure of a son withdrawing money without permission by a woman with intact cognition who asks for secrecy
stem: An 82-year-old woman attends for low mood with her son, who answers most questions. Seen alone, she says he takes money from her account without asking and shouts when she questions it. She is not afraid to go home and asks you to tell no one.

data_table.Examination: Mild reactive low mood; MoCA 27/30; weighs options and communicates a consistent choice; no injuries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Telephone the police today to report the financial abuse she describes
Raise the allegation with her son at the end of the consultation
Document, assess her safety and capacity, and refer to advocacy with consent
Apply to the civil and administrative tribunal for a financial management order
Accept her request for secrecy and treat the low mood with medication

subtopic_detail: Foster child who does not seek comfort from carers but plays reciprocally with peers and uses imaginative play
stem: A 6-year-old boy has lived with the same foster carers since age three, after removal for severe neglect. His carer says he does not come to her when hurt or frightened, accepts comfort stiffly, seems flat and rarely shows pleasure at home. His teacher says he plays chasing games with two friends and spent last week running an elaborate pretend restaurant.

data_table.Examination: Good social reciprocity and spontaneous imaginative play in the interview, no overfamiliarity with strangers

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for an autism spectrum assessment as the first step
Refer the child and carer for attachment focused dyadic therapy
Commence low dose risperidone for his flat affect and withdrawal
Refer for individual play therapy without carer involvement
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for his flat affect
