subtopic_detail: Eighteen months of aggression, fire setting and cruelty to a pet in a boy who concentrates well in class
stem: A 9-year-old boy is referred after a third school suspension this year. Over 18 months he has twice started fires in the shed, hit smaller children, and his mother found the family cat with its whiskers cut off. He says flatly that he does not care whether the children were hurt.

data_table.School: Sits still, attends a 40 minute lesson, completes written work; aggression is planned
data_table.Examination: Restricted affect, no remorse, no psychotic or depressive symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence methylphenidate and titrate over four weeks with teacher ratings
Commence low dose risperidone to reduce his aggression while awaiting therapy
Refer his mother to structured parent management training with a school plan
Refer him for individual anger management counselling for twelve sessions
Notify child protection because cruelty to animals indicates maltreatment

subtopic_detail: New dyspepsia in an older man taking an anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation who has added an antidepressant and a self bought analgesic
stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed six weeks after starting sertraline for depression, with his mood improved. For three weeks he has taken supermarket ibuprofen twice daily for knee pain, and for the past week has had burning epigastric discomfort after meals. He takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation, and has had no melaena or haematemesis.

data_table.Examination: Mild epigastric tenderness, no guarding, conjunctivae not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 139 g/L (130 to 180), ferritin 96 micrograms/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Cease the apixaban and substitute aspirin, continuing the other two medicines
Cease the ibuprofen, review his knee pain with a safer analgesic and reassess
Cease the sertraline and substitute a different antidepressant class
Add a proton pump inhibitor and continue all three medicines
Switch the apixaban to warfarin with monitoring and continue the other two

subtopic_detail: Choosing an antipsychotic for a man on high dose opioid substitution whose corrected QT interval is already 480 milliseconds
stem: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable off antipsychotics for two years, has relapsed over the past month with persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations. He has taken methadone 120 mg daily for eight years and is abstinent from other drugs. He has no cardiac symptoms and no family history of sudden death.

data_table.Investigations: Corrected QT interval 480 ms, potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Halve the methadone dose over a week before starting any antipsychotic
Commence intramuscular haloperidol and repeat the electrocardiogram afterwards
Correct his potassium and magnesium, then commence aripiprazole
Commence high dose quetiapine titrated rapidly, with weekly electrocardiograms
Withhold antipsychotics and offer psychological therapy until the interval falls

subtopic_detail: Seeing people in the house three weeks after an increase in a dopamine agonist in a man with established Parkinson disease
stem: A 76-year-old man with nine years of Parkinson disease sees people standing in the hallway in the evenings. He describes them clearly, knows they are not real and is not frightened. His dopamine agonist dose was increased three weeks ago. There has been no fever, urinary symptom, fall or daytime drowsiness.

data_table.Examination: Oriented with sustained attention, Montreal Cognitive Assessment 25 of 30, unchanged from eight months ago
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, urine microscopy no organisms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone, titrating to the hallucination frequency
Reduce and withdraw the dopamine agonist with his neurologist
Commence low dose olanzapine at night and review him in four weeks
Commence low dose quetiapine and keep the dopamine agonist unchanged
Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor and neuropsychological assessment

subtopic_detail: Persecutory beliefs emerging on week two of sight saving high dose steroid treatment that cannot be withdrawn
stem: A 71-year-old woman was started on prednisolone 60 mg daily twelve days ago for giant cell arteritis. Over four days she has become convinced that staff are recording her conversations and plotting against her, and last night she tried to leave the ward. The dose cannot be reduced for weeks without risking her sight.

data_table.Examination: Fully orientated, attention sustained, no fluctuation across three nursing shifts, fixed persecutory beliefs
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 8 mg/L (<5), sodium 137 mmol/L, glucose 9.8 mmol/L, brain computed tomography with atrophy only

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Stop the prednisolone and treat the arteritis with an anti-inflammatory
Manage as a hyperactive delirium with orientation measures alone
Start a low dose atypical antipsychotic and continue the sight saving steroid
Commence lithium with level monitoring to prevent further disturbance
Transfer to an acute psychiatric unit for management of the psychosis

subtopic_detail: Registrar colleague smelling of alcohol while rostered to the ward with a slurred handover witnessed by two staff
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar on an evening shift. During handover a fellow registrar rostered to the ward until midnight smells strongly of alcohol, slurs several words and twice loses his place in the patient list. The nurse in charge quietly tells you she noticed the same thing last Friday.

When you speak to him privately he becomes upset, says he had two drinks at lunch because his marriage has broken down, insists he is fine to work and begs you not to say anything. He is due to review two involuntary patients tonight and holds the ward pager.

data_table.Examination: Slurred speech with an unsteady gait on walking to the office, alcohol on the breath, tearful and reactive affect, no suicidal ideation elicited on direct questioning, orientated with no gross cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Accept his reassurance, offer to review any complex patients with him tonight and encourage him to seek help from his general practitioner
Advise him to complete this shift and then take personal leave, and agree that nothing needs to be reported if he starts treatment this week
Ask the nurse in charge to observe him for the remainder of the shift and document any further concerns for discussion at the next team meeting
Remove him from clinical duties now by escalating to the on call consultant, arrange his safe transport home and make a mandatory notification
Arrange an immediate breath alcohol test and take no further action if the reading falls below the legal limit for driving a motor vehicle

subtopic_detail: Episodes labelled as panic attacks that bring pallor and severe hypertension and that worsened after an antidepressant was started
stem: A 42-year-old woman is referred with treatment resistant panic disorder. For eighteen months she has had twenty minute episodes of palpitations, headache and drenching sweats. Her husband says she goes chalk white during them. They come without warning, including from sleep, and she avoids nothing. Venlafaxine started eight weeks ago has made them worse. She has lost 6 kg in a year.

data_table.Examination: Pale with cool peripheries, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function normal, fasting glucose 6.9 mmol/L, left ventricular hypertrophy on electrocardiogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase the venlafaxine and add a short benzodiazepine course
Measure plasma free metanephrines, withhold venlafaxine, refer to endocrinology
Commence a non selective beta blocker for the cardiovascular symptoms
Refer for further psychological therapy and add an antihypertensive
Arrange abdominal computed tomography before any biochemical testing

subtopic_detail: Adult requesting assessment for lifelong inattention with no documented childhood history
stem: A 27-year-old software tester describes losing track of tasks, missing deadlines and rereading paragraphs for as long as he can remember. A colleague taking stimulant medication suggested the diagnosis. He drinks alcohol at weekends only and sleeps seven hours.

data_table.Examination: Cooperative, frustrated but reactive affect, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Online self rating scale in the likely range; full blood count and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing to establish the diagnosis
Accept the rating scale, diagnose him today and refer for skills training
Treat as anxiety with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Seek collateral evidence of childhood symptoms before diagnostic assessment
Trial methylphenidate and use the response to confirm the diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Psychosis persisting for several weeks after the mood episode has resolved
stem: A 23-year-old woman was admitted six weeks ago elated, sleeping two hours nightly and convinced she had been chosen to reform banking. Mood and sleep settled within a fortnight. For the past four weeks, while euthymic, she has believed bank staff speak about her in code and has heard two voices commenting on her actions. She has had two similar admissions, living independently between them.

data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative on each admission

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, given the systematised belief about bank staff
Bipolar affective disorder in remission, with slowly resolving psychosis
Schizoaffective disorder, given psychosis persisting while mood is normal
Schizophrenia, with mood symptoms reactive to the psychotic experiences
Substance induced psychotic disorder from unreported stimulant use

subtopic_detail: Return to driving three weeks after a first episode of psychosis while still symptomatic
stem: A 20-year-old apprentice is reviewed three weeks after discharge following a first psychotic episode, treated with risperidone. He has resumed driving to work. He still believes a particular car is following him and feels sedated in the mornings. He holds an unconditional private licence.

data_table.Examination: Alert but slowed, flat mood with reactive affect, persecutory delusion held with moderate conviction, mild bradykinesia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about driving?

options.text: Advise him not to drive now, document this and explain the reporting obligations
Allow private driving if he avoids night driving and long trips
Notify the licensing authority immediately without telling him
Reduce the risperidone and let him drive once he feels alert
Tell him the diagnosis permanently disqualifies him from driving

subtopic_detail: Purging several times weekly at normal body weight with dental erosion in a young adult
stem: A 20-year-old student has made herself vomit after eating for two years, three or four times a week, after episodes of eating far more than she intends. She weighs herself several times daily and judges herself almost entirely on her shape.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, palatal erosion of the upper incisors, mild parotid enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily
Dietitian review with self help materials alone, deferring other treatment
Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and fluoxetine 60 mg daily
Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and sertraline 50 mg daily
Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy and bupropion 150 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Escalating online gambling losses with borrowing and concealment over twelve months
stem: A 42-year-old man attends at his wife's insistence. Over the past year he has bet on sport through a phone application, staking more to recover losses. He has a loan she does not know about, is restless when he tries to stop and has lied about the money. He feels hopeless about the debt but denies intent to harm himself.

data_table.Examination: Mood low with reactive affect, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to a financial counsellor and review him in three months
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the gambling later
Advise blocking software and deposit limits, and review in six weeks
Refer for gambling focused cognitive behavioural therapy and assess suicide risk
Start naltrexone, referring for psychological therapy only if it fails

subtopic_detail: Obsessive compulsive symptoms unchanged after six weeks on a low dose serotonergic antidepressant
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 29-year-old teacher six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg daily for obsessive compulsive disorder. She has intrusive thoughts about contamination and washes her hands until they crack, spending about three hours a day on rituals.

She has taken the tablet every day without missing a dose and reports no adverse effects beyond mild nausea in the first week. She has been on a waiting list for psychological therapy since the last visit and has not yet been seen. She estimates that nothing has changed and asks whether the medication is the wrong one for her.

data_table.Examination: Cracked and erythematous skin over both hands, mood mildly low with reactive affect, obsessions and compulsions described with good insight, no psychotic features, no suicidal ideation
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a regular benzodiazepine to relieve the distress associated with the intrusive thoughts and review her when a therapy appointment becomes available
Increase the sertraline dose and continue for at least twelve weeks at the higher dose before judging whether this medication has failed her
Switch to a different selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a starting dose and review the response after a further six weeks of treatment
Add a low dose antipsychotic as an augmenting agent now and continue the current sertraline dose, reviewing the combination after a further six weeks
Stop the sertraline and rely on exposure and response prevention alone once a place becomes available, reviewing her again when therapy has commenced

subtopic_detail: Mute immobile inpatient with waxy flexibility refusing food for two days
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted eight days ago with a relapse of schizophrenia had his olanzapine increased four days ago. For two days he has not spoken, sits in the same chair for hours and has eaten nothing. When staff raise his arm it stays where they leave it.

data_table.Examination: Mute with staring, posturing against gravity, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, palpable bladder
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (40-320), WCC 8.2 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Stop olanzapine and start bromocriptine with dantrolene for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Give a parenteral lorazepam challenge and observe over the following hours
Increase the olanzapine dose further to treat the underlying psychotic relapse
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy, withholding other psychotropic medication
Start intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding with no medication change

subtopic_detail: Refusal of all food because of a delusion that it has been poisoned
stem: A 51-year-old man with schizophrenia stopped his depot antipsychotic six months ago. At a home visit he has eaten almost nothing for five days, certain that all food and water in the house is contaminated by a neighbour who wants him dead. He refuses hospital, saying nothing is wrong with him.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104 /min, BP 102/64 mmHg with a postural fall
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, weight down 6 kg in four months; oriented, no insight into the risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Assess his capacity and arrange involuntary assessment under the Mental Health Act
Accept his refusal and arrange community mental health follow up this week
Apply to the guardianship tribunal to consent to admission for him
Restart his depot antipsychotic today with his sister's consent
Admit to a medical ward for rehydration, deferring psychiatric assessment

subtopic_detail: Sodium of 121 in a man with schizophrenia who drinks water compulsively through the day
stem: A 46-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia has had a brief generalised seizure on the ward. Staff report he carries a two litre bottle everywhere and drinks from bathroom taps at night. He is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Examination: No focal deficit, no oedema; weight 3.1 kg above yesterday
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 121 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 254 mosmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 84 mosmol/kg, urea 2.1 mmol/L, thyroid function and cortisol normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give hypertonic saline in boluses until the sodium rises by ten mmol/L
Start demeclocycline and continue to allow free access to fluid
Give normal saline with furosemide to remove excess free water
Cease the antipsychotic and observe the sodium over coming days
Restrict fluid with supervision, monitor sodium and record daily weights

subtopic_detail: Sedation and hypersalivation two weeks after a man stable on clozapine stopped smoking
stem: A 38-year-old man stable on clozapine for four years was admitted two weeks ago to a smoke free ward and has not smoked since, having previously smoked 30 a day. He was started on nicotine patches. His mother says he sleeps most of the day, is unsteady on his feet and soaks two pillowcases with saliva each night.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96 /min, BP 108/66 mmHg with postural fall
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, pooling saliva, unsteady gait, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.8 x10^9/L, neutrophils 4.1 x10^9/L, troponin normal, QTc 428 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe an anticholinergic and a morning stimulant for the sedation
Cease clozapine immediately and start another antipsychotic
Advise him to resume smoking at his previous level and review
Measure the plasma clozapine concentration and reduce the dose
Attribute the symptoms to the nicotine patches and cease them

subtopic_detail: Lip smacking and tongue movements after eight years of antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatrist reviewing a 59-year-old woman with schizophrenia who has taken the same first generation antipsychotic for eight years. Her psychotic symptoms have been well controlled and she lives independently.

Her daughter has noticed repetitive chewing and lip smacking movements over the past six months, which stop briefly when attention is drawn to them and disappear during sleep. The woman herself is not distressed by them but has started avoiding meals out because food falls from her mouth. There is no tremor, no rigidity and no subjective restlessness, and she takes no anticholinergic medication.

data_table.Examination: Repetitive chewing, lip smacking and tongue protrusion, mild choreiform movements of the fingers, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no akathisia, gait normal, dentures fit well
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and copper studies within normal limits, magnetic resonance imaging of the brain not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start propranolol titrated to effect for the abnormal movements and review her in six weeks, continuing the current antipsychotic at its present dose
Continue the current treatment unchanged with six monthly movement rating scales, since she reports no distress and her psychotic illness is well controlled
Reduce the dose of the current antipsychotic where the illness allows or switch to an agent with lower risk, and consider a vesicular monoamine transporter inhibitor
Increase the dose of the current antipsychotic, since higher dopamine blockade suppresses the movements and will improve her ability to eat in public
Start benzatropine to counter the abnormal movements and review her in six weeks to assess whether the chewing and lip smacking have improved

subtopic_detail: Neutrophils of 1.2 in a man monitored under a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol on clozapine
stem: A 34-year-old man of West African ancestry has had schizophrenia in remission on clozapine for three years. After haematology review he was registered two years ago under a benign ethnic neutropenia protocol, with baseline neutrophils of 1.3 to 1.6 when well and a normal bone marrow. He feels well, with no fever or sore throat.

data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.2 x10^9/L, WCC 3.6 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), Hb 148 g/L, platelets 262 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and add lithium to raise the neutrophil count
Continue clozapine unchanged and give granulocyte colony stimulating factor
Continue under his modified protocol thresholds, counting more often, with haematology advice
Cease clozapine permanently and start a different antipsychotic this week
Withhold clozapine for a week with daily counts before resuming treatment

subtopic_detail: Waist circumference rising by fourteen centimetres with a fasting glucose of 6.4 after ten months of olanzapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old man in a community clinic ten months after his first episode of psychosis. He has been taking olanzapine and his symptoms have remitted, and he has returned to a part time job.

He tells you he is sleeping well and is pleased with his progress, though his clothes no longer fit. He smokes ten cigarettes a day. He has no personal history of diabetes, and his father developed type 2 diabetes at fifty. He walks his dog most days but has stopped playing indoor soccer.

data_table.Examination: Weight 96 kg having been 78 kg at initiation, body mass index 30 kg/m2, waist circumference 104 cm having been 90 cm at initiation, blood pressure 132/84 mmHg, no acanthosis nigricans, no tremor or rigidity, no abnormal involuntary movements
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), glycated haemoglobin 42 mmol/mol (less than 42), total cholesterol 6.2 mmol/L (less than 5.5), triglycerides 2.8 mmol/L (less than 1.7), high density lipoprotein 0.9 mmol/L (greater than 1.0), liver function and full blood count within normal limits, prolactin 340 mIU/L (less than 400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine unchanged and review his weight and metabolic profile again in twelve months' time
Cease the antipsychotic entirely, since he has been in remission for most of the past ten months
Discuss switching to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic burden, alongside lifestyle support and metformin
Halve the olanzapine dose and add a low dose of quetiapine at night to maintain the overall antipsychotic effect
Refer for bariatric surgery assessment given the weight gain and the developing impairment of glucose tolerance

subtopic_detail: Corrected calcium of 2.72 with a normal lithium level and stable mood after nine years of maintenance treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar conducting an annual review of a 53-year-old woman who has taken lithium for nine years for bipolar affective disorder. She has had no episode of mania or depression in seven years and works full time as a teacher.

She reports mild thirst but no polyuria, no tremor and no nausea. She takes no other regular medication and has not used non-steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. She reports some aching in her wrists and knees and general tiredness which she attributes to the school term.

data_table.Examination: Weight stable at 68 kg, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, fine physiological tremor only, no goitre, no dry skin or hair thinning, no proximal weakness, mood euthymic with normal speech and thought form
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L taken twelve hours post dose (0.6-0.8 maintenance), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90) and stable over five years, estimated glomerular filtration rate 74 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone 3.2 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), corrected calcium 2.72 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 8.4 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for endocrine assessment of hypercalcaemia while continuing lithium and monitoring the calcium
Reduce the lithium dose to achieve a level of 0.4 to 0.5 mmol/L and repeat the calcium in three months
Cease lithium immediately and commence sodium valproate as a substitute mood stabilising agent for her
Attribute the fatigue and aching to subclinical hypothyroidism and commence thyroxine replacement therapy now
Reassure her that these results are expected on long term lithium and repeat the full panel in twelve months

subtopic_detail: Repeated relapse on patches alone in a heavy smoker with treated depression who wants the most effective option
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 47-year-old woman who wants to stop smoking. She smokes twenty five cigarettes a day, lights her first within five minutes of waking, and has made four attempts in the past six years using nicotine patches alone, relapsing each time within a fortnight.

She has a history of recurrent depression, currently well controlled on sertraline for two years with no recent symptoms. She has no history of seizures, no cardiovascular disease and no renal impairment. She has read online that one of the tablets used for quitting causes psychiatric problems and asks you about this directly.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 25 kg/m2, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, chest clear on auscultation, no clubbing, mood euthymic with no suicidal ideation on direct questioning
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry shows a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted with a normal ratio, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to recommend?

options.text: Varenicline commenced one week before her chosen quit date, with review of mood at two and four weeks
Bupropion started two weeks before her quit date and continued for a total of nine weeks of treatment
A higher strength nicotine patch used alone, with the dose increased in proportion to her daily cigarette count
Behavioural counselling through a telephone quit service alone, with no pharmacotherapy prescribed at this stage
A nicotine vaping product obtained on prescription, used as the sole aid for the next three months of her attempt

subtopic_detail: Request to conceive within a year while taking sodium valproate that has controlled mania for six years
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 27-year-old woman with bipolar affective disorder type one who has been stable on sodium valproate for six years, following two admissions with mania before that. She tells you she and her partner hope to start trying for a baby within the next twelve months.

She is currently euthymic, works as a physiotherapist and has good insight into her illness. She has never taken lithium. She uses no contraception at present and says she does not want to risk becoming unwell again, having been in hospital twice.

data_table.Examination: Mood euthymic with reactive affect, no psychotic features, speech normal in rate and volume, sleep seven to eight hours nightly, no suicidal ideation, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function tests and renal function within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the lowest effective dose and add high dose folic acid five milligrams daily before conception
Plan a switch to an alternative mood stabiliser with effective contraception maintained throughout the transition
Stop valproate immediately without replacement and monitor her mood fortnightly until she becomes pregnant
Continue valproate and arrange detailed fetal morphology ultrasound at eighteen weeks once she conceives
Advise her to stop valproate as soon as she has a positive pregnancy test and review her urgently at that point

subtopic_detail: Escalating threats in an emergency department cubicle after verbal de-escalation and an offer of oral medication have failed
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 32-year-old man brought in by police under the state mental health act after neighbours reported him shouting at passing cars. He is known to the service with schizophrenia and stopped his medication three months ago.

He is pacing his cubicle, shouting that staff are working for the people following him, and has punched the wall twice. Two nurses have spent twenty minutes attempting verbal de-escalation and have offered him oral olanzapine, food and a quiet space, all of which he has refused. He is now standing over a nurse with a clenched fist. A security team is present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Grazed knuckles with no deformity, pupils equal at 4 mm and reactive, no ataxia or nystagmus, no head injury reported by police, unable to complete cognitive assessment owing to agitation
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 6.1 mmol/L, point-of-care testing otherwise deferred owing to the level of agitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue verbal de-escalation without medication, since sedation should be avoided in an undifferentiated presentation
Give intravenous midazolam in repeated increments until he is sufficiently settled for a full physical examination
Give intramuscular droperidol with physical restraint only as long as needed, then continuous monitoring afterwards
Ask the police to remove him from the department and return him once he is calm enough to be assessed safely
Place him in mechanical restraints in a seclusion room and observe without giving any medication for four hours

subtopic_detail: QRS duration of 128 milliseconds three hours after an overdose taken with a rising drowsiness and a normal blood pressure
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 19-year-old woman brought in by ambulance three hours after telling her flatmate she had swallowed a handful of her mother's tablets following a relationship breakdown. The flatmate has brought in an empty bottle labelled amitriptyline 50 mg.

She was drowsy but rousable on arrival and has become harder to wake over the last twenty minutes. She has taken no alcohol and no other medication. She has no history of cardiac disease and no previous overdose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 12, pupils dilated at 6 mm and sluggish, skin dry and flushed, bowel sounds reduced, no focal neurological deficit, bladder palpable
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 128 milliseconds and a prominent terminal R wave in lead aVR, venous pH 7.34 (7.32-7.42), bicarbonate 21 mmol/L (22-32), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), paracetamol level not detected, capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and prepare for intubation with ongoing electrocardiographic monitoring
Give intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and improve her conscious state before further assessment
Give intravenous amiodarone to control the tachycardia and reduce the risk of progression to a ventricular rhythm
Administer activated charcoal orally now and repeat the dose in four hours to reduce ongoing drug absorption
Observe with continuous cardiac monitoring and treat only if she develops seizures or a ventricular arrhythmia

subtopic_detail: Three days of mutism with waxy limb posturing and refusal of food in a woman with a long history of severe depression
stem: A 58-year-old woman with recurrent severe depression, who stopped her antidepressant four months ago, was found by her daughter sitting in a chair, not speaking and not eating. She was admitted three days ago and has taken nothing orally for two days. The medical workup is complete.

data_table.Examination: Mute, limbs remain where they are placed, resists passive eye opening, grasps the examiner's hand when asked not to, no rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Bloods, calcium and thyroid function normal; creatine kinase 210 U/L; brain imaging and electroencephalogram unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed encephalitis pending lumbar puncture
Give a lorazepam challenge and observe over ten to thirty minutes
Start an antipsychotic for the posturing of a psychotic depression
Recommence her previous antidepressant at the dose she took before
Insert a nasogastric tube and observe for a further 72 hours

subtopic_detail: Fever with lower limb clonus and hyperreflexia developing within eight hours of a dose increase and a new analgesic
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 41-year-old man brought in by his wife because he has become agitated, sweaty and shaky through the course of today. He has taken sertraline for two years and his general practitioner increased the dose four days ago.

Yesterday he saw a locum for back pain and was prescribed a new analgesic, which he started last night and has taken three doses of. His wife says he was completely well at breakfast and that the shaking began around lunchtime. He takes no other medication and does not use illicit drugs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124 beats per minute, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and restless but oriented, pupils dilated at 6 mm, skin diaphoretic, sustained clonus at both ankles with hyperreflexia more marked in the legs than the arms, no lead-pipe rigidity, tremor of both hands
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 640 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, capillary glucose 6.2 mmol/L, electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with a normal QRS and corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene and commence active cooling, treating this as a malignant hyperthermic reaction
Cease the offending agents, give intravenous benzodiazepines and fluids with active cooling and monitoring
Give intravenous bromocriptine and continue the sertraline, treating this as a neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Give empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and aciclovir after lumbar puncture, treating this as a central nervous infection
Give a single dose of an antipsychotic for the agitation and continue observation on the short stay unit overnight

subtopic_detail: Longstanding inattention with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death before the age of forty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a 14-year-old boy referred with longstanding inattention. Teacher and parent rating scales are concordant, symptoms have been present since early primary school across home and school, and a psychologist has documented impairment in two settings.

His mother mentions in passing that he fainted at football training twice this season, each time while running, and that he recovered within a minute. She adds that her brother died suddenly at thirty eight while jogging and that no cause was ever found. The boy sleeps well and there is no snoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Height and weight on the fiftieth centile, no murmur audible at rest, no abnormal precordial heave, peripheral pulses normal, no marfanoid features, neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence methylphenidate at a low dose and monitor pulse and blood pressure at each subsequent clinic review
Commence atomoxetine instead of a stimulant, on the basis that it does not carry any cardiovascular risk
Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology with an electrocardiogram, deferring stimulant medication until assessed
Arrange behavioural parent training and classroom accommodations, and review the syncope only if it recurs
Arrange a tilt table test to confirm vasovagal syncope before starting stimulant medication for his inattention

subtopic_detail: anticipating a drug level change when a heavy smoker on an antipsychotic metabolised by the same enzyme decides to quit
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 38-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine for three years with no positive symptoms and is working part time. He smokes thirty cigarettes a day and has decided to stop, motivated by a friend's recent heart attack.

His most recent clozapine level two months ago was in the mid therapeutic range and his white cell count and absolute neutrophil count have been within normal limits at every monitoring visit. He takes no other regular medication, drinks no alcohol and uses no caffeine beyond one coffee daily. He has no constipation and no sedation at present. He tells you he wants to stop abruptly this weekend and asks whether there is anything he should know. His observations and physical examination are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: No sedation, no sialorrhoea, no abdominal distension, bowels opening daily
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level in the mid therapeutic range two months ago, white cell count and absolute neutrophil count within normal limits
data_table.Substance use: Thirty cigarettes daily, no alcohol, one coffee daily

lead_in: What is the most important action as he stops smoking?

options.text: Advise him to delay the quit attempt until his mental state has been stable for a further twelve months
Monitor the clozapine level closely and reduce the dose as required in the weeks after cessation
Monitor the clozapine level closely and increase the dose as required in the weeks after cessation
Advise against nicotine replacement therapy because it maintains the enzyme induction he is losing
Increase the frequency of white cell and neutrophil monitoring because cessation raises agranulocytosis risk

subtopic_detail: first line treatment choice for post-traumatic symptoms in a resettled refugee who requires an interpreter and has ongoing visa uncertainty
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic. A 34-year-old man who arrived in Australia two years ago as a refugee attends with his cousin, who has been translating for him at appointments. He describes nightmares about detention and beatings, waking sweating most nights, and avoiding the news and any uniformed officer.

He startles violently at doors closing, feels constantly on edge, and has stopped attending English classes because crowds frighten him. These symptoms have been present since arrival and have not improved. He has no current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms and no alcohol or other substance use. He sleeps about four hours a night. His visa status is unresolved and he has a hearing in five months. He has no medical comorbidity, takes no medication, and physical examination and observations are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, hypervigilant, startles to noise outside the room, no psychomotor retardation, physical examination within normal limits
data_table.Mental state: No current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, no substance use, sleeping about four hours nightly
data_table.Social: Resettled refugee, unresolved visa status with a hearing in five months, attending with a family member interpreting

lead_in: What would you recommend first?

options.text: Deferral of all treatment until his visa hearing concludes, with supportive review every month
A single session of structured debriefing about the detention experiences followed by watchful waiting
Trauma-focused psychological therapy with a professional interpreter engaged for every session
A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a standard starting dose with review in four weeks
A short course of a benzodiazepine at night to restore sleep before any other intervention is started

subtopic_detail: initial response to an adolescent disclosing persistent gender incongruence with coexisting low mood in a general clinic
stem: A 15-year-old assigned female at birth has identified as male since age eleven and used he and him pronouns for three years. He binds his chest daily and is distressed by breast development and menstruation. His mood has been low most days for three months.

data_table.Mental state: Anhedonia, passive thoughts that life is not worth living without plan, no self-harm
data_table.Social: Attending school, family supportive, socially transitioned for three years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue in clinic today
Advise the family to discourage social transition for now
Arrange a karyotype and hormonal profile before referral
Treat the depression while referring to a specialist gender service
Treat the depression first, revisiting gender distress after recovery

subtopic_detail: weight to give a written advance care directive when a NSW patient is later detained and objects to one medication
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar admitting a 44-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, detained in a NSW mental health facility with persecutory delusions and four nights without sleep. Eighteen months ago, while well, she wrote an advance care directive declining olanzapine because of weight gain and preferring aripiprazole, which has worked twice. She nominated her sister as designated carer. She now refuses oral medication and has thrown a chair.

data_table.Mental state: Persecutory delusions about staff, agitated, refusing oral medication
data_table.Investigations: Observations and physical examination normal, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: How should her directive influence your prescribing?

options.text: Disregard it, since detention overrides any previously recorded treatment preference
Disregard it, since a directive lapses twelve months after it is written
Follow it only if her designated carer agrees with the preference recorded
Follow it only if she can explain and confirm the preference right now
Prescribe her preferred agent unless contraindicated, recording your reasoning

subtopic_detail: disposition decision for a patient with repeated superficial self-harm presentations who requests admission during a crisis
stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with superficial forearm lacerations after an argument, now sutured. This is her fifth presentation in three months. She has borderline personality disorder and asks to be admitted because she cannot face going home.

data_table.Mental state: Settling, no current suicidal intent or plan, not intoxicated
data_table.History: Weekly dialectical behaviour therapy, two sessions missed; three previous admissions each followed by escalating self-harm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Structured safety plan and return to her therapy team this week
Admission to an acute inpatient unit for containment and observation
A benzodiazepine for crisis use with clinic follow up next month
Start a mood stabiliser for affective instability and review in two weeks
Discharge with advice to return only if suicidal intent develops

subtopic_detail: collapse at a dance event with hyperthermia and a low sodium after a recreational stimulant and large volumes of water
stem: An 18-year-old woman is brought in from a music festival after a seizure lasting ninety seconds. Friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy four hours ago, danced continuously and drank large volumes of water. She is drowsy and confused.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 136 /min, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, temperature 40.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, flushed and diaphoretic
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145), creatine kinase 3200 units/L (40-200)

lead_in: What are the two most urgent interventions?

options.text: Mannitol for cerebral oedema and phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis
Hypertonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling
Isotonic saline for the sodium and active external cooling
Fluid restriction for the sodium and paracetamol for the fever
Hypertonic saline for the sodium and dantrolene as first line

subtopic_detail: reframing a long history of anxiety and burnout in an adult woman whose difficulties are better explained by lifelong social camouflaging
stem: A 29-year-old woman has had generalised anxiety and recurrent depression since age 19, with partial response to two antidepressants and cognitive behavioural therapy. She rehearses conversations, copies colleagues' mannerisms and needs two days alone after a work social event. She has lifelong intense interests in timetables, finds seams and fluorescent lighting painful, and eats the same four meals.

data_table.History: School reports described her as quiet with no concerns; exhausted since a recent promotion
data_table.Mental state: No psychotic symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a low dose antipsychotic for her sensory symptoms and rigid eating
Reassure her that her normal school reports exclude the diagnosis
Refer for a developmental history and neurodevelopmental assessment
Switch to a third antidepressant from a different class
Refer for assessment of an emerging personality disorder

subtopic_detail: explaining a positive bedside inconsistency sign to a patient with sudden leg weakness and normal imaging
stem: A 41-year-old woman developed sudden right leg weakness five days ago and cannot weight bear. She has no psychiatric history and says she was told the scans were normal so nothing is wrong.

data_table.Examination: Give-way weakness of right hip flexion, right hip extends involuntarily on resisted left hip flexion, sensory loss ending abruptly at the inguinal crease
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance brain and whole spine, nerve conduction studies and inflammatory markers all normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Document suspected feigning and arrange covert observation
Repeat the spinal imaging with contrast before explaining
Start an antidepressant and review her mood in four weeks
Explain the positive bedside sign and refer for physiotherapy
Explain that the investigations are normal and discharge her

subtopic_detail: fever and tachycardia in the third week of an antipsychotic titration where the cardiac and neuroleptic explanations require different immediate actions
stem: A 27-year-old man on day 18 of a clozapine titration, now 250 mg at night, has two days of fever, lethargy and vomiting. He has treatment resistant schizophrenia.

data_table.Examination: Alert, normal tone with no rigidity or clonus, no focal infective source
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), C-reactive protein 68 mg/L (<5), troponin I 640 nanograms/L (<20), creatine kinase 190 units/L (40-200)
data_table.Cardiac: Echocardiogram ejection fraction 44 per cent with global hypokinesis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cease clozapine, start bromocriptine and dantrolene, and transfer to intensive care
Continue clozapine, attribute the fever to benign pyrexia and monitor daily
Cease clozapine and start broad spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis
Withhold two doses and resume at a lower dose with weekly troponin
Cease clozapine permanently, transfer for cardiac monitoring and involve cardiology

subtopic_detail: choosing smoking cessation pharmacotherapy for a heavily dependent smoker with treated depression and a previous failed nicotine patch attempt
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 48-year-old man who wants to stop smoking. He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 17 and lights his first within five minutes of waking.

He made one attempt two years ago using a 21 mg nicotine patch alone and relapsed at day four with strong cravings, particularly in the evenings. He has major depressive disorder that has been stable for three years on sertraline 100 mg daily, with no hospital admissions and no self-harm. He drinks two standard drinks most nights and has no other substance use. He has no seizure history, no eating disorder, and his renal function is within normal limits. He is motivated and has set a quit date in three weeks' time, and he asks what will give him the best chance this time.

data_table.Smoking history: 25 cigarettes daily for 31 years, first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking, one previous attempt with patch monotherapy relapsing at day 4
data_table.Mental health: Major depressive disorder stable for 3 years on sertraline 100 mg daily, no admissions or self-harm
data_table.Investigations: Renal and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy would you recommend as first line for this quit attempt?

options.text: Varenicline commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
A 21 mg nicotine patch commenced on the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
Bupropion commenced one week before the quit date and continued for twelve weeks
Nicotine lozenges used on demand for cravings without any scheduled background therapy
Increasing the sertraline to 150 mg daily as antidepressants also assist smoking cessation

subtopic_detail: responding to a rising thyroid stimulating hormone on long term lithium in a patient whose mood has been stable for years
stem: A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for nine years with no mood episode for seven years. Over four months she has felt the cold, gained 5 kg and become constipated.

data_table.Examination: Small diffuse non-tender goitre, dry skin, delayed ankle reflex relaxation
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6 to 0.8), thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free thyroxine 9.8 pmol/L (10 to 26)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for thyroid ultrasound and fine needle aspiration
Continue lithium and start thyroxine titrated to thyroid function
Cease lithium, switch to sodium valproate and recheck thyroid function
Reduce the lithium dose to achieve a level near 0.4 mmol/L
Repeat thyroid function in three months before treating

subtopic_detail: advising an adult newly started on a stimulant about driving obligations and dose timing for shift work
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27-year-old man four weeks after starting methylphenidate for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder diagnosed this year. He reports better focus at work, is sleeping adequately, and has had no appetite loss beyond a mild reduction at lunch.

He drives a courier van for a living on a commercial licence and works rotating shifts including a night shift block every third week. He asks whether he has to tell anyone about the medication, and says a workmate told him that being on a stimulant would cost him his licence. He has no history of substance misuse, no cardiac symptoms, and no family history of sudden cardiac death. His blood pressure today is 128/78 with a pulse of 82, unchanged from baseline, and his weight is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: No tremor, normal cardiovascular examination, weight unchanged from baseline
data_table.Treatment: Methylphenidate started 4 weeks ago with symptomatic improvement and adequate sleep
data_table.Occupation: Commercial licence courier driver on rotating shifts including night shift every third week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about his driving?

options.text: Notification is only required if he has a crash or receives an infringement while taking the medication
He should switch to atomoxetine, since non stimulant treatment removes any notification requirement
He must notify the driver licensing authority, and treated stable illness is generally compatible with driving
No notification is required because stimulant medication is prescribed and lawfully obtained
He should stop driving commercially while taking any stimulant and change to a private licence

subtopic_detail: identifying the medication cause of a low sodium in an older adult started on an antidepressant three weeks earlier
stem: A 76-year-old woman started sertraline 50 mg daily three weeks ago for a first depressive episode. Her daughter reports three days of muddled thinking, unsteadiness and a fall. She also takes perindopril, unchanged for six years.

data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no postural drop, unsteady gait; abbreviated mental test score 6 out of 10, previously 9
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 119 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 468 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline, give intravenous sodium chloride and recheck the sodium
Switch to mirtazapine today and leave fluid intake unchanged
Arrange computed tomography of the head before changing medication
Cease sertraline, restrict fluid and recheck the sodium in 48 hours
Continue sertraline, cease perindopril and recheck the sodium in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: choosing between behavioural and pharmacological treatment for long standing sleep onset difficulty maintained by compensatory habits
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 39-year-old teacher who has had difficulty falling asleep for the past 14 months, most nights of the week. She takes about 90 minutes to get to sleep and feels unrefreshed and irritable during the day.

Her sleep diary shows she goes to bed at 9 pm to give herself the best chance, stays in bed reading on her phone until she feels sleepy, gets up at 6.30 am, and naps for 40 minutes most afternoons. She drinks one coffee at breakfast and none after midday. She has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas and her partner confirms this, no restless legs, and no low mood, anhedonia or anxiety on direct questioning. Her thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits and she takes no regular medication. She asks for something to help her sleep.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, Mallampati class 1, no goitre
data_table.Sleep diary: Bed at 9 pm, sleep onset latency about 90 minutes, rise at 6.30 am, afternoon nap of about 40 minutes most days, total sleep time about 6 hours in 9.5 hours in bed
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What would you recommend as first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night for two weeks with a plan to review and taper
Prescribe modified release melatonin 2 mg nightly for thirteen weeks with review at completion
Prescribe low dose amitriptyline 10 mg at night and review the response in four weeks
Arrange overnight polysomnography before deciding on treatment for her sleep difficulty
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including stimulus control and sleep restriction

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a persistent grief reaction from a depressive episode fourteen months after a bereavement
stem: A 58-year-old woman is referred 14 months after her adult son died in a workplace accident. She yearns for him daily, spends hours with his photographs, has kept his bedroom unchanged and avoids their mutual friends.

data_table.Symptoms: Yearning, preoccupation and identity disruption, present most days for 14 months
data_table.Negative findings: Appetite, sleep and enjoyment of gardening preserved; no guilt or suicidal ideation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for grief focused psychotherapy targeting the loss and avoidance
Start an antidepressant and review the response in six weeks
Reassure her that this is normal grief and review in six months
Prescribe a short benzodiazepine course for distress at home
Refer for eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing for the death

subtopic_detail: recognising a motor syndrome mistaken for worsening psychosis when antipsychotic escalation has made it worse
stem: A 24-year-old man admitted eight days ago with relapsed schizophrenia had olanzapine increased from 10 mg to 20 mg daily four days ago. Over 48 hours he has stopped speaking and eats only when food is placed in his mouth.

data_table.Examination: Mute and immobile, holds a posture in which his arm is placed, resists passive movement with matching force, echolalia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (60 to 220)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start nasogastric feeding and reassess the mental state afterwards
Withhold the olanzapine and give a lorazepam challenge
Increase the olanzapine to 30 mg daily for negative symptoms
Start intravenous dantrolene and bromocriptine in a high dependency bed
Arrange urgent brain imaging and lumbar puncture before treatment

subtopic_detail: reviewing an established anticonvulsant mood stabiliser when a woman of reproductive age discloses she is no longer using contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for four years and has had no mood episode in three years, having previously had two manic admissions.

Today she tells you she stopped her oral contraceptive three months ago because she and her partner would like to start a family within the year, and she has not told anyone at the service. She has had no mood symptoms, sleeps well and is working. She takes no other medication and no folate supplement. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test in clinic today is negative. She asks whether she should just keep taking the valproate until she actually falls pregnant and then stop it.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative today, full blood count and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Medication and history: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years, no mood episode for 3 years, two previous manic admissions, contraception ceased 3 months ago, no folate supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue valproate and restart reliable contraception, deferring pregnancy until the illness is longer in remission
Cease valproate today and manage her without any mood stabiliser while she tries to conceive
Plan a switch to a mood stabiliser suitable in pregnancy and start high dose folate now
Continue valproate and stop it as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive, with folate then
Continue valproate at a reduced dose of 500 mg daily with high dose folate supplementation

subtopic_detail: selecting parenteral sedation for escalating aggression after verbal measures and oral medication have been refused
stem: A 32-year-old man brought in by police is pacing, shouting and has kicked a trolley across the corridor. Twenty minutes of de-escalation has failed and he has twice refused oral olanzapine. Police report three days of methamphetamine use. No electrocardiogram has been possible. He now advances on a nurse with a clenched fist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, no focal signs or head injury
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management now?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly, repeated every 10 minutes until sedated
Withhold sedation until an electrocardiogram excludes a prolonged QT interval
Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly with anaesthetic support on standby
Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous monitoring after restraint
Offer oral diazepam 10 mg with a further period of verbal de-escalation

subtopic_detail: selecting first line treatment for involuntary movements and vocalisations in an adolescent whose school is demanding they be stopped
stem: A 13-year-old boy's school asks that his shoulder shrugging, eye blinking and throat clearing be stopped because they disrupt the classroom. They began at age seven, different ones come and go over months, and they are worse when he is tired. He can hold them back briefly but the urge builds until he lets it out.

data_table.Examination: Movements observed, suppressible with rebound, no chorea, normal tone
data_table.Negative findings: No obsessions or compulsions, no academic or social impairment, only mild distress to him

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence risperidone and titrate against the frequency of the movements
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for compulsive behaviour
Advise suppression in class and reward successful suppression at home
Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging and an antistreptolysin O titre
Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention with habit reversal training

subtopic_detail: responding to new agitation in residential care when an antipsychotic is requested and a reversible precipitant has not been sought
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to prescribe risperidone for an 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease who has become agitated and resistive over the past five days, shouting during personal care and pushing a carer's hand away during showering.

He has lived there for two years with no previous behavioural concerns and no history of aggression. Staff say the behaviour happens almost entirely during showering and toileting and that he settles within minutes once left alone in his chair. They report he has been eating less and that his urine has smelled strong, although a dipstick two days ago showed leucocytes with no nitrites and he has no fever or dysuria. He started oxybutynin three weeks ago for urinary frequency, prescribed by a locum. His usual medications are donepezil, perindopril and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 126/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Calm when seated, distressed only during personal care, dry mouth, abdomen soft with a fullness suprapubically, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick two days ago with leucocytes and no nitrites, no fever or dysuria
data_table.Medications: Donepezil, perindopril, atorvastatin, and oxybutynin started 3 weeks ago for urinary frequency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for a reversible precipitant including urinary retention and review the oxybutynin
Start trimethoprim 300 mg at night for seven days to treat a urinary tract infection
Start oxazepam 7.5 mg before showering to reduce distress during personal care episodes
Increase the donepezil dose and arrange review by the dementia behaviour advisory service
Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the behaviour after two weeks of treatment

subtopic_detail: deciding on inpatient medical admission for a young person with restrictive eating when the weight alone does not meet the usual threshold
stem: A 17-year-old woman has six months of food restriction and compulsive exercise. She weighs 52 kg at 168 cm (body mass index 18.4), down from 68 kg six months ago, and insists she is not underweight. She fainted once while running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38 /min sitting, blood pressure 98/56 sitting and 74/48 standing, temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cool peripheries, lanugo hair, cannot rise from a squat unaided
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), corrected QT interval 468 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluoxetine with psychiatric outpatient follow up in two weeks
Urgent medical admission for cardiac monitoring and refeeding
Outpatient family based treatment with weekly weight and electrolytes
Oral potassium replacement, stop running and review in one week
Reassurance that her body mass index is healthy, with dietitian review

subtopic_detail: attributing persistent psychotic symptoms between mood episodes when a stimulant history offers a competing explanation
stem: A 29-year-old man has two years of case notes recording three episodes: two of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting about a month each, and one depressive episode of ten weeks. He believed a government agency was inserting thoughts into his mind during all three. He used methamphetamine two to three times a week until fourteen months ago.

data_table.Course: Euthymic for four months with normal sleep, activity and speech, while thought insertion and a commenting voice have continued throughout
data_table.Substance history: Fortnightly supervised urine drug screens negative for fourteen months
data_table.Treatment: Quetiapine 400 mg at night throughout, no missed doses on pharmacy records

lead_in: Which diagnosis best accounts for this presentation?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
Schizoaffective disorder of the bipolar type
Methamphetamine induced psychotic disorder
Schizophrenia with a superimposed depressive episode

subtopic_detail: Recognition and initial management of lithium toxicity precipitated by an NSAID interaction
stem: A 42-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has one week of tremor and drowsiness. She has taken lithium 900 mg nocte for six years, stable at 0.7 mmol/L. Two weeks ago she started ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor, 3 beats ankle clonus, ataxic gait, no rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Whole bowel irrigation via nasogastric tube for 6 hours
Reduce lithium to 450 mg nocte and stop the ibuprofen
Activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube, then observe
Stop lithium and ibuprofen, intravenous saline, nephrology review
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine

subtopic_detail: Recognition and immediate management of serotonin syndrome from an SSRI plus tramadol co-prescription
stem: A 38-year-old man taking sertraline 100 mg daily has two days of tremor, agitation and diarrhoea. Tramadol 50 mg four times daily was started four days ago.

data_table.Neurology: Agitated, diaphoretic, dilated pupils; spontaneous ankle clonus, hyperreflexia lower more than upper limbs, no rigidity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Intravenous methylene blue, with intensive care admission for monitoring
Intramuscular bromocriptine and dantrolene, then intubation for muscle rigidity
Intramuscular haloperidol for agitation, continuing both drugs at reduced dose
Intravenous flumazenil for assumed benzodiazepine co-ingestion, pending drug screen
Stop sertraline and tramadol, give diazepam, cool actively, consider cyproheptadine

subtopic_detail: Interpretation of clozapine haematological monitoring and decision to continue or interrupt therapy
stem: A 34-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg nocte for four years. He is well, with no fever or sore throat. Routine 4-weekly bloods were taken yesterday.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in clozapine management?

options.text: Empirical filgrastim daily for five days, continuing clozapine unchanged
Stop clozapine and admit for daily full blood counts and antibiotics
Reduce clozapine to 300 mg nocte with monthly full blood counts
Continue clozapine, repeat the count in a week, screen for infection
Stop clozapine and switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte the same day

subtopic_detail: Choice of benzodiazepine for alcohol withdrawal in the setting of established cirrhotic liver disease
stem: A 58-year-old man has drunk 15 standard drinks daily for 20 years and stopped 36 hours ago. He has alcoholic cirrhosis with a MELD of 14. He is agitated and diaphoretic with visual hallucinations of small animals.

data_table.Mental state: Alcohol Withdrawal Scale 14, coarse tremor, no seizures, no encephalopathy
data_table.Bloods: Platelets 82 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, albumin 28 g/L, bilirubin 40 micromol/L

lead_in: Which benzodiazepine regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intramuscular midazolam 5 mg two hourly
Oral diazepam 20 mg every two hours
Oral oxazepam 30 mg every four hours
Oral chlordiazepoxide 25 mg every four hours
Intravenous phenobarbital 130 mg two hourly

subtopic_detail: First-line antidepressant selection and monitoring in a depressed adolescent with suicidal ideation but no intent
stem: A 15-year-old girl has eight weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and 3 kg weight loss. She has passive thoughts of not wanting to wake up, with no plan or intent. Six weeks of weekly cognitive behavioural therapy has not helped. She has never taken psychotropic medication.

data_table.Mental state: Tearful, psychomotor slowing, hopelessness, no psychotic features
data_table.History: No family history of bipolar disorder

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral sertraline 25 mg daily titrated to 50 mg
Oral fluoxetine 10 mg daily titrated to 20 mg
Oral venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily titrated to 75 mg
Continue psychological therapy and defer pharmacotherapy
Admit to an adolescent inpatient psychiatric unit

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic choice in a first-episode psychosis in a young man with metabolic and adherence considerations
stem: A 21-year-old man has six weeks of paranoid delusions that his housemates are poisoning his food, third person auditory hallucinations and social withdrawal. He has smoked five to ten cones of cannabis daily for three years. He says he will not take a medication that causes weight gain.

data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.4%, QTc 420 ms, urine cannabinoids only

lead_in: Which oral antipsychotic is most appropriate to commence?

options.text: Olanzapine 5 mg at night, increased to 10 mg after one week
Aripiprazole 10 mg daily, increased to 15 mg after one week
Haloperidol 2 mg twice daily, increased to 5 mg twice daily
Risperidone 1 mg twice daily, increased to 3 mg twice daily
Clozapine 12.5 mg daily, titrated upwards over two weeks

subtopic_detail: Emergency department risk assessment and disposition for repeated self-harm in emotionally unstable personality disorder
stem: A 26-year-old woman with emotionally unstable personality disorder presents after superficial cutting of the forearm, her fifth presentation in three months, each after an interpersonal stressor. She attends weekly dialectical behaviour therapy, and her case manager agrees she is at her usual baseline.

data_table.Wound: Superficial, clean edges, no sutures needed
data_table.Mental state: Tearful, denies suicidal ideation, not intoxicated
data_table.Supports: Mother and partner at home overnight, safety plan in her bag

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with next-day case manager contact and safety plan review
Admit involuntarily to an acute psychiatric unit for 72 hours
Admit to a short stay unit and start quetiapine 100 mg nocte
Admit voluntarily to a psychiatric intensive care unit for 48 hours
Discharge with general practitioner review next week and no other contact

subtopic_detail: Recognition and management of refeeding hypophosphataemia during nutritional rehabilitation of severe anorexia nervosa
stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa was admitted 48 hours ago for nutritional rehabilitation at a body mass index of 12.8 kg/m2. Nasogastric feeding began at 20 kcal/kg/day. She reports new fatigue and leg weakness.

data_table.Bloods (48 h): Phosphate 0.42 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.0), potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease the feed and give intravenous dextrose with intravenous phosphate
Continue the feed at 20 kcal/kg/day and give oral phosphate three times daily
Increase the feed to 40 kcal/kg/day and give oral phosphate twice daily
Reduce the feed to 10 kcal/kg/day and give intravenous phosphate, magnesium and potassium
Continue the feed and defer correction until phosphate falls below 0.3 mmol/L

subtopic_detail: Second-generation antipsychotic metabolic monitoring schedule
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 29-year-old man 3 months after commencing olanzapine 15 mg orally each evening for a first episode of schizophrenia. He has stopped hearing voices and is looking for work. His weight has risen from 82 kg to 90 kg over the 3 months, his waist circumference is 102 cm, and he smokes 10 cigarettes daily. He has no personal or family history of diabetes and does not drink alcohol.

Baseline fasting glucose was 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and fasting lipids were within normal limits. Blood pressure today is 132/84 mmHg. He asks how often he now needs blood tests since he is feeling well and has commenced full-time TAFE study.

data_table.Weight trajectory: 82 kg baseline to 90 kg at 3 months; waist circumference 102 cm
data_table.Baseline metabolics: Fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); fasting lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate metabolic monitoring plan at this visit?

options.text: Repeat fasting glucose and lipids now, then every 3 months for the first year on treatment
Defer any fasting bloods until 12 months after commencement then repeat glucose and lipids
Order an oral glucose tolerance test today and only recheck fasting bloods if the OGTT is impaired
Rely on annual GP well person checks for metabolic surveillance while he remains on olanzapine
Measure only weight and blood pressure quarterly and skip fasting bloods while glucose remains normal

subtopic_detail: Ward monitoring for deterioration in treated catatonia
stem: A 41-year-old man with catatonia has improved partly on regular lorazepam and stays on the mental health unit. You are writing his monitoring plan for the coming days.

data_table.Observations: HR 92, BP 126/78, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 37.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Four hourly temperature and pulse with a daily creatine kinase
Daily weight, a fluid balance chart and a weekly full blood count
Continuous cardiac monitoring with twelve hourly electrocardiograms
Daily electroencephalography until the catatonic signs resolve
Twice weekly observations and a repeat computed tomography scan

subtopic_detail: Managing a lapse after the quit date
stem: A 41-year-old woman stopped smoking five weeks ago on varenicline with Quitline support. At a party on Saturday she smoked three cigarettes and has not smoked since. She telephones, upset, asking whether to stop the medicine.

data_table.Treatment: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily, week 5 of 12
data_table.Since the lapse: No cigarettes for three days; cravings mild

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Continue varenicline to twelve weeks and review the triggers with her
Stop varenicline and restart the whole course after a new quit date
Continue varenicline and add a 21 mg nicotine patch for cover
Stop varenicline and switch to bupropion for the remaining weeks
Continue varenicline and extend the course to twenty-four weeks from today

subtopic_detail: Lithium chronic toxicity precipitants
stem: A 62-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly for 24 years has three days of nausea, coarse tremor and unsteady gait, with confusion today. Her general practitioner added ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily 10 days ago. She has also been drinking cranberry juice.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor, truncal ataxia
data_table.Bloods: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L (was 0.7); urea 12.4 mmol/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 78)

lead_in: Which is the most likely precipitant of this toxicity?

options.text: Age related decline in glomerular filtration rate over 24 years of treatment
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory blockade of prostaglandins reducing renal lithium clearance
Cranberry juice inducing hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 metabolism of lithium
Sodium depletion redistributing lithium from erythrocytes to the plasma
Cumulative interstitial nephritis from decades of lithium causing tubular resistance

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnostic criteria and functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practice registrar assessing a 27-year-old graphic designer who describes lifelong difficulty finishing projects, chronic lateness, and losing wallets and keys weekly. She was described in Year 4 school reports as bright but not applying herself. She has been terminated from two jobs in the last 3 years for missed deadlines and now spends most weekend evenings catching up on work she was unable to complete on weekdays. She has never taken stimulant medication.

She scored 5 on the PHQ-9, 4 on the GAD-7, and 22 on the Adult ADHD Self Report Scale part A. Her collateral history from her mother confirms restlessness and inattention in primary school despite average academic ability. She uses no alcohol, cannabis, or stimulants. Thyroid function, ferritin, and full blood count are within normal limits. She asks whether she meets criteria for adult ADHD.

data_table.Onset history: Restlessness and inattention documented from Year 4 reports and by mother
