data_table.Functional impairment: Two employment terminations in 3 years; weekend catch up work

lead_in: Which criterion is the most decisive in confirming DSM-5 adult ADHD in this presentation?

options.text: Symptoms present in more than one setting with clear functional impairment and childhood onset
A positive Adult ADHD Self Report Scale total score above 20 with contemporaneous PHQ-9 below 10
A positive short trial response to methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily over 2 weeks
An informant confirmed history of restlessness during adolescence rather than primary school onset
Neuropsychological testing showing global working memory in the low average range on formal measures

subtopic_detail: Borderline personality disorder first line treatment
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman on the second visit after her third emergency department presentation this year with self cutting. Her forearms show 20 or more parallel superficial cuts of varying age. She describes 5 years of unstable relationships, intense fear of abandonment, chronic emptiness, dissociative episodes lasting hours after arguments, and impulsive spending. She meets 7 of the 9 DSM-5 borderline personality disorder criteria.

Her mood is reactive rather than sustained: PHQ-9 12, GAD-7 14. She has no manic history and no psychotic symptoms. She uses alcohol only socially, no illicit substances. She has been prescribed quetiapine 100 mg nightly by her GP and sertraline 50 mg daily by a previous psychiatrist; she reports neither helped. She asks what treatment is actually going to help.

data_table.Presentations this year: Three ED attendances with self cutting
data_table.Current medications: Quetiapine 100 mg nocte; sertraline 50 mg daily (both unhelpful)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate primary treatment recommendation?

options.text: Add low dose olanzapine 5 mg nightly for mood instability and emptiness while continuing sertraline
Refer for structured, time limited psychotherapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy or mentalisation based therapy
Admit to the acute psychiatric inpatient unit for a planned 4 to 6 week stabilisation and behavioural monitoring
Increase sertraline to 200 mg daily and reassess for reduction in cutting frequency in 6 weeks
Refer to a private hypnotherapist for weekly regression work on early attachment relationships

subtopic_detail: Electroconvulsive therapy pre-anaesthesia considerations
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar planning a course of electroconvulsive therapy for a 68-year-old woman with severe treatment resistant depression (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale 32) who has stopped eating and lost 12 percent body weight over 2 months. She has failed sequential trials of sertraline, venlafaxine, mirtazapine and lithium augmentation. She has a history of atrial fibrillation on apixaban 5 mg twice daily, hypertension on perindopril, and had a coronary artery bypass graft 5 years ago. Her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 52 percent.

She had an anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago with complete recovery of neurological function. Her partner has consented on her behalf under the Mental Health Act after a formal capacity assessment. Vital signs are pulse 78 regular, blood pressure 148/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C.

data_table.Depression severity: HDRS 32; 12 percent weight loss in 2 months; stopped eating
data_table.Cardiac history: AF on apixaban; CABG 5 years ago; EF 52 percent
data_table.Recent event: Anterior circulation ischaemic stroke 4 weeks ago, complete recovery
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 148/86, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate action before proceeding with ECT?

options.text: Cancel the ECT course permanently because recent ischaemic stroke is an absolute contraindication
Continue apixaban unchanged as it does not increase risk during ECT and requires no perioperative planning
Substitute intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg with sertraline 200 mg orally as an alternative treatment plan
Proceed with ECT tomorrow because delaying more than 4 weeks after stroke removes the elevated risk
Defer ECT until at least 4 to 6 weeks post stroke with cardiology and neurology review of risk

subtopic_detail: Valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy prevention
stem:
You are the outpatient psychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder currently well on sodium valproate 1000 mg orally twice daily for 3 years, and lithium was previously stopped for polyuria. She has had no manic or depressive episodes for 26 months and is engaged to be married. She and her partner would like to start trying to conceive in the next 12 months. She has never previously discussed contraception with her psychiatrist. Her partner uses condoms inconsistently.

Her weight is 74 kg, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and full blood count, electrolytes, and liver function tests are within normal limits. She has no personal or family history of neural tube defects. She is very concerned that any change in medication will trigger a relapse and asks what to do next.

data_table.Current medication: Sodium valproate 1000 mg twice daily for 3 years
data_table.Mood stability: No manic or depressive episodes for 26 months
data_table.Contraception: Condoms used inconsistently by partner only

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Refer urgently for perinatal psychiatry review to plan a switch to a safer mood stabiliser preconception
Continue valproate at the current dose and add high dose folate 5 mg daily until conception
Cease valproate abruptly today and start lamotrigine 25 mg daily titrated over the next 6 weeks
Continue valproate but add long-acting reversible contraception until she stops planning pregnancy
Reduce valproate to 500 mg twice daily to lower teratogenic risk and continue at this dose during pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic discrimination among short duration psychoses
stem:
You are the community mental health team registrar reviewing a 22-year-old university student 3 weeks after his acute admission for hearing derogatory voices, believing his housemates were poisoning his water, and 4 days of not sleeping. He had never before had psychiatric contact. On admission urine drug screen was negative and MRI brain was unremarkable. He was started on olanzapine 10 mg nightly and voices and delusions resolved within 8 days; sleep normalised.

He was discharged home after 12 days with complete symptom resolution. He remains well today with no residual positive or negative symptoms. Total duration of psychotic symptoms from onset to full resolution was 12 days. He has no family history of psychotic illness, no substance use in the last 6 months confirmed by hair testing at admission, and no recent bereavement or trauma. He asks what the diagnostic label is now.

data_table.Symptom duration: 12 days total from onset to resolution
data_table.Response: Complete resolution on olanzapine 10 mg within 8 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic label at this stage?

options.text: Schizophrenia with active phase symptoms controlled by second generation antipsychotic therapy
Schizophreniform disorder with good prognostic features and complete symptom resolution on therapy
Brief psychotic disorder with symptom duration between 1 day and 1 month with return to prior functioning
Substance induced psychotic disorder related to unreported hallucinogen exposure prior to admission
Delusional disorder with persecutory type since his beliefs about being poisoned were the dominant feature

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance rapid tranquillisation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in the emergency department attending a 34-year-old woman brought in by police after threatening staff at a supermarket. She is known to services with schizoaffective disorder, currently on paliperidone long-acting injection given 5 weeks ago. She is pacing, shouting, and refusing all oral medications. Verbal de-escalation over 15 minutes has been unsuccessful. She has no known allergies, is not pregnant (bhCG negative from urine), has never had NMS, and is otherwise physically well.

Vital signs (obtained during a brief cooperative moment) are pulse 108, blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Point-of-care glucose 6.2 mmol/L. Weight is estimated at 65 kg. Security officers and 4 nursing staff are present. There is no intravenous access.

data_table.Presentation: Agitated, pacing, verbally threatening; refuses oral medication
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 138/86, RR 22, SpO2 97% RA, temp 36.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial parenteral pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg alone as monotherapy without concurrent benzodiazepine at this time
Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg concurrently with intramuscular midazolam 5 mg into the same deltoid muscle
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg with promethazine 50 mg in a single deltoid muscle injection
Intramuscular ziprasidone 20 mg pending intravenous access for potential propofol induction if needed
Intramuscular ketamine 4 mg per kg as a single dose to achieve immediate dissociative sedation onset

subtopic_detail: Cannabis induced vs primary psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 19-year-old man 6 weeks after admission for auditory hallucinations and paranoid delusions. On admission urine drug screen was positive for THC only, and hair testing at 3 cm covered the preceding 3 months and was positive for high potency cannabis (used 3 to 5 times daily). He was started on risperidone 2 mg twice daily and voices resolved by day 4.

He has been abstinent from cannabis since discharge (confirmed by weekly urine drug screens, all negative for 6 weeks) and remains on risperidone 2 mg twice daily. He still reports intermittent low grade suspiciousness and hears his name called once or twice weekly, though he is otherwise functioning at work and university. He has no family history of psychotic illness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4) and prolactin 780 mIU/L (60 to 620) are within normal limits and mildly elevated respectively.

data_table.Substance use: Abstinent 6 weeks (weekly UDS negative); prior heavy high potency use

lead_in: What does the persistence of these symptoms most strongly suggest?

options.text: Reasonable expectation of substance induced psychotic disorder that will resolve with more time abstinent
Primary psychotic disorder in the schizophrenia spectrum with cannabis acting as an environmental trigger
Prolactinoma related psychosis given the modestly elevated prolactin of 780 mIU/L on risperidone therapy
Ongoing covert cannabis use with false negative urine drug screens each week from insufficient sensitivity
Persistent hallucinogen perception disorder from previous LSD use rather than cannabis specific effects here

subtopic_detail: Anorexia nervosa refeeding syndrome prevention
stem: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa weighs 39 kg at 168 cm (BMI 13.8), having taken no more than 200 kcal daily for four weeks and lost 12 kg in six months. She is admitted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 42 supine, 68 standing; systolic blood pressure 96 falling to 78 mmHg on standing; temperature 35.6 degrees C
data_table.Bloods: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L, phosphate 0.72 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for the first 72 hours?

options.text: Full nutrition at 40 kcal/kg/day, replacing electrolytes only if deficits appear
Feed at 10 to 20 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and empirical phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Refuse admission and refer to a community dietitian for weekly weight review
Intravenous 10 per cent glucose for the first 24 hours before any feeding
Nasogastric feeding at 60 mL per hour from admission, replacing electrolytes if abnormal

subtopic_detail: Early intervention in psychosis family involvement
stem:
You are the early psychosis service registrar reviewing a 20-year-old university student 6 weeks after his first admission for schizophrenia. He is on aripiprazole 15 mg daily, positive symptoms have resolved, and he wants to return to living with his parents while he resumes engineering studies. His parents ask what they can do to reduce the chance of relapse. He consents to their involvement in his care.

He scores 4 on the PHQ-9, has no substance use, and family assessment shows warmth, but the father expresses high levels of criticism when his son does not respond immediately to requests. Mother is highly reassuring and takes over daily tasks he can manage. Both parents are anxious about future relapse and ask what to do at home. He agrees a family meeting would help. Vital signs and metabolic screen are within normal limits.

data_table.Recovery stage: 6 weeks post first admission; positive symptoms resolved
data_table.Family climate: Warmth present; father high critical comments; mother overinvolved

lead_in: Which family based intervention has the strongest evidence for reducing relapse in first episode psychosis?

options.text: Weekly individual supportive counselling for parents only, delivered separately from the patient
A single family psychoeducation session at discharge covering illness basics and warning signs
Structured family intervention over 3 or more months addressing expressed emotion, problem solving, and psychoeducation
Referral of both parents to a chronic mental illness carer support group with peer led format only
Removing the patient from family home into a residential rehabilitation program for 12 months

subtopic_detail: Autism spectrum disorder in adult women
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29-year-old woman for assessment of what she wonders is autism. She reports lifelong difficulty in social groups (she can manage one to one but finds groups exhausting), intense special interests (marine biology since age 6, currently a competitive knitter with detailed knowledge of yarn weights), a need for predictable routines (rings her sister the same time every Thursday), and sensory overload in supermarkets that she manages with noise cancelling headphones.

She scored 32 on the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-10 not shown), scored 42 on the Ritvo Autism Asperger Diagnostic Scale Revised, and describes exhaustion after long social days that she calls masking. Her school reports describe her as a well behaved bright student who kept to herself. She has no learning disability. Screening scores: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 8. She uses no alcohol or illicit substances. She has never had a psychiatric diagnosis previously.

data_table.Core features: Social exhaustion; special interests; routines; sensory overload
data_table.Development: School reports describe reserved bright student

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to make a confident DSM-5 diagnosis?

options.text: Prescribe an SSRI first line for probable social anxiety disorder and reassess autism features in 6 months
Advise she does not meet DSM-5 criteria because her school reports describe a well behaved child without concern
Order genetic testing (chromosomal microarray) as the primary confirmatory diagnostic test in a well adult
Refer for structured multidisciplinary assessment using DSM-5 criteria including collateral developmental history
Prescribe methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg twice daily as a therapeutic trial for likely ADHD comorbidity

subtopic_detail: Conversion vs factitious vs malingering discrimination
stem: A 34-year-old teacher developed right leg weakness abruptly four days ago after witnessing a playground injury. She cannot weight bear. She wants to return to work and has no financial incentive.

data_table.Neurology: Right hip flexion and knee extension 0/5 on direct testing, but the leg moves spontaneously in bed; Hoover sign positive
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance brain and whole spine and nerve conduction studies normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate DSM-5 diagnosis and next step?

options.text: Malingering; discharge with a letter to her insurer and no further input
Factitious disorder; admit for behavioural observation to detect feigning
Functional neurological disorder; physiotherapy, psychology and a clear explanation
Somatic symptom disorder; start duloxetine and refer to a pain clinic
Occult demyelination; repeat imaging with gadolinium and lumbar puncture

subtopic_detail: Relapse prevention pharmacotherapy choice with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54-year-old man 10 days after completing a medically supervised inpatient alcohol withdrawal. His usual pattern before admission was 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade. He is highly motivated to stay abstinent and lives with his supportive wife. He is not on opioid pain relief and has no personal or family history of seizures.

Investigations from admission show ALT 96 U/L (under 40), AST 128 U/L (under 40), gamma-GT 320 U/L (under 60), bilirubin 26 micromol/L (under 20), albumin 34 g/L (33 to 47), INR 1.1, platelets 132 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), and a FibroScan reports significant liver fibrosis without established cirrhosis. eGFR is 88 mL/min/1.73 m2. His BMI is 26 kg/m2 and there is no ascites or peripheral oedema. He has not previously tried any relapse prevention medication.

data_table.Alcohol history: 15 standard drinks daily for over a decade; 10 days abstinent post-withdrawal
data_table.LFTs: ALT 96; AST 128; gamma-GT 320; bilirubin 26; albumin 34; INR 1.1; platelets 132
data_table.Support: Living with supportive wife; not on opioids; no seizure history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate relapse prevention pharmacotherapy to commence?

options.text: Oral acamprosate 666 mg three times daily as first-line maintenance in significant liver fibrosis
Oral disulfiram 200 mg daily under supervised administration by his wife
Oral gabapentin 300 mg three times daily titrated to 600 mg three times daily as sole therapy
Oral naltrexone 50 mg daily starting today with LFT monitoring at 4 weeks
Continued oral diazepam 5 mg three times daily as chronic maintenance to prevent relapse

subtopic_detail: Postnatal depression pharmacotherapy in a breastfeeding woman
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman at her 8 week postnatal check. She reports 6 weeks of persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and thoughts that her baby would be better off without her. She denies any active plans to harm herself or the baby. Her EPDS score is 21 and she is exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant. She had a similar depressive episode after her first child that responded to sertraline.

She has no other medical history and is on no regular medications. She is engaged with the maternal and child health nurse and her partner is supportive and home each evening. She would like to continue breastfeeding and asks whether medication is compatible.

data_table.Presentation: 6 weeks persistent low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep independent of baby
data_table.Passive suicidality: Thoughts baby would be better off without her; no active plan or intent
data_table.EPDS score: 21 with item 10 marked as denying active plans
data_table.Feeding: Exclusive breastfeeding of healthy term infant
data_table.History: Previous PND responded well to sertraline
data_table.Supports: Engaged with MCH nurse; supportive partner

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Cease breastfeeding and commence fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily as the primary antidepressant
Arrange inpatient mother-baby unit admission today for severe postnatal depression
Commence sertraline 25 mg orally daily uptitrated to 50 to 100 mg daily and continue breastfeeding
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone without pharmacotherapy for the next 6 weeks
Prescribe temazepam 10 mg at night to address the sleep disturbance and review in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Clozapine initiation monitoring for neutropenia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community mental health team commencing clozapine on a 32-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who has failed adequate trials of risperidone and olanzapine. He is registered with a clozapine monitoring program. He lives independently with his mother and has weekly community mental health contact. He has no medical comorbidities and no family history of blood dyscrasias.

Baseline investigations before starting: white cell count 6.4 x 10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), absolute neutrophil count 3.8 x 10^9/L (2.0 to 7.5), haemoglobin 148 g/L (135 to 175), platelets 260 x 10^9/L (150 to 400), fasting glucose 4.6 mmol/L, ECG showing sinus rhythm with QTc 420 ms. He is not febrile and there are no signs of infection.

data_table.Diagnosis: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia after failed risperidone and olanzapine
data_table.Baseline FBC: WCC 6.4; ANC 3.8; Hb 148; platelets 260 (all within reference)
data_table.Metabolic and cardiac: Fasting glucose 4.6; ECG sinus with QTc 420 ms
data_table.Support and monitoring: Community mental health weekly; registered clozapine monitoring program

lead_in: What is the most appropriate schedule for full blood count monitoring in the first year of clozapine therapy?

options.text: Daily neutrophil count for the first 2 weeks then weekly for the remainder of the first year
Full blood count only when clinical symptoms of infection develop during therapy
Weekly full blood count for 4 weeks then monthly thereafter for the duration of treatment
Weekly full blood count for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 52 weeks, then monthly ongoing
Fortnightly full blood count from the outset then monthly after 12 months of treatment

subtopic_detail: Generalised anxiety disorder first-line pharmacotherapy in an older adult
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 74-year-old woman with 6 months of persistent worry about her adult children, restlessness, muscle tension, difficulty falling asleep, and irritability that has curtailed her activities. She lives alone and has hypertension well controlled on perindopril. She has osteopenia but no other medical comorbidities. Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min and her sodium is 138 mmol/L (135 to 145). She is not on any regular psychotropic medication.

Her GAD-7 score is 15 and PHQ-9 is 6. She has never had suicidal thoughts. She is otherwise engaged, cognitively intact on brief bedside testing, and reports no falls in the last year. She has read patient information on cognitive behavioural therapy and is willing to try either medication or therapy, and can access both.

data_table.Presentation: 6 months of worry, restlessness, muscle tension, insomnia, irritability
data_table.Comorbidities: Hypertension on perindopril; osteopenia; no falls in past year
data_table.Function: Cognitively intact; lives alone; activities curtailed by worry

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication to consider?

options.text: Oral escitalopram 5 mg daily uptitrated to 10 mg with 2 week review and sodium check at 4 weeks
Oral amitriptyline 25 mg at night uptitrated as needed for anxiety and sleep
Oral pregabalin 75 mg twice daily titrated to 150 mg twice daily as monotherapy
Oral diazepam 5 mg twice daily as ongoing maintenance therapy for the anxiety symptoms
Oral quetiapine 25 mg at night titrated to 100 mg for anxiolysis and sleep

subtopic_detail: Explaining catatonia and its likely course to a family
stem: You have diagnosed catatonia in a 58-year-old woman with major depression and started regular lorazepam. Her husband asks what he should expect over the next few days.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: mute, immobile, catalepsy present; conscious state clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate information to give him?

options.text: Most patients improve markedly on benzodiazepines within days
Improvement is unlikely without electroconvulsive therapy first
Catatonia settles by itself once the mood episode is treated
Antipsychotic medication is the mainstay and starts tomorrow
Recovery usually needs several months of inpatient rehabilitation

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose ECG interpretation and sodium bicarbonate threshold
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of about 3 g of amitriptyline. She was found drowsy at home and gave the drug history en route. She has a background of major depressive disorder, and has recently been changed from sertraline to amitriptyline for chronic pain. She takes no other medication and drank no alcohol today.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and orientated when awake. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a tall R wave in aVR of 5 mm. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34, PaCO2 32 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Activated charcoal was declined at scene.

data_table.Ingestion: About 3 g amitriptyline 90 minutes ago; no coingestants; drowsy but rousable
data_table.Vitals: HR 130; BP 92/56; RR 20; SpO2 96 percent; T 36.8
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; QRS duration 140 ms; R wave in aVR 5 mm
data_table.ABG: pH 7.34; PaCO2 32; HCO3 18; Na 138; K 3.8; lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the tachycardia and to prevent ventricular arrhythmia
Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally as her level of consciousness permits
Give a 20 percent intralipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus as first-line therapy for the overdose
Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg for the reduced level of consciousness
Give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg intravenously and titrate serum pH to 7.5

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy-prevention program
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder in remission on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily and quetiapine 100 mg nightly for 2 years. She reports 6 months of stable mood without hypomanic or depressive symptoms. She now tells you that her partner and she have started trying for a pregnancy 8 weeks ago and she does not want to change medications because 'nothing has ever worked as well'.

She has no other medical history. She is using no contraception. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test today is negative. She has full capacity for the discussion, understands she is in remission, and has an existing psychiatric care plan and mental health team engagement. She is currently on the state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program.

data_table.Diagnosis and history: Bipolar I in remission 6 months; stable on valproate 1000 mg plus quetiapine 100 mg for 2 years
data_table.Reproductive intent: Actively trying to conceive; no contraception; LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Program status: Enrolled in state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program
data_table.Insight: Full capacity; aware of remission; declines medication change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Recommend cross-titration off valproate to lithium or lamotrigine and effective contraception until switch is complete
Continue valproate at the same dose and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily as adequate teratogen prevention
Stop valproate today without a substitute mood stabiliser and monitor mood clinically for the next 4 weeks
Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a lower teratogenic dose while she attempts to conceive
Continue valproate and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy as the sole added support during conception

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic selection in first episode psychosis
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community early intervention team. A 19-year-old university student is referred by his general practitioner with a 6 week history of paranoid ideas that his housemates are recording him, hearing voices commenting on his actions, and social withdrawal. He is a rugby player who cares about his fitness. His mother has hypothyroidism.

On mental state examination he is guarded but cooperative, with thought disorder and second person auditory hallucinations. He has no suicidal ideation and no aggressive plans. His weight is 78 kg, height 182 cm, waist circumference 82 cm.

Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.2 percent (less than 5.7), total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L, ECG QTc 402 ms. He is antipsychotic naive and consents to treatment. He asks specifically about medication that will not cause weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 14/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Weight 78 kg; height 182 cm; waist 82 cm; guarded; thought disorder; second person auditory hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 4.8 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.2%; total cholesterol 4.6 mmol/L; ECG QTc 402 ms
data_table.History: Antipsychotic naive; concerned about weight gain

lead_in: Which antipsychotic is the most appropriate first line choice?

options.text: Aripiprazole 10 mg orally in the morning, titrated according to symptomatic response
Olanzapine 5 mg orally at night, titrated according to symptomatic response
Haloperidol 5 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response
Clozapine 25 mg orally at night with a weekly full blood count for monitoring
Quetiapine 300 mg orally at night, titrated to symptomatic response

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring and renal decline
stem: A 58-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for 22 years, with levels of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L. She is euthymic and has no polyuria or thirst. She takes occasional ibuprofen and recently started perindopril.

data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L; creatinine 118 micromol/L (was 92) (45-90); eGFR 48 (was 68) mL/min/1.73 m^2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Stop lithium and switch to sodium valproate, with nephrology review
Reduce the lithium dose, cease ibuprofen, review perindopril, refer to nephrology
Increase the lithium dose to target a level between 0.8 and 1.0 mmol/L
Add hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily and repeat the level in a week
Continue unchanged and repeat renal function in twelve months

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of SSRI discontinuation from depressive relapse
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 34-year-old woman who is 5 days into stopping paroxetine 20 mg daily after 14 months of treatment for a first episode of major depression. She stopped abruptly against advice when she felt too well to continue. She reports dizziness, brain zaps, and irritability over the last 3 days.

On assessment she has no anhedonia, her sleep is normal, appetite normal, energy has been high, and she has been enjoying her hobbies. There is no suicidal ideation and no hopelessness. She scores 4 on the PHQ-9.

Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C. No focal neurological findings. She is worried that her illness is returning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84/min; BP 122/76 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 99% RA; T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: No anhedonia; sleep normal; appetite normal; enjoying hobbies; no suicidal ideation; PHQ-9 score 4; no focal neurology
data_table.History: Stopped paroxetine 20 mg after 14 months, 5 days ago; dizziness, brain zaps, irritability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose depressive relapse, increase paroxetine to 40 mg daily and add cognitive behavioural therapy referral
Reassure that the symptoms will resolve within a few days without any medication and review in 4 weeks
Switch immediately to fluoxetine 20 mg to bridge the discontinuation because of its long half life
Explain that these are discontinuation symptoms, restart paroxetine at the usual dose and taper over 6 to 8 weeks
Refer urgently to psychiatry as the symptoms are likely a paroxetine hypersensitivity reaction

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose triage
stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking about 3 g of amitriptyline. She is drowsy but rousable, warm and dry, with dilated pupils.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 /min, BP 96/58 mmHg, T 37.1 degrees C, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm, QTc 468 ms; VBG pH 7.32, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; glucose 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g orally with four hours of ward cardiac monitoring
Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg, then reassess the airway and conscious state
Gastric lavage and an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion over 20 minutes
Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose to prevent seizures
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 per cent bolus with continuous telemetry

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and treatment considerations
stem: A 28-year-old accountant has lifelong difficulty concentrating, worse since starting a demanding role six months ago, with missed deadlines, restlessness and interrupting others. School reports at age 8 described him as fidgety and easily distracted.

data_table.Examination: No depressive or anxious cognitions, no history of mania
data_table.Investigations: Adult ADHD Self Report Scale Part A 5 of 6 positive; thyroid function and iron studies normal
data_table.Driving: Drives daily, no crashes in 3 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for diagnostic assessment
Start dexamfetamine 5 mg twice daily, review in 2 weeks
Diagnose generalised anxiety disorder and start sertraline
Advise him to stop driving until treatment starts
Refer for neuropsychological testing before any diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Clozapine neutropenia interpretation and action
stem: A 44-year-old Aboriginal man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has taken clozapine 400 mg nightly for eight years in remission. His registered benign ethnic neutropenia baseline averages 1.9 x10^9/L. He is asymptomatic with no fever or sore throat.

data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.3 x10^9/L (2.0-8.0), white cell count 3.6 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 138 g/L, platelets 232 x10^9/L; neutrophils 1.9 x10^9/L five days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine and admit for haematology assessment
Continue clozapine and repeat the full blood count within 2 days
Add lithium to raise the neutrophil count and recheck in 2 weeks
Give filgrastim and continue clozapine with more frequent counts
Reduce clozapine to 200 mg nightly and recheck in 3 to 5 days

subtopic_detail: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy and mood stabiliser choice
stem: A 30-year-old woman at six weeks of a planned pregnancy has bipolar I disorder with two previous manic episodes requiring inpatient care. She has been well on lithium 1000 mg at night for four years. She wishes to continue her medication if it is safe.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no perceptual disturbance
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, TSH 2.6 mIU/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her mood stabiliser?

options.text: Cease lithium and switch to sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily
Switch to lamotrigine 200 mg daily for its safer teratogenic profile
Continue lithium at the lowest effective dose with a fetal echocardiogram at 20 weeks
Cease lithium for the first trimester and restart it after 14 weeks
Cease lithium and start olanzapine 10 mg at night to avoid teratogenicity

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance on a mental health unit
stem: A 30-year-old man admitted with schizoaffective disorder is pacing the corridor, shouting and standing over staff. A quiet space, reduced stimulation and repeated verbal de-escalation have not settled him. He is not currently assaulting anyone and says he will take a tablet.

data_table.Medications: Olanzapine daily, no regular benzodiazepine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer oral lorazepam and observe closely
Give intramuscular droperidol immediately
Give intramuscular olanzapine immediately
Place him in seclusion and observe closely
Apply physical restraint and observe closely

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
stem: A 38-year-old man has acute confusion and shaking that began 8 hours ago. He started sertraline 100 mg daily three weeks ago and took tramadol 100 mg for back pain 12 hours ago. He takes no antipsychotic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, BP 158/98 mmHg, RR 24 /min, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, lower limb clonus with hyperreflexia, pupils 6 mm, tone increased in the legs only
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L (30-250), sodium 138 mmol/L, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from the sertraline and tramadol interaction
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requiring bromocriptine and dantrolene
Malignant hyperthermia from ryanodine receptor sensitivity
Anticholinergic toxidrome from an overdose of tramadol
Central pontine myelinolysis from rapid sodium correction

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant choice in a breastfeeding mother with moderate MDD postpartum
stem: A 31-year-old woman is 8 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding. For 3 weeks she has had low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, poor appetite and guilt about not bonding. She has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby, no intrusive obsessional thoughts and no bipolar history.

data_table.Screening: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale 18, self-harm item negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological plan?

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily, review in 2 weeks
Sertraline 25 mg orally daily, increasing to 50 mg after 7 days
Paroxetine 20 mg orally daily, review in 2 weeks
Venlafaxine 75 mg orally daily, review in 2 weeks
Amitriptyline 25 mg orally at night, review in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Baseline investigations before commencing lithium
stem: A 34-year-old man with bipolar I disorder had a first manic episode six weeks ago and is now euthymic on olanzapine. He has no medical history and has agreed to start lithium after informed discussion.

data_table.Examination: Blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, weight 78 kg; no tremor or goitre

lead_in: Which baseline investigations are most appropriate before commencing lithium?

options.text: Urea electrolytes creatinine, thyroid function, liver function, fasting lipids and echocardiogram
Urea electrolytes creatinine, thyroid function, 24 hour urinary creatinine clearance and lipids
Urea electrolytes creatinine, thyroid function, calcium, full blood count, beta hCG where indicated and electrocardiogram
Urea electrolytes creatinine, thyroid function, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and magnesium
Urea electrolytes creatinine, thyroid function, full blood count and a plain chest radiograph

subtopic_detail: Baseline and monitoring requirements before clozapine commencement
stem: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia has persistent hallucinations and delusions despite adequate adherent trials of risperidone and olanzapine, each for 8 weeks. He agrees to start clozapine. He has no blood dyscrasia or cardiac disease.

data_table.Baseline: Full blood count, troponin, electrocardiogram and echocardiogram normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate haematological monitoring schedule?

options.text: Monthly full blood count for 18 weeks, then 3 monthly thereafter
Weekly full blood count for 4 weeks, then monthly thereafter
Fortnightly full blood count for 18 weeks, then monthly thereafter
Weekly for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 12 months, then monthly
Weekly for 6 weeks, then fortnightly for 6 weeks, then monthly

subtopic_detail: Discriminating neuroleptic malignant syndrome from serotonin syndrome
stem: A 42-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has 24 hours of confusion, fever and rigidity. Haloperidol 5 mg twice daily was started one week ago, and he has taken paroxetine 40 mg daily for two years. He has taken no tramadol, triptan or illicit drug.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 158/98 mmHg, temperature 39.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Lead-pipe rigidity in all four limbs, hyporeflexia, no clonus, diffuse sweating, mute
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 8600 U/L (less than 200), white cells 14 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from paroxetine, atypical because of dopamine blockade
Encephalitis with autonomic dysregulation after a viral prodrome
Malignant hyperthermia after halogenated anaesthetic exposure
Anticholinergic toxicity from the anticholinergic burden of haloperidol
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome from recently commenced haloperidol

subtopic_detail: Recognition of postpartum psychosis requiring immediate admission
stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought in by her partner 8 days after her first birth. For two days she has slept under two hours a night, believing her baby was switched at hospital and is watched through the smoke alarm. She whispered today that she must protect the baby from the alarm.

data_table.Examination: Agitated, pressured speech, distractible, fleeting suicidal ideation
data_table.History: Cousin with postpartum psychosis; no personal bipolar history
data_table.Disposition: Refusing admission, wants to take the baby home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Involuntary admission to a mother and baby unit under the Mental Health Act
Community perinatal follow up within 24 hours, remaining at home
Sertraline 25 mg daily with perinatal team review in 48 hours
Oral diazepam 10 mg tonight with perinatal follow up in 48 hours
Child protection notification with outpatient psychiatric review next week

subtopic_detail: Treating the underlying mood episode once catatonia has responded
stem: A 30-year-old woman's catatonia resolved on regular lorazepam but she remains profoundly depressed. Her file records a hypomanic episode two years ago. She has taken venlafaxine for six months.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: depressed mood, marked retardation, no catatonic signs, no psychotic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Taper venlafaxine and start quetiapine for bipolar depression
Increase the venlafaxine dose and continue the lorazepam cover
Add lithium to venlafaxine and check a level in five days
Cease all psychotropic medication and reassess her in two weeks
Switch venlafaxine to sertraline at an equivalent daily dose

subtopic_detail: Long term lithium monitoring and hypercalcaemia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 46-year-old woman in the community clinic. She has bipolar I disorder and has taken lithium carbonate 750 mg nightly for 12 years with no relapse in that time. She feels well and adherent.

She mentions six months of constipation and vague aches. Her general practitioner has sent through a routine annual panel taken 12 hours post dose. She takes no diuretic, calcium supplement or vitamin D. Her thyroid function is within normal limits and she has had no recent immobilisation or fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 126/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.68 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); corrected calcium 2.74 mmol/L (2.10-2.60); phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.75-1.50)
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90); eGFR 68 mL/min/1.73m2; TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Measure serum parathyroid hormone alongside a repeat corrected calcium level
Reduce the lithium dose by 25 per cent and recheck the trough level in one week
Cease lithium today and substitute sodium valproate as maintenance monotherapy
Commence a thiazide diuretic to lower urinary calcium and repeat the panel monthly
Arrange a bone mineral density scan and start weekly oral alendronate therapy

subtopic_detail: Establishing that a persecutory belief is unfounded before diagnosing
stem: A 39-year-old man tells you his landlord has entered his flat repeatedly and moved his belongings. He shows photographs of a window left ajar. He works, sleeps and socialises as usual.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, linear speech, no hallucinations, belief held with conviction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Seek collateral history from his partner and the property manager
Commence an oral antipsychotic and review him again in four weeks
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any treatment
Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis today
Reassure him the belief is untrue and arrange routine follow up

subtopic_detail: Persistent psychosis after confirmed cannabis abstinence
stem:
You are the registrar in a youth mental health service seeing a 19-year-old apprentice. Seven weeks ago he presented with persecutory beliefs and second person auditory hallucinations after two years of daily high potency cannabis use.

He stopped cannabis at that first presentation and has attended weekly, with supervised urine screens negative for cannabinoids on each of the last five visits. Despite this, he still hears two voices commenting through the day and believes his supervisor is recording him. He has withdrawn from his football team and his mother reports he now speaks little at home. He is sleeping and eating, and denies any plan to harm himself or others.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: guarded, restricted affect, ongoing auditory hallucinations, reduced spontaneous speech
data_table.Investigations: Five consecutive supervised urine drug screens negative; full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue abstinence monitoring alone and review again in a further four weeks
Refer to the drug and alcohol service for relapse prevention as the sole intervention
Prescribe diazepam 5 mg twice daily for anxiety and arrange supportive counselling
Commence a long-acting injectable antipsychotic at the first treatment appointment
Commence oral risperidone with baseline metabolic screening and early psychosis referral

subtopic_detail: Autism recognition in an adult woman presenting as treatment resistant anxiety
stem:
You are the psychiatrist seeing a 24-year-old graphic designer referred with anxiety that has not responded to sertraline, escitalopram or venlafaxine at adequate doses and durations over three years.

She describes exhaustion after workplace social events, and says she rehearses conversations beforehand and copies phrases from colleagues. Fluorescent lighting and the office air conditioner noise are intolerable to her, and she has worn the same brand of clothing since childhood because of the fabric. Her mother reports she lined up her toys by colour and had one intense interest at a time throughout primary school. Her anxiety is worst when routines change at short notice, and she has no history of trauma, panic attacks or compulsions.

data_table.Examination: Mental state: anxious, limited spontaneous eye contact, precise and detailed speech, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Augment the current antidepressant with low dose aripiprazole and review in six weeks
Refer for a structured multidisciplinary autism diagnostic assessment with a developmental history
Diagnose borderline personality disorder and refer for dialectical behaviour therapy skills
Commence a stimulant trial for possible inattentive presentation attention deficit disorder
Increase the venlafaxine to the maximum tolerated dose and add graded exposure therapy

subtopic_detail: Emergency department management of recurrent self harm in borderline personality disorder
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar at 11 pm. A 26-year-old woman with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder has presented after superficially cutting her forearm following an argument with her partner. The wounds are clean, not bleeding and do not need suturing.

This is her fifth presentation in four months. She describes chronic emptiness and says she wants to be admitted because she cannot face going home. On assessment she describes no suicidal intent or plan, and her only access to means is household items. She is not intoxicated. She has an allocated community case manager and a scheduled appointment in four days. Her last two admissions were each followed by an escalation in self-harm within a week of discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Four superficial linear forearm lacerations, haemostatic; mental state distressed, reactive affect, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Blood alcohol not detected; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Dress the wounds, develop a written crisis plan with her and bring forward the community appointment
Admit to the acute inpatient unit for a planned two week period of containment and observation
Commence quetiapine 100 mg at night for affective instability and review in the clinic weekly
Commence sodium valproate as a mood stabiliser and arrange serum level monitoring in a fortnight
Discharge with printed crisis line numbers and advise her to attend the existing appointment as booked

subtopic_detail: Assessment of an asylum seeker with insomnia and nightmares
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a refugee health clinic seeing a 29-year-old man who arrived in Australia 14 months ago and holds a bridging visa pending a protection decision. He speaks limited English and attends with his cousin, who has been translating.

He reports four months of broken sleep, frightening dreams most nights and headaches. He was detained and beaten in his country of origin. He describes worsening symptoms since a visa interview six weeks ago and worries constantly about his brother, who remains overseas. He describes no suicidal ideation, and takes neither alcohol nor any medication. His full blood count, iron studies, vitamin D and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Mental state: subdued, tearful when describing detention, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, vitamin D and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 15 mg at night for sleep and review the response in four weeks
Continue with the cousin interpreting and start trauma-focused therapy at the next visit
Rebook with a professional interpreter and refer to the state torture and trauma service
Prescribe temazepam 10 mg nightly for two weeks and reassess the sleep diary afterwards
Refer to a private psychologist under a mental health treatment plan without further arrangements

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological management of acute behavioural disturbance after failed de-escalation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 28-year-old man was brought in by police after threatening staff at a service station. He is pacing, shouting and has struck a wall. Twenty minutes of verbal de escalation in a low stimulus room by two senior nurses has not settled him, and he has refused oral medication twice.

No collateral history is available and there are no records under the name he has given. There is no intravenous access. He is not visibly intoxicated, has no obvious injury and is able to walk unaided. A capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. He continues to advance towards staff and a code has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 148/86, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); no venous access established; no prior records available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Intravenous diazepam 10 mg given slowly once access has been secured by the team
Intramuscular droperidol 10 mg with continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring afterwards
Intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg followed immediately by intramuscular midazolam 5 mg
Intramuscular haloperidol 10 mg combined with intramuscular promethazine 50 mg
Physical restraint by five trained staff with reassessment for medication in thirty minutes

subtopic_detail: Initial approach to a request for gender affirming hormone therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 19-year-old trans man who has lived in his affirmed gender for three years, uses he and him pronouns at work and with family, and has had a legal name change. He requests testosterone therapy.

He describes persistent distress about chest and menstrual bleeding, and says this has been consistent since age 13. He has no psychotic symptoms, substance use, self-harm or suicidal ideation. He works full time and has supportive parents. He has not previously seen a psychiatrist and asks whether a psychiatric assessment is required before he can start. His blood pressure and body mass index are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Mental state: euthymic, engaged, no psychotic features, no cognitive impairment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Require twelve months of psychiatric assessment before any hormone therapy can be considered
Commence testosterone undecanoate today and arrange follow up bloods in three months
Commence sertraline for the reported distress and revisit hormone therapy after three months
Refer to a public gender clinic and take no further action until that appointment occurs
Arrange baseline haematocrit, lipids and liver function and discuss fertility preservation options

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose with QRS widening and hypotension
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 22-year-old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking an unknown quantity of her grandmother's amitriptyline. She was drowsy on arrival and has become progressively less responsive over the last ten minutes.

She had one self-limiting generalised seizure in the ambulance. She takes no other medication and there is no alcohol detected. Intravenous access is established and she is being preoxygenated with a plan for intubation. Her serial electrocardiograms show a progressively widening QRS complex and a rightward terminal axis in lead aVR. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.22 with a bicarbonate of 15 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 82/48, RR 26, SpO2 97% on 15 L oxygen, temperature 36.4
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 152 ms, terminal R wave in aVR 4 mm; venous pH 7.22 (7.32-7.42); bicarbonate 15 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Blood tests: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); potassium 3.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); paracetamol not detected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading infusion to prevent recurrence of the seizure
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over twenty minutes for the broad complex tachycardia
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion titrated to a mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol by rapid bolus with repeat boluses guided by the QRS
Intravenous lipid emulsion 20 per cent given as a bolus then infusion over thirty minutes

subtopic_detail: Arranging involuntary assessment from general practice
stem: A 33-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder attends your Newcastle practice with her sister. She has eaten almost nothing for three weeks because she believes her food is poisoned, has lost 7 kg, and refuses hospital. She sees nothing wrong and will not take medication.

data_table.Mental state: Guarded, fixed belief food is contaminated, no insight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Complete a mental health certificate today
Arrange a community review appointment tomorrow
Ask her sister to consent to the admission
Apply to the Guardianship Division for an order
Ask police to take her into protective custody

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hyponatraemia after recreational stimulant use
stem:
You are the emergency registrar at a regional hospital during a music festival. A 21-year-old woman is brought in after collapsing. Friends say she took two tablets sold as ecstasy about six hours ago and has been dancing since, drinking large amounts of water because she was told to stay hydrated.

She had a witnessed generalised seizure lasting 90 seconds in the ambulance and remains drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 11. She is not rigid, her pupils are 5 mm and reactive, and there is no clonus. Her potassium, creatinine, glucose and calcium are within normal limits, and her creatine kinase is 340 U/L. Her sodium has come back at 118 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 106/62, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 11, pupils 5 mm reactive, no rigidity, no clonus, no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135-145); creatine kinase 340 U/L (30-200); potassium, creatinine, glucose and corrected calcium within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day with four hourly sodium monitoring on the ward
Hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride 100 mL bolus intravenously with repeat sodium checks
Intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride one litre over one hour then reassess the sodium
Intravenous dantrolene 1 mg/kg with active external cooling and temperature monitoring
Subcutaneous desmopressin 2 micrograms with strict hourly fluid balance charting overnight

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of catatonia in severe depression
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to see a 58-year-old man on a medical ward. He was admitted three days ago with reduced oral intake. He has a history of recurrent major depression and stopped his mirtazapine two months ago.

He has not spoken since admission. Nursing staff report he holds his right arm in whatever position it is placed for several minutes, resists passive movement of his neck, and has been observed to repeat the last words said to him. He has taken no fluids for 24 hours. He is on no antipsychotic and no dopamine antagonist of any kind. His temperature is 36.8, his white cell count and inflammatory markers are within normal limits, and computed tomography of the brain shows no acute abnormality.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/84, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Mutism, waxy flexibility of the right arm, negativism on passive neck movement, echolalia
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 480 U/L (30-200); white cell count and C reactive protein within normal limits; CT brain no acute abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence olanzapine 5 mg at night for the mutism and negativism observed on the ward
Insert a nasogastric tube for feeding and observe the mental state for a further 48 hours
Administer a lorazepam 2 mg challenge and reassess the clinical signs after fifteen minutes
Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy tomorrow morning without a preceding medication trial
Restart mirtazapine at the previous dose and refer for a psychiatry outpatient appointment

subtopic_detail: Functional neurological disorder diagnosis and initial management
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old childcare worker with three weeks of right leg weakness. She cannot walk unaided and has needed carer support at home. She is distressed and frightened about the cause.

On examination her right hip extension is 2 out of 5 on direct testing, but her right hip extends fully against your hand when you ask her to flex the left hip against resistance. Her gait is dragging with the leg held stiffly and does not vary with distraction tasks in the way she reports. Reflexes are symmetrical and plantar responses are flexor. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and whole spine performed yesterday is unremarkable, and her B12, thyroid function and inflammatory markers are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Right hip extension 2/5 on direct testing but full on contralateral hip flexion against resistance; symmetrical reflexes; flexor plantar responses
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and whole spine unremarkable; vitamin B12, thyroid function and C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the spinal imaging with contrast in six weeks and review the results in clinic
Explain that all investigations are normal and that there is no physical cause for the weakness
Admit to the psychiatric unit for assessment of an underlying unresolved psychological conflict
Refer for formal assessment of deliberate symptom production before offering any active treatment
Demonstrate the positive clinical sign to her and refer for specialist physiotherapy led retraining

subtopic_detail: Medical instability thresholds for admission in adolescent anorexia nervosa
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 17-year-old girl in clinic with her mother. Over eight months she has restricted her intake and now eats one meal daily. Her weight has fallen from 58 kg to 40 kg at a height of 168 cm.

She walks to school and plays no sport. She denies bingeing, vomiting and laxative use, and a urinary electrolyte screen shows no evidence of purging. She is oriented and her mood is described as flat but she has no suicidal ideation. She is enrolled in a family based treatment program with a fortnightly appointment. Her observations and bloods have just returned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 38, BP 82/50 lying with a fall to 68/44 on standing, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 35.4
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus bradycardia, QTc 486 ms; potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.70-1.10)
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 14.2 kg/m2; cool peripheries; no oedema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit today for cardiac monitoring, electrolyte correction and supervised low rate refeeding
Continue family based treatment and increase the review frequency to twice weekly instead
Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg nightly to reduce eating related anxiety and support weight gain
Refer to the adolescent day program starting next week with weekly weight and observation checks
Arrange outpatient dietetic review with a target intake of 2500 kilocalories daily from tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring and intervention
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 26-year-old man in the early psychosis clinic. He presented 12 weeks ago with a first episode of psychosis and started olanzapine 10 mg nightly. His positive symptoms have fully remitted, he has returned to his apprenticeship and he is keen to stay on the current treatment.

He has gained 7 kg since starting and his waist circumference has risen from 89 cm to 104 cm. He has no family history of diabetes and no personal history of an eating disorder. His fasting bloods were taken this morning after a documented 10 hour fast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 128/80, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.0-5.4); HbA1c 44 mmol/mol (less than 42); triglycerides 2.6 mmol/L (less than 1.7)
data_table.Blood tests: Renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence metformin alongside a structured diet and exercise program
Switch olanzapine to aripiprazole with a cross taper over four weeks
Refer to a dietitian for review and repeat the panel in twelve months
Commence orlistat and arrange fasting lipids again in three months
Reduce olanzapine to 5 mg nightly and continue current lifestyle advice

subtopic_detail: Valproate in women of childbearing potential
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 23-year-old woman in the outpatient clinic. She has bipolar I disorder and has been euthymic for 18 months on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily, after two admissions for mania in her late teens.

She tells you she married three months ago and hopes to conceive within the next year. She is using no contraception. She has never taken lamotrigine or lithium, and she has had no depressive episodes. Her most recent valproate level, full blood count and liver function are within normal limits.

data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily; no other regular medicines
data_table.Investigations: Serum valproate within therapeutic range; full blood count, liver function and beta human chorionic gonadotropin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue valproate at the current dose and start high dose folate 5 mg daily
Halve the valproate dose now and review her mood state again in three months
Arrange reliable contraception and cross titrate valproate to an alternative agent
Cease valproate today and review her again once she has a positive pregnancy test
Maintain valproate and refer for detailed fetal morphology once she conceives

subtopic_detail: Clozapine and smoking cessation interaction
stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health team reviewing a 41-year-old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia. He has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for six years with good symptom control and normal neutrophil counts throughout.

He smokes 25 cigarettes a day and has decided to stop entirely from next Monday, having been accepted into a quit program. He asks whether anything needs to change. He takes no other regular medicines, drinks no alcohol and has had no recent illness or dose change.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 118/74, RR 15, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 450 mg daily in divided doses
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 3.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); renal function and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Make no change to clozapine and review his mental state again in three months
Increase clozapine by 100 mg daily to offset the loss of a nicotine effect
Substitute nicotine replacement therapy indefinitely to keep the interaction stable
Withhold clozapine on the quit date and restart at the same dose after one week
Measure the clozapine plasma level and plan a staged dose reduction as he stops

subtopic_detail: Adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with comorbid depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 29-year-old accountant referred with lifelong inattention, disorganisation and difficulty completing tasks. School reports from age eight describe the same pattern, and a structured assessment supports a diagnosis of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.

Over the past four months he has also had persistent low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking and passive thoughts that life is not worth living, with no plan or intent. He has never taken psychotropic medication. He drinks two standard drinks weekly and uses no other substances. His thyroid function and full blood count are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation, reactive but predominantly low affect, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment approach?

options.text: Start lisdexamfetamine and add an antidepressant only if his mood fails to lift
Treat the depressive episode first and reassess the attention symptoms afterwards
Start atomoxetine and lisdexamfetamine together to cover both symptom clusters
Offer psychological skills coaching alone and review his progress in six months
Decline to diagnose attention deficit disorder until his mood has been in remission

subtopic_detail: Post traumatic stress disorder in a refugee patient
stem:
You are the registrar in a community mental health clinic seeing a 34-year-old man who arrived in Australia two years ago on a humanitarian visa. He describes nightly nightmares, intrusive daytime images of events during his detention overseas, avoidance of news broadcasts and constant scanning of his surroundings.

Symptoms have been present for 14 months and he now sleeps about four hours a night. His preferred language is Dari and a professional interpreter is present. He describes no hallucinations outside the intrusive imagery, no elevated mood and no substance use. He is housed, has permanent residency and is not facing any visa determination.

data_table.Examination: Hypervigilant, startles at corridor noise, mood anxious with congruent affect, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence prazosin at night and review the frequency of his nightmares in a month
Commence quetiapine at night given the severity of his sleep disturbance
Commence sertraline and arrange a further medical review again in four weeks
Refer for trauma-focused psychological therapy delivered with an accredited interpreter
Provide supportive counselling and psychoeducation and reassess him in three months

subtopic_detail: Carer collateral history and confidentiality
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in an outpatient clinic. Your patient is a 33-year-old man with schizophrenia who is currently well, working part time and taking paliperidone. He has full decision making capacity on assessment today.

His mother telephones the clinic. She says he has stopped answering her calls, has been awake all night for a week and has been talking about neighbours reading his thoughts. She asks you what medication he is on and whether his dose has changed. Your patient told you at his last visit that he does not want his family given any information about his care, and he has not repeated or withdrawn that instruction.

data_table.Examination: At last review two weeks ago: euthymic, no delusions elicited, insight preserved, capacity intact
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone long-acting injection, dose unchanged for eight months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the mother's call?

options.text: Record her account in full and explain that you cannot disclose his clinical details
Tell her the medication name and dose because she is his nominated primary carer
Decline the call entirely and advise her to raise her concerns with her son directly
Disclose his details on the basis that a relapse constitutes a serious imminent threat
Ask her to obtain his written consent before you will accept any further information

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38-year-old woman is brought in 90 minutes after taking what her partner estimates was about 30 amitriptyline 25 mg tablets. She is drowsy but rousable and answers questions.

Her pupils are 6 mm and sluggish and her mouth is dry. Her blood pressure has been stable since arrival and she has had no seizure. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.36. Serial electrocardiograms show the QRS duration lengthening from 96 ms on arrival to 118 ms now, with a terminal R wave in lead aVR.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 112/70, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, dry mucous membranes, pupils 6 mm sluggish, no clonus
data_table.Investigations: QRS 118 ms with terminal R wave in aVR; venous pH 7.36; paracetamol not detected; potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give activated charcoal 50 g orally now that she is able to answer questions
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes and repeat the tracing
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol as a bolus and reassess the tracing
Give intravenous lipid emulsion 20 per cent at 1.5 mL/kg and observe for one hour
Give intravenous flumazenil 200 mcg and titrate against her conscious state

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and the lorazepam challenge
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to review a 57-year-old woman on a medical ward. She was admitted three days ago with reduced oral intake. Over the past week she has become mute, holds her left arm in whatever position it is placed, and resists passive movement of her neck.

She has a history of severe depression and was started on olanzapine 10 mg nightly by her general practitioner two weeks ago. She has not eaten for 48 hours. Her creatine kinase is 180 U/L, she has been afebrile throughout, and there is no rigidity in her lower limbs or autonomic instability.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 124/78, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility of the left arm, negativism on neck movement, staring, no lower limb rigidity
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 180 U/L (30-190); white cell count, renal function and calcium within normal limits; computed tomography of the brain unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase olanzapine to 20 mg nightly and review her presentation again tomorrow
Commence dantrolene and bromocriptine and transfer her to a high dependency bed
Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram before commencing any psychotropic treatment
Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and refer her for daily psychology
Cease olanzapine and give a lorazepam challenge with a planned response assessment

subtopic_detail: Repeated relapse after stopping oral antipsychotic treatment
stem: A 27-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder has had four admissions in three years. Each followed him stopping oral paliperidone within weeks of discharge. He responds well and tolerates it while taking it, says he simply forgets, and is willing to keep having treatment.

data_table.Medications: Oral paliperidone, dispensing records show long gaps
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative, fasting glucose 4.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Offer a long-acting injectable antipsychotic
Commence clozapine for treatment resistance
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy alone
Increase the oral paliperidone dose further
Add lithium to the oral paliperidone regimen

subtopic_detail: Autism recognition in adult women previously diagnosed with a personality disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman referred after four emergency presentations in two years with distress and self-harm. She carries a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder made at age 22 and has completed a full dialectical behaviour therapy program with no measurable change.

Her distress episodes consistently follow open plan office days, unexpected roster changes and shopping centre visits, and settle within hours once she is alone in a quiet room. She describes a stable and consistent sense of who she is, has had one relationship for nine years, and denies any fear of abandonment. She reports rehearsing conversations in advance since primary school and copying the mannerisms of colleagues to appear at ease. Her mother describes lining up objects and intense narrow interests throughout childhood.

data_table.Examination: Reciprocal eye contact effortful and consciously maintained, literal interpretation of questions, no dissociation observed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, thyroid function and urine drug screen within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat a further course of dialectical behaviour therapy with a different therapist
Commence a mood stabiliser to reduce the frequency of her emotional dysregulation
Diagnose a complex post-traumatic presentation and refer for trauma-focused therapy
Refer for a structured autism diagnostic assessment including a developmental history
Provide brief supportive contact and discharge her back to her general practitioner

subtopic_detail: Gender affirming care pathway in a young adult
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 19-year-old man in an outpatient clinic. He was assigned female at birth, has lived and worked in his affirmed gender for three years, and has used his current name on all documents for two of those years.

He asks to start testosterone. He had a depressive episode at 16 that has been in full remission on sertraline 50 mg daily for two years. He describes a consistent and long standing sense of his gender, has a supportive partner and household, and reports no suicidal ideation. He has never had gender affirming hormone therapy and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic features, capacity to consent intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and lipids within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Require a further 12 months of psychotherapy before considering any referral onward
Refer him for gender affirming hormone therapy assessment and continue his sertraline
Cease his sertraline first so that his baseline mood state can be properly established
Advise a documented period of real life experience before any medical treatment starts
Defer any decision until he turns 21 given the permanence of some hormonal effects

subtopic_detail: Advance care directives and designated carers in NSW
stem: A 38-year-old woman is recovering from her third episode of psychosis and nearing discharge from a NSW unit. She has capacity today. She tells you haloperidol caused a frightening dystonic reaction last admission and that olanzapine suited her on both other occasions.
