She wants this followed if she becomes unwell again, and wants her brother rather than her father contacted and involved.

data_table.Examination: No psychotic symptoms, insight good, capacity intact on assessment
data_table.Medications: Olanzapine 15 mg nightly, well tolerated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to give effect to her wishes?

options.text: Record her preferences as a clinical file note for future treating teams
Apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying olanzapine as her treatment
Ask her general practitioner to add a haloperidol allergy alert instead
Support a written advance care directive and a designated carer nomination
Explain that her stated preferences cannot bind a future treating team

subtopic_detail: Culturally safe engagement and social and emotional wellbeing
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar at a regional hospital. A 22-year-old Aboriginal man is referred by the emergency department after presenting with three months of low mood, poor sleep and heavy alcohol use following the death of an uncle.

He attended one appointment at the clinic last year and did not return. Today he sits at the edge of the room, gives brief answers and twice says he wants to leave. He denies current suicidal intent and is not intoxicated. He mentions that most of his family live four hours away and that he has been staying with different cousins since the funeral.

data_table.Examination: Guarded, minimal eye contact, no psychotic features, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, thyroid function and blood alcohol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate approach to this consultation?

options.text: Offer to involve an Aboriginal health worker and ask who he wants present today
Complete a full structured psychiatric history today before he leaves the department
Commence an antidepressant now and arrange telephone review again in four weeks
Detain him under the mental health act until a full risk assessment can be finished
Refer him to a drug and alcohol service alone and defer mental health review entirely

subtopic_detail: Antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24-year-old woman who has taken risperidone 4 mg daily for eight months for a psychotic illness that is now in full remission. She is adherent and wants to stay well.

She reports that her periods stopped five months ago and that both breasts leak a small amount of milky fluid when pressed. She has never been pregnant and a pregnancy test today is negative. She takes no other medication, has no headache and has no visual field defect on confrontation testing. Her thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Visual fields full to confrontation, no galactorrhoea at rest, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 1850 mIU/L (less than 500); beta human chorionic gonadotropin not detected; thyroid function and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary before altering her medication
Add cabergoline weekly and continue risperidone at her present effective dose
Switch her to aripiprazole with a cross taper and repeat the prolactin afterwards
Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive to restore her menstrual bleeding pattern
Cease risperidone entirely and monitor her mental state closely over the next month

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant selection with a cytochrome P450 2D6 interaction
stem:
You are the consultation liaison registrar asked to advise on a 52-year-old woman attending the breast clinic. She completed treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer 10 months ago and takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily, which is planned to continue for five years.

Over the past three months she has had persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor concentration and early morning waking, and she scores in the moderate range on a depression rating scale. She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no history of mania, takes no other regular medicines, and her renal function, liver function, sodium and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Medications: Tamoxifen 20 mg daily
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145); renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
Fluoxetine 20 mg daily, increasing to 40 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
Bupropion 150 mg daily, increasing to 300 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
Duloxetine 30 mg daily, increasing to 60 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated
Escitalopram 10 mg daily, increasing to 20 mg daily after two weeks if tolerated

subtopic_detail: Long term benzodiazepine deprescribing in an older patient
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 71-year-old woman who has taken temazepam 20 mg nightly for six years, originally prescribed after a bereavement.

She has fallen twice in the past three months, both times when getting up overnight, and sustained a wrist fracture on the second occasion. She says the tablets no longer help her sleep but that she cannot manage without them and becomes anxious if she misses a dose. Her cognition is normal on formal testing, her postural blood pressure drop is 6 mmHg, and her vision, vitamin D and renal function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 70, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Gait steady in daylight, no peripheral neuropathy, cognitive screening normal
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and vitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her temazepam?

options.text: Continue temazepam at the current dose and install home rails and night lighting
Substitute an equivalent diazepam dose and reduce it gradually over several months
Cease temazepam tonight and prescribe temazepam 10 mg for occasional rescue use
Replace temazepam with nightly quetiapine 25 mg and review her sleep in one month
Replace temazepam with nightly melatonin and give her written sleep hygiene advice

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant continuation during breastfeeding
stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 30-year-old woman who is six weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding a healthy term infant.

She has recurrent major depressive disorder with three previous episodes, one of which required admission. She has taken fluoxetine 20 mg daily for four years, remained on it through pregnancy, and has stayed well throughout including the past six weeks. Her infant is feeding well, is gaining weight along the fiftieth centile and is neurologically normal at the six week check. She asks whether she should stop or change her medication now that she is feeding.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, mother and infant interaction warm and responsive
data_table.Investigations: Edinburgh postnatal depression scale score 4; full blood count, iron studies and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her medication?

options.text: Stop fluoxetine now and restart it promptly if any depressive symptoms return
Switch to sertraline because it produces the lowest relative infant dose available
Halve the dose to 10 mg daily to reduce the total quantity reaching her infant
Continue fluoxetine unchanged and support her to keep breastfeeding as she wishes
Continue fluoxetine and advise her to change to formula feeding to avoid exposure

subtopic_detail: Delusional disorder versus schizophreniform and brief psychotic disorder
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 46-year-old electrician brought in by his wife. For eight months he has been certain she is having an affair with a neighbour, and he checks her phone, odometer and laundry daily and has begun following her car.

He has continued to run his business without difficulty, meets his contract deadlines and is described by his employees as unchanged in every other respect. He has no hallucinations, his speech is organised, his self care is intact and his mood is not elevated or depressed. His wife confirms the accusations have no basis and that nothing else about him has altered. His urine drug screen is negative and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Speech organised and goal directed, affect reactive, no hallucinations, no negative symptoms, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; magnetic resonance imaging of the brain unremarkable; full blood count, renal function, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Delusional disorder, jealous type, with function preserved outside the belief itself
Schizophreniform disorder, given the eight month duration of psychotic symptoms
Brief psychotic disorder, given the abrupt onset of a clearly circumscribed belief
Paranoid personality disorder with pervasive suspiciousness of his wife and others
Obsessive compulsive disorder with poor insight driving his repeated checking rituals

subtopic_detail: Gamma hydroxybutyrate withdrawal
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 28-year-old man brought in by friends with agitation and tremor. He has been using a clear liquid he buys in a small bottle and doses every two to three hours around the clock, including overnight, for the past eight months.

His last dose was three hours ago, taken because he woke with the same symptoms. He is sweating, tremulous and repeatedly tries to get off the trolley. He has already received diazepam 20 mg orally in divided doses over the past hour with no discernible change. His breath has no alcoholic smell, his blood alcohol is not detected, and his blood glucose is 5.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 168/96, RR 24, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoresis, disoriented to time and place, visual hallucinations of insects
data_table.Investigations: Blood alcohol not detected; blood glucose 5.8 mmol/L (3.0-7.7); sodium, potassium and creatinine within normal limits; creatine kinase 340 U/L (30-190)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give oral thiamine and manage him with hourly observation in the short stay unit
Give intramuscular olanzapine 10 mg and repeat once after 30 minutes if required
Escalate to high dose intravenous diazepam titrated in a monitored critical care area
Commence an intravenous fluid infusion and reassess his agitation in two hours
Commence a buprenorphine and naloxone film and observe for symptom improvement

subtopic_detail: Acute behavioural disturbance in Parkinson disease
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call. A 74-year-old man admitted two days ago with a urinary tract infection has become acutely agitated overnight. He is pulling at his intravenous line, has struck out at a nurse and cannot be redirected by verbal reassurance or by his wife.

He has Parkinson disease treated with levodopa and carbidopa, and his mobility depends on it. He is disoriented to place and time, and his attention fluctuates markedly over minutes. Reorientation, dimmed lighting and the removal of unnecessary lines have already been tried without effect, and he now poses an immediate risk to himself and to staff. His oxygen saturation, blood glucose, sodium and calcium are within normal limits and he is not in urinary retention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 142/84, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating attention, disoriented, resting tremor and rigidity, no focal neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Sodium, potassium, calcium, blood glucose and liver function within normal limits; bladder scan 40 mL

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate choice for immediate sedation?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
Olanzapine 5 mg intramuscularly, repeated once after 30 minutes if required
Risperidone 0.5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
Diazepam 5 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated
Quetiapine 25 mg orally, repeated once after 30 minutes if he remains agitated

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy with a psychiatric history
stem:
You are the registrar in a general practice clinic seeing a 44-year-old woman who smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has done so since she was 17. She wakes at night to smoke and lights her first cigarette within five minutes of waking.

She has tried nicotine patches alone twice and relapsed within a fortnight on both occasions. She has a history of a single depressive episode eight years ago, treated with sertraline and in full remission for seven years off all medication. She has no history of seizures, no eating disorder and no current depressive symptoms. Her renal function and liver function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 130/82, RR 15, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no suicidal ideation, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Renal function, liver function, full blood count and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate first choice?

options.text: Nicotine patch 21 mg daily used alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
Bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then twice daily for nine further weeks
Varenicline titrated over the first week and continued for 12 weeks after quitting
Nicotine lozenges used as required alone for 12 weeks with behavioural support
Behavioural counselling and quitline referral alone with no pharmacotherapy offered

subtopic_detail: Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy with hepatic impairment
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital drug and alcohol service reviewing a 55-year-old man three days after an admission for decompensated alcohol related liver disease. He has completed uncomplicated withdrawal management and is now medically stable.

He has been drinking about 20 standard drinks daily for 15 years and states that his goal is complete abstinence. His most recent imaging and bloods confirm established cirrhosis with a bilirubin of 46 micromol/L, an albumin of 29 g/L and an international normalised ratio of 1.6. He takes no opioids and has no renal impairment. He has never taken pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 118/70, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Palmar erythema, spider naevi, no asterixis, no ascites on examination
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 46 micromol/L (less than 20); albumin 29 g/L (35-50); international normalised ratio 1.6 (0.9-1.3); creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: Which pharmacotherapy is the most appropriate choice to support abstinence?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg daily commenced now and continued for at least six months
Disulfiram 200 mg daily commenced now and continued with supervised dosing
Diazepam 5 mg twice daily continued as maintenance to reduce his craving for alcohol
Topiramate titrated slowly to 100 mg twice daily as first line relapse prevention
Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily commenced now that withdrawal has resolved

subtopic_detail: Substance induced depressive disorder versus independent major depression
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 39-year-old man in the outpatient clinic, four weeks after an inpatient admission for alcohol withdrawal.

On admission he described eight months of low mood, hopelessness, poor sleep and thoughts that his family would be better off without him. Those eight months coincided exactly with an escalation from 10 to 30 standard drinks daily after he lost his job. He has now been continuously abstinent for four weeks, verified by carbohydrate deficient transferrin, and has taken no antidepressant at any stage. Today he reports that his mood, sleep, appetite and outlook have all returned to normal and he denies any suicidal thoughts. He had no depressive symptoms during a previous two year period of abstinence in his twenties.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic with reactive affect, no psychomotor change, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Carbohydrate deficient transferrin within the abstinent range; liver function improving; thyroid function, full blood count and vitamin B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder in early remission following his recent hospital admission
Alcohol induced depressive disorder that has resolved with sustained abstinence
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood precipitated by the loss of his employment
Persistent depressive disorder with a superimposed alcohol use disorder developing
Protracted alcohol withdrawal syndrome producing his ongoing affective disturbance

subtopic_detail: Refeeding syndrome during inpatient nutritional rehabilitation
stem:
You are the medical registrar caring for a 19-year-old woman admitted three days ago for nutritional rehabilitation. Her body mass index is 13.4 kg/m2 and she had eaten almost nothing for the preceding two weeks.

Nasogastric feeding was commenced on admission and she is now receiving 1400 kilocalories a day. She has taken thiamine and a multivitamin since admission. This morning she reports calf cramps and feels short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. Her chest is clear on auscultation, her jugular venous pressure is not elevated and there are no peripheral oedema or crackles. Her electrocardiogram shows a corrected QT interval of 470 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 52, BP 96/60, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no oedema, proximal weakness on standing from a chair
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.38 mmol/L (0.75-1.50); potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10); corrected QT interval 470 ms; creatinine and glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Stop nasogastric feeding entirely and resume it once her electrolytes have normalised
Increase her caloric intake as planned and repeat the electrolyte panel tomorrow
Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation with normal saline and monitor her hourly
Continue feeding at a reduced rate and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium
Replace phosphate alone and continue the current feeding rate without other changes

subtopic_detail: Lithium continuation in early pregnancy
stem:
You are the registrar in a perinatal mental health clinic seeing a 32-year-old woman who has just discovered she is seven weeks pregnant. The pregnancy is wanted and she intends to continue it.

She has bipolar I disorder with four previous manic episodes, two of which required involuntary admission and one of which followed an abrupt cessation of treatment. She has been well for five years on lithium carbonate 900 mg nightly and has never responded to any other agent. Her lithium level is 0.72 mmol/L, her renal and thyroid function are within normal limits, and she has no other medical history. She asks whether she should stop the lithium immediately.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, insight intact, no psychotic features
data_table.Investigations: Serum lithium 0.72 mmol/L (0.6-0.8); creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate and thyroid function within normal limits; dating ultrasound consistent with seven weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding her lithium?

options.text: Continue lithium with more frequent level monitoring and arrange a detailed cardiac scan
Cease lithium immediately and monitor her mental state weekly through the pregnancy
Cross taper lithium to sodium valproate over four weeks and monitor her levels
Cross taper lithium to lamotrigine over four weeks and continue it through delivery
Halve the lithium dose for the first trimester and restore the full dose afterwards

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity after an antidepressant switch
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 34-year-old woman brought in by her partner with agitation and shaking that began six hours ago.

Her general practitioner stopped fluoxetine 40 mg daily last week and started tranylcypromine four days ago. She takes no other regular medication and no illicit substances. On examination her jaw is not rigid, her limbs move freely against gravity, and inducible clonus is present at both ankles with ocular clonus also seen. Her lower limb tone is markedly greater than her upper limb tone. Her creatine kinase is 620 U/L and she has had no recent antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 126, BP 158/94, RR 26, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Inducible ankle clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, lower limb tone greater than upper limb, diaphoresis, mydriasis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 620 U/L (30-190); sodium, potassium, creatinine and blood glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give dantrolene and bromocriptine and admit her to a critical care bed for cooling
Restart fluoxetine at a lower dose and continue tranylcypromine under observation
Cease both antidepressants, give benzodiazepines and add oral cyproheptadine
Give a single dose of intravenous haloperidol and observe her for two hours
Give paracetamol for the fever and observe her overnight on the short stay unit

subtopic_detail: Clozapine induced myocarditis in the initiation window
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 25-year-old man on day 18 of a clozapine titration for treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is now taking 250 mg daily and his psychotic symptoms have improved.

Over the past two days he has felt increasingly tired and short of breath walking to the dining room, which he could do comfortably last week. He has no cough, no pleuritic pain and no calf swelling. His neutrophil count has remained normal throughout and his chest radiograph shows no consolidation. His troponin and C reactive protein were both normal at baseline before clozapine was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 104/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 37.8
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation, no murmur, no calf tenderness, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 340 ng/L (less than 16); C reactive protein 78 mg/L (less than 5); neutrophils 4.6 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5); eosinophils 0.9 x10^9/L (less than 0.5); chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue clozapine at the current dose and repeat the troponin again in 48 hours
Halve the clozapine dose and arrange an outpatient echocardiogram within two weeks
Withhold clozapine tonight and recommence the titration if he improves by morning
Commence empirical intravenous antibiotics and continue the clozapine titration
Cease clozapine immediately and arrange an urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review

subtopic_detail: Chronic insomnia first line treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44-year-old accountant who has had trouble getting to sleep and staying asleep on five nights a week for nine months. She lies awake for up to two hours and then watches the clock, and she is irritable and unproductive at work.

She drinks one coffee before midday and uses no alcohol or other substances. She has no depressive or anxiety disorder on structured assessment, her thyroid function is within normal limits, and her partner has never heard her snore or stop breathing. A sleep diary shows eight and a half hours in bed for about five and a half hours of sleep, and she has already removed her phone from the bedroom without benefit.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no goitre, mental state examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function, full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia including sleep restriction
Prescribe temazepam at night for four weeks and review her sleep diary after that
Prescribe low dose amitriptyline at night and review her symptoms in four weeks
Prescribe melatonin modified release nightly and review her symptoms in four weeks
Provide written sleep hygiene advice alone and review her sleep diary in six weeks

subtopic_detail: Gambling disorder identification and initial management
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 38-year-old man referred after presenting to his general practitioner with insomnia and low mood. On questioning he describes betting on sport through a phone application most evenings, increasing his stakes over two years to chase losses.

He has hidden a personal loan from his partner and has twice tried to stop for a month without success. He drinks two standard drinks a week and uses no other substances. He denies current suicidal intent but says he has thought that his family would be better off without him, and his mood improves on days when he does not bet.

data_table.Examination: Mildly anxious, no psychomotor retardation, no psychotic features, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence an antidepressant for the depressive symptoms and review in four weeks
Commence naltrexone and arrange psychiatric review of his mood in four weeks
Refer for structured psychological therapy with safety assessment and self-exclusion advice
Advise him to disclose the debt to his partner and review his progress in six weeks
Admit to an inpatient unit for supervised withdrawal from gambling behaviours

subtopic_detail: Initial approach to an adult seeking gender affirming care
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 24-year-old trans woman referred by her general practitioner for an opinion before starting feminising hormone therapy. She has identified as female since her mid teens, has socially transitioned for two years and uses her chosen name at work.

She describes persistent low mood and social anxiety that she attributes to family rejection and to workplace misgendering, with no self-harm and no psychotic symptoms. She has capacity, is not intoxicated and has read reputable material about the effects and limits of hormone therapy. Her general practitioner has asked whether her mood symptoms mean treatment should be deferred.

data_table.Examination: Mood mildly low with reactive affect, no thought disorder, no suicidal intent, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, liver function, renal function and thyroid function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Defer hormone therapy until her depressive and anxiety symptoms have fully remitted
Request a two year documented real life experience before supporting hormone therapy
Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the gender question in six months
Advise that psychiatric assessment is mandatory before any hormone can be prescribed
Support hormone therapy now and treat her mood symptoms alongside it

subtopic_detail: Family intervention where relapse follows household conflict
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 23-year-old man with schizophrenia three weeks after discharge following his second admission in a year. He lives with his parents and takes paliperidone by monthly depot injection, with confirmed administration of every dose.

He has no positive symptoms currently and his negative symptoms are stable. His mother describes daily arguments in which she tells him he is lazy and should try harder, and both parents say they are exhausted and do not understand the illness. He uses no substances, urine drug screening is negative, and his admissions both followed periods of escalating conflict at home.

data_table.Examination: No hallucinations or delusions elicited, affect blunted, insight partial, no extrapyramidal signs
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen negative; full blood count, renal function and metabolic panel within normal limits

lead_in: What intervention is most likely to reduce his risk of relapse?

options.text: Increase the depot dose and review his mental state again in four weeks
Add an oral antipsychotic alongside the depot to broaden his relapse protection
Arrange supported independent accommodation to remove him from the household
Refer him for individual cognitive behavioural therapy for his negative symptoms
Offer structured family intervention with psychoeducation over at least ten sessions

subtopic_detail: Choosing the NSW instrument for recording preferences and carer involvement
stem: You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, well and working three months after a manic episode that required involuntary admission in NSW. Olanzapine was intolerably sedating during that admission and another agent suited her. She wants her objection to olanzapine known if she relapses, and her sister rather than her estranged father contacted. She has capacity and asks what she can put in place now.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychotic features, insight good, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.7 mmol/L, renal and thyroid function normal

lead_in: What should you advise her to put in place?

options.text: A community treatment order drafted now for use if she relapses later
An enduring guardianship appointment giving her sister all treatment decisions
A written advance care directive plus a designated carer nomination form
An olanzapine allergy alert recorded in her electronic medical record
A signed refusal of future involuntary treatment lodged with the Tribunal

subtopic_detail: Autism recognised late in an adult woman
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 29-year-old primary school teacher referred with two years of worsening anxiety and exhaustion. She has been treated for generalised anxiety disorder with two serotonin reuptake inhibitors and eighteen sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy with minimal change.

She describes rehearsing conversations in advance, needing two hours alone after work before she can speak to anyone, and intense distress at unplanned changes to her timetable. She has had the same three narrow interests since childhood and describes finding fluorescent lighting and classroom noise physically painful. Her school reports described her as quiet and well behaved with no learning difficulty, and her younger brother was diagnosed as autistic at age six.

data_table.Examination: Anxious, good eye contact, articulate and rehearsed conversational style, no thought disorder
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, thyroid function, iron studies and B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add a third serotonin reuptake inhibitor trial at a higher dose for twelve weeks
Refer for a structured multidisciplinary autism assessment including developmental history
Diagnose social anxiety disorder and refer for group exposure based therapy
Diagnose avoidant personality disorder and refer for schema focused psychotherapy
Commence a low dose antipsychotic to reduce her sensory and anxiety symptoms

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine deprescribing after a fall
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to advise on the medicines of a 78-year-old woman admitted after a fall at home with a wrist fracture. She has taken temazepam 20 mg nightly for eleven years, started after her husband died.

She says she cannot sleep without it and has tried stopping twice, each time abandoning the attempt after three sleepless nights. She does not drink alcohol, has no current depressive episode and scores normally on formal cognitive testing. Her postural blood pressures show no significant drop and her vision was reviewed last month.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 134/78 lying and 130/76 standing, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Mildly unsteady tandem gait, no focal neurology, Mini-Mental State Examination 29 out of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, calcium, thyroid function and B12 within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her temazepam?

options.text: Continue temazepam at the current dose as she has taken it safely for many years
Stop temazepam now while she is an inpatient with nursing support overnight
Substitute zopiclone at an equivalent dose to reduce her falls risk overnight
Negotiate a gradual taper with psychological support for sleep alongside it
Add mirtazapine at night and continue temazepam until her sleep has settled

subtopic_detail: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia in residential care
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar asked to review an 84-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease in residential care. Over three weeks he has become agitated and resistive during the evening shower, at times pushing staff away, and this is the only time the behaviour occurs.

Staff report that his sleep, continence and appetite are unchanged. He has been assessed by the medical officer, who found normal observations, normal bloods and no constipation. His regular medicines are unchanged and include no analgesia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 138/76, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Alert, no delirium features, crepitus and tenderness in both knees on passive movement
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function, calcium and C-reactive protein within normal limits; urinalysis shows no infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Trial regular paracetamol with a modified shower routine and behavioural charting
Start risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily and review his behaviour in four weeks
Start oxazepam before showering and review his behaviour again in two weeks
Start citalopram for underlying depression and review his behaviour in four weeks
Arrange transfer to a specialist behavioural unit for ongoing assessment and care
